Cancer consequence: cells proliferate uncontrollably; the G1 restriction point is the primary checkpoint preventing replication of cells with unrepaired DNA or inappropriate growth signals. Rb is a classic tumor suppressor. 1 pt for complete G1/S mechanism with all four named components; 1 pt for Rb mutation effect and cancer relevance.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Proto-oncogenes: promote growth in regulated manner; gain-of-function mutations (point mutation, amplification) → oncogenes → constitutive growth signals → dominant (one mutant allele sufficient). Tumor suppressors: brake cell division; loss-of-function mutations (both alleles, two-hit) → remove brakes → recessive at cellular level.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Compare proto-oncogenes and tumor suppressors: normal function, how mutations drive cancer, dominant vs. recessive.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Proto-oncogenes: (i) Normal function — encode proteins that promote cell growth, division, and survival in a regulated fashion: growth factors (PDGF), growth factor receptors (EGFR), intracellular signal transducers (RAS, Raf), transcription factors (Myc), cell cycle regulators. (ii) Mutation mechanism — gain-of-function mutations convert proto-oncogenes to oncogenes: point mutation (RAS G12V permanently active), gene amplification (Myc overexpressed), chromosomal translocation (BCR-ABL fusion), or promoter upregulation → constitutively active growth signaling. (iii) Dominant — one mutant allele is sufficient to drive abnormal proliferation (the gain-of-function allele dominates the wild-type). Tumor suppressor genes: (i) Normal function — encode proteins that restrain cell division, promote apoptosis, repair DNA, or maintain cell contact inhibition: Rb (G1 brake), p53 (DNA damage guardian), BRCA1/2 (DNA repair), APC (Wnt pathway brake). (ii) Mutation mechanism — loss-of-function mutations via point mutation, deletion, or epigenetic silencing eliminate the protein's brake function. (iii) Recessive (at cellular level / two-hit hypothesis) — both alleles must be inactivated to lose tumor suppressive function (one functional copy is usually sufficient). 1 pt per gene type with all three components correct.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Intrinsic pathway: DNA damage → BH3-only proteins inhibit Bcl-2 → Bax/Bak permeabilize mitochondria → cytochrome c released → apoptosome → caspase-9 → executioner caspases → cell death. Cancer evasion example: Bcl-2 overexpression blocks cytochrome c release.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe the intrinsic apoptosis pathway; explain how cancer cells evade apoptosis.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Intrinsic pathway: DNA damage or other intracellular stress → activates BH3-only pro-apoptotic Bcl-2 family proteins (Bim, Bid, Puma) → these inhibit anti-apoptotic proteins (Bcl-2, Bcl-xL) → releases pro-apoptotic proteins Bax/Bak from inhibition → Bax/Bak oligomerize and permeabilize the outer mitochondrial membrane (MOMP) → cytochrome c released from mitochondrial intermembrane space into cytoplasm → cytochrome c + Apaf-1 + procaspase-9 → apoptosome complex → activates caspase-9 → activates executioner caspases (caspase-3, 6, 7) → cleave cellular substrates (DNA, cytoskeletal proteins, etc.) → apoptosis. (ii) Cancer cell evasion (any ONE mechanism): (1) Overexpression of Bcl-2 or Bcl-xL — blocks cytochrome c release; (2) Loss of Bax/Bak function via mutation; (3) p53 mutation or MDM2 amplification — p53 cannot activate Puma/Bim; (4) Activation of IAP (inhibitor of apoptosis proteins) that block caspase activation; (5) Elevated survival signaling (PI3K-Akt pathway phosphorylates Bad, keeping Bcl-2 active). 1 pt for correctly tracing intrinsic pathway with cytochrome c and caspases; 1 pt for one specific evasion mechanism.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: E6 degrades p53 → cells cannot arrest at DNA damage checkpoints → mutations accumulate → cancer. E7 inactivates Rb → same as Rb mutation → E2F free → bypass G1 checkpoint. Vaccine prevents HPV infection before viral integration; cannot remove integrated viral DNA or reverse p53/Rb inactivation in infected cells → prevention only, not treatment.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain E6/p53, E7/Rb mechanisms; explain why HPV vaccine is cancer prevention not treatment.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) p53 normal function: activated by DNA damage, oncogene activation, or hypoxia → induces transcription of p21 (CDK inhibitor, halts cell cycle) and pro-apoptotic genes → allows DNA repair or triggers apoptosis if damage is irreparable → prevents accumulation of mutations. E6 degrades p53 → cells with DNA damage cannot halt the cycle → mutations accumulate → cancer. (ii) E7 binds and functionally inactivates Rb → same as Rb loss-of-function: E2F is constitutively free → G1 checkpoint bypassed → cells replicate uncontrollably without growth factor signals. Mechanistically identical to Rb mutation in cancer cells. (iii) HPV vaccine is cancer prevention because: it prevents HPV infection before it occurs. Once HPV integrates into the host genome (occurring years to decades before cancer develops), the viral E6 and E7 genes become permanently expressed → p53 and Rb are continuously targeted. The vaccine cannot remove integrated viral DNA or restore p53/Rb function in already-infected cells. Cancer treatment would require eliminating already-transformed cells; prevention targets the infectious cause before transformation can begin. 1 pt for E6/p53 + E7/Rb mechanisms; 1 pt for prevention vs. treatment distinction with molecular reasoning.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Describe the four levels of protein structure, identifying the types of bonds or interactions that maintain each level. Explain how the primary structure ultimately determines the final three-dimensional shape of a protein.

(b) The graph shows enzyme activity versus pH for three different enzymes: pepsin (stomach), amylase (saliva), and trypsin (small intestine).
    (i) Identify the optimal pH for each enzyme and explain why each enzyme functions best at its particular pH in its biological context.
    (ii) Explain the molecular basis for why enzyme activity decreases sharply at pH values far from the optimum.

(c) A researcher observes that an enzyme's reaction rate is the same whether the substrate is molecule X or the closely related molecule Y, but the enzyme binds X with much higher affinity than Y. Explain this observation using the induced-fit model of enzyme-substrate interaction. Include the concepts of activation energy and the transition state.

(d) A mutation substitutes a nonpolar valine for a charged glutamate residue in the active site of an enzyme. Predict the effect of this mutation on: (i) substrate binding; (ii) catalytic rate; and (iii) the enzyme's stability at high temperatures. Justify each prediction.
stimulus:
Enzyme activity vs. pH data:
Enzyme   | Optimal pH | Active range
Pepsin   |    2.0     |  1.0 – 3.5
Amylase  |    7.0     |  6.0 – 8.5
Trypsin  |    8.0     |  7.0 – 9.0

Protein structure review:
• Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds (covalent) between carboxyl and amino groups
• The R-group (side chain) determines each amino acid's chemical properties
• Proteins fold spontaneously in aqueous environments, driven largely by hydrophobic interactions
• Chaperone proteins assist folding of large or complex proteins in the cell
title: APBIO-FRQ-L-011

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Primary: peptide bonds (covalent), amino acid sequence. Secondary: H-bonds, alpha helix/beta sheet. Tertiary: hydrophobic interactions, disulfide bonds, H-bonds, ionic bonds. Quaternary: multiple polypeptides. Primary sequence determines shape via R-group chemistry → hydrophobic collapse, charge interactions.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe all four levels of protein structure with bonds/interactions; explain how primary structure determines shape.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Four levels: (1) Primary — sequence of amino acids joined by covalent peptide bonds; (2) Secondary — local folding into alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets stabilized by hydrogen bonds between backbone NH and C=O groups; (3) Tertiary — overall 3D folding of the whole polypeptide; stabilized by hydrophobic interactions (nonpolar R-groups cluster inside away from water), disulfide bonds (covalent, between cysteine R-groups), ionic bonds (between oppositely charged R-groups), hydrogen bonds between R-groups, and van der Waals forces; (4) Quaternary — association of two or more polypeptide subunits; same types of interactions as tertiary. How primary determines shape: the specific sequence of R-groups creates a unique pattern of hydrophobic, hydrophilic, charged, and polar residues → these interact with each other and with water in specific ways → the polypeptide folds into the lowest free-energy conformation → the 3D shape is determined. Denaturation (disrupting non-covalent interactions by heat or pH) causes unfolding, demonstrating that the primary sequence contains all information needed to specify 3D structure.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Pepsin optimal pH 2 (acidic stomach); amylase optimal pH 7 (neutral saliva); trypsin optimal pH 8 (alkaline small intestine). pH away from optimum changes ionization state of active site R-groups → disrupts substrate binding and catalysis → at extreme pH, denaturation occurs.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Identify optimal pH for each enzyme; explain molecular basis of pH sensitivity.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Pepsin optimal pH 2.0 — functions in the highly acidic stomach (HCl lowers pH to 1-3); digestive enzymes require the pH of their secretion site. Amylase optimal pH 7.0 — functions in saliva and neutral oral environment. Trypsin optimal pH 8.0 — functions in the slightly alkaline small intestine (bicarbonate from pancreas raises pH). (ii) Molecular basis: enzyme active site geometry and catalytic residues depend on the ionization state of amino acid R-groups (e.g., histidine pKa ~6, carboxylates pKa ~4, lysine pKa ~10). At pH far from optimum: H⁺ or OH⁻ alters the protonation state of active site residues → changes charge distribution and H-bonding capacity → disrupts substrate binding and/or catalytic mechanism → enzyme activity falls. At extreme pH: disrupts ionic bonds and H-bonds throughout the protein → tertiary structure destabilizes → denaturation. 1 pt for correct optimal pH identification with biological context; 1 pt for molecular basis (ionization of R-groups).

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Induced fit: substrate binding induces conformational change that positions catalytic residues. X binds tightly; Y binds weakly. But once either induces the active conformation, the active site stabilizes the transition state equally → same rate (kcat). Enzyme lowers Ea by stabilizing the transition state; this is independent of initial substrate affinity (Km).
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain same reaction rate but different affinity using induced-fit model; include activation energy and transition state.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Induced fit model: enzyme active site is not perfectly rigid; substrate binding causes conformational change in the enzyme that optimally positions catalytic residues around the substrate. For X (high affinity): strong initial binding, optimal induced-fit conformational change → active site perfectly positions catalytic residues around X → effective stabilization of transition state → low activation energy → fast reaction. For Y (low affinity): weaker initial binding (poor shape/charge complementarity before conformational change), but induced-fit conformation still achieves sufficient catalytic positioning to stabilize transition state comparably to X → once bound, catalytic rate is similar. Same kcat (catalytic rate constant) but higher Km for Y (lower affinity). Activation energy: enzyme lowers the activation energy (Ea) by stabilizing the high-energy transition state intermediate → the enzyme active site provides an environment (correct charge, H-bond donors/acceptors) that complements the transition state geometry even when substrate binding is weaker, explaining similar reaction rates despite different affinities.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: (i) Substrate binding: decreased affinity (Km increases) — lost ionic interaction with substrate. (ii) Catalytic rate: decreased kcat — lost catalytic residue (if glutamate was acid/base catalyst). (iii) Thermal stability: may increase (more hydrophobic interior) or decrease (if salt bridge lost) — either acceptable with sound reasoning.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Predict effect of nonpolar-for-charged mutation on substrate binding, catalytic rate, and thermal stability.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Substrate binding: if the substrate has a charged group that normally interacts with the glutamate in the active site, replacing glutamate with nonpolar valine eliminates that ionic/H-bond interaction → reduced substrate binding affinity (increased Km) → fewer productive enzyme-substrate complexes formed. (ii) Catalytic rate: if the glutamate participates directly in catalysis (as a general acid/base or nucleophile), replacing it with nonpolar valine eliminates catalytic function → dramatically reduced kcat (catalytic rate) → if glutamate was not directly catalytic but only binding, effect on kcat may be modest. Either prediction is acceptable if reasoning is consistent. (iii) Thermal stability: paradoxically, this substitution might INCREASE thermal stability. Nonpolar amino acids are more hydrophobic → if this residue is buried, adding a nonpolar side chain could strengthen the hydrophobic core and reduce entropy-driven unfolding. Alternatively: if this glutamate formed a salt bridge with another charged residue, removing it could destabilize structure at high temperature. Accept either direction if reasoning is mechanistically sound. 1 pt for any two predictions with sound mechanistic reasoning; 1 pt for the third.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Using the Michaelis-Menten data in Table 1, determine the approximate Km and Vmax for this enzyme. Explain the biological significance of each value — what does Km tell you about an enzyme's affinity for its substrate, and what does Vmax tell you about an enzyme population?

(b) Table 2 shows the same enzyme's kinetics in the presence of inhibitor A and inhibitor B.
    (i) Classify each inhibitor as competitive or noncompetitive, and justify your classification using the Km and Vmax data.
    (ii) Describe the molecular mechanism of each type of inhibition, including where each inhibitor binds and how it reduces enzyme activity.

(c) The enzyme threonine deaminase is inhibited by isoleucine, the end product of the metabolic pathway that begins with threonine. Explain how this represents allosteric regulation and feedback inhibition. Include: the difference between the allosteric site and the active site, and the conformational change mechanism.

(d) Temperature affects enzyme activity in a characteristic bell-shaped curve.
    (i) Explain why enzyme activity increases from 0°C to the temperature optimum.
    (ii) Explain why enzyme activity decreases sharply above the temperature optimum.
    (iii) Predict how a thermophilic bacterium's enzyme would differ structurally from a mesophilic enzyme performing the same function, and explain the structural basis for thermal stability.
stimulus:
Table 1: Enzyme kinetics (no inhibitor)
[Substrate] μM | Reaction rate (μmol/min)
     10         |        10
     20         |        16.7
     40         |        25
     80         |        33.3
    160         |        40
    500         |        47.6
   1000         |        49.5
   5000         |        50.0

Table 2: Kinetics with inhibitors (1 mM each)
               | Vmax (μmol/min) | Km (μM)
No inhibitor   |       50        |   40
Inhibitor A    |       50        |   120
Inhibitor B    |       25        |   40
title: APBIO-FRQ-L-012

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Vmax ≈ 50 μmol/min (plateau at high [S]). Km ≈ 40 μM (rate = Vmax/2 = 25, occurs at [S] = 40). Km = inverse of affinity (low Km = high affinity). Vmax = maximum rate when all active sites saturated = kcat × [E]total.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Determine Km and Vmax from data; explain biological significance of each.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: From the data: Vmax ≈ 50 μmol/min (reaction rate plateaus at ~50 at high [S]). Km = [S] at which reaction rate = Vmax/2 = 25 μmol/min. From table: rate = 25 at [S] = 40 μM → Km ≈ 40 μM. Biological significance: Km — the Michaelis constant is an inverse measure of enzyme-substrate affinity. Low Km = high affinity (enzyme reaches half-Vmax at low [S]); high Km = low affinity. Km approximates the dissociation constant of the E-S complex under many conditions. It indicates how efficiently the enzyme captures substrate at physiological concentrations. Vmax — the maximum velocity when all enzyme active sites are saturated with substrate. Vmax = kcat × [E]total, where kcat is the turnover number (reactions per enzyme per second). Vmax reflects the total catalytic capacity of the enzyme population (depends on both enzyme concentration and intrinsic catalytic rate). 1 pt for correct Km (40 μM) and Vmax (50 μmol/min) with method shown; 1 pt for correct biological interpretation of both.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Inhibitor A: competitive (Km increases, Vmax unchanged) — binds active site, competes with substrate; overcome by high [S]. Inhibitor B: noncompetitive (Km unchanged, Vmax decreases) — binds allosteric site, reduces kcat regardless of substrate concentration.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Classify inhibitors A and B; describe molecular mechanism of each.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Inhibitor A: Km increases (40→120 μM), Vmax unchanged (50 μmol/min) → COMPETITIVE inhibitor. Inhibitor B: Km unchanged (40 μM), Vmax decreases (50→25 μmol/min) → NONCOMPETITIVE inhibitor. (ii) Competitive inhibition mechanism: competitive inhibitor is structurally similar to substrate and binds reversibly to the active site; it competes with substrate for the same binding site. At high [S], excess substrate outcompetes the inhibitor → Vmax is eventually reached (unchanged). But higher [S] is needed to achieve half-Vmax → apparent Km increases. Noncompetitive inhibition mechanism: inhibitor binds to the allosteric site (different from active site), whether or not substrate is bound; binding induces a conformational change that reduces the catalytic efficiency of the active site (reduces kcat). Because the inhibitor does not compete with substrate, adding more substrate cannot overcome it → Vmax decreases. Substrate still binds with the same affinity (Km unchanged). 1 pt for correct classification with justification; 1 pt for correct mechanism of both.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Threonine deaminase has active site (threonine binds) and allosteric site (isoleucine binds) — physically separate. Isoleucine binding causes conformational change → active site shape altered → reduced threonine binding or catalysis → less isoleucine produced → negative feedback. Prevents overproduction.
accepted_variants: allosteric site separate from active site
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain allosteric regulation and feedback inhibition using threonine deaminase / isoleucine.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Allosteric regulation: the enzyme has two distinct sites — the active site (where threonine binds and is converted to α-ketobutyrate, the first step toward isoleucine biosynthesis) and the allosteric (regulatory) site (where isoleucine binds as an inhibitor). These sites are physically separate and do not overlap. Feedback inhibition mechanism: when isoleucine accumulates (end product of the pathway), isoleucine binds the allosteric site of threonine deaminase → induces a conformational change in the enzyme's tertiary/quaternary structure → changes the shape of the active site → reduces affinity for threonine (or reduces kcat) → enzyme activity decreases → less isoleucine is produced. This is negative feedback: the end product of a pathway inhibits an enzyme early in that same pathway. Significance: prevents overproduction of isoleucine; maintains metabolic balance without wasteful synthesis; response is rapid (no transcription needed — direct protein-level regulation). Difference from active site: allosteric site does not bind substrate and does not perform catalysis; it is a regulatory site that modulates active site conformation through cooperative conformational changes.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Below optimum: more kinetic energy → faster substrate-enzyme collisions → higher rate. Above optimum: thermal energy breaks non-covalent bonds → denaturation → active site disrupted → activity lost irreversibly. Thermophile enzymes: more disulfide bonds, proline residues, denser hydrophobic core, salt bridges → resist denaturation at high temperature.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain temperature optimum bell curve; predict thermophile enzyme structural differences.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Below optimum: increasing temperature increases average kinetic energy of both substrate and enzyme molecules → more frequent and energetic collisions between substrate and active site → more productive enzyme-substrate encounters per unit time → reaction rate increases. (ii) Above optimum: thermal energy exceeds the strength of non-covalent bonds (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, ionic bonds) holding the enzyme in its functional 3D shape → protein denatures (unfolds) → active site geometry is disrupted → enzyme loses catalytic function → activity drops sharply. This is irreversible denaturation (unlike reduced activity at low temperature, which is reversible). (iii) Thermophilic enzyme adaptations: more disulfide bonds (covalent, highly stable), more proline residues in loops (restricts backbone flexibility, reducing entropy-driven unfolding), denser hydrophobic core (more hydrophobic amino acids buried, stronger hydrophobic interactions), more ionic bonds (salt bridges) especially at surface, fewer flexible loops that can denature first. Functional result: higher energy (temperature) required to overcome the stabilizing forces → higher temperature optimum. 1 pt for molecular explanation of each side of the curve; 1 pt for thermophile adaptations.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) A pancreatic acinar cell synthesizes and secretes the digestive enzyme trypsinogen. Trace the complete pathway of a trypsinogen molecule from its synthesis to its secretion from the cell. Name each organelle or cellular structure involved, describe what happens to the protein at each step, and identify the type of membrane-bounded vesicle used for each transport step.

(b) The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) has functions distinct from the rough ER (RER). Describe THREE specific functions of the SER in a liver cell and explain the molecular basis for one of those functions.

(c) Lysosomes are membrane-bounded organelles containing acid hydrolases. Explain:
    (i) How lysosomal enzymes are targeted to lysosomes rather than being secreted from the cell.
    (ii) Why lysosomal enzymes do not destroy the lysosome's own membrane.
    (iii) What happens when a lysosome fuses with an autophagosome.

(d) A researcher treats cells with brefeldin A, a drug that disrupts COP-I vesicle formation and collapses the Golgi apparatus back into the ER. Predict and explain the effect of this treatment on: (i) secretion of a newly synthesized extracellular protein; (ii) delivery of lysosomal enzymes to lysosomes; (iii) the morphology of the ER in treated cells.
stimulus:
The endomembrane system consists of the nuclear envelope, endoplasmic reticulum (rough and smooth), Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, vacuoles, and plasma membrane. These compartments are functionally connected by vesicular transport.

Key vesicle types:
• COPII vesicles: ER → Golgi (anterograde transport)
• COPI vesicles: Golgi → ER (retrograde retrieval) and intra-Golgi transport
• Clathrin-coated vesicles: Golgi → lysosomes (via mannose-6-phosphate receptor); plasma membrane → endosomes (endocytosis)

Golgi apparatus: proteins are modified (glycosylation patterns altered, proteolytic processing), sorted, and packaged. Cis face receives vesicles from ER; trans face sends vesicles toward destinations.
title: APBIO-FRQ-L-013

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Ribosome on RER → ER lumen (signal peptide, glycosylation, folding) → COPII vesicle → Golgi (further modification) → secretory vesicle → exocytosis at plasma membrane.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Trace trypsinogen from synthesis to secretion naming organelles, events, and vesicle types.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Complete pathway: (1) Ribosome (on rough ER) — trypsinogen synthesized by ribosome; signal peptide directs ribosome to RER; polypeptide threaded into ER lumen as it is synthesized; signal peptide cleaved. (2) Rough ER lumen — initial N-linked glycosylation; protein folding assisted by chaperones (BiP/GRP78); disulfide bonds formed; quality control (misfolded proteins retained/degraded). (3) COPII vesicle buds from ER → transported to cis-Golgi. (4) Golgi apparatus (cis → medial → trans) — further glycosylation modifications; protein sorted and packaged in trans-Golgi network. (5) Secretory vesicle (dense-core or constitutive secretory vesicle) buds from trans-Golgi → transported to plasma membrane. (6) Exocytosis — vesicle fuses with plasma membrane; trypsinogen released into pancreatic duct lumen. Note: trypsinogen is secreted as an inactive zymogen (activated to trypsin in the small intestine by enteropeptidase) — accept if student notes this.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Three SER functions in liver: lipid synthesis; drug detoxification (CYP450 enzymes hydroxylate hydrophobic drugs → more water-soluble); glycogen metabolism (glucose-6-phosphatase). Molecular basis example: CYP450 uses O₂ + NADPH to hydroxylate lipophilic compounds → increases polarity → excreted.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe three SER functions in liver cells; explain molecular basis of one.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Three SER functions in liver cells: (1) Lipid synthesis — SER synthesizes phospholipids and cholesterol; enzymes embedded in SER membrane catalyze lipid synthesis using acetyl-CoA and fatty acid precursors. (2) Drug detoxification / xenobiotic metabolism — cytochrome P450 enzymes (CYP450) in SER oxidize lipid-soluble drugs, toxins, and steroids → convert to more water-soluble forms for excretion (glucuronidation). Molecular basis: CYP450 enzymes use O₂ and NADPH to insert hydroxyl groups into hydrophobic substrates → increases polarity → facilitates conjugation reactions → more water-soluble metabolite excreted in bile or urine. (3) Glycogen metabolism — glucose-6-phosphatase embedded in SER membrane dephosphorylates glucose-6-phosphate → free glucose enters bloodstream. (4) Calcium storage/release — SER sequesters Ca²⁺; IP₃ signaling triggers Ca²⁺ release from SER. Any three with one molecular explanation earns full credit.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: (i) Mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag on lysosomal enzymes recognized by M6P receptors in trans-Golgi → clathrin vesicle to lysosome. (ii) Luminal glycocalyx protects membrane; hydrolases require acidic pH inactive at neutral cytoplasmic pH. (iii) Autophagosome fuses with lysosome → contents degraded → monomers recycled.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain lysosomal enzyme targeting, membrane protection, and autophagy.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Targeting: lysosomal hydrolases are glycoproteins synthesized in the RER and processed in the Golgi; a specific modification — addition of mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag — marks these enzymes as lysosomal. In the trans-Golgi, M6P receptors recognize the M6P tag and package enzymes into clathrin-coated vesicles destined for late endosomes/lysosomes rather than secretory vesicles. Without this tag (or with M6P receptor mutations), enzymes are secreted extracellularly instead. (ii) Membrane protection: lysosomal membrane lipids are heavily glycosylated on the luminal face (glycocalyx of the inner membrane) → carbohydrate coat protects membrane proteins and lipids from acid hydrolases; lysosomal membrane proteins (LAMPs, LIMPs) are specifically resistant to degradation; acidic pH is maintained by V-type H⁺-ATPase pumping protons in. Hydrolases require low pH to function — the neutral cytoplasm inactivates any leaked enzymes. (iii) Autophagy: autophagosome (double membrane) engulfs damaged organelles or cytoplasmic proteins; outer membrane of autophagosome fuses with lysosome → autolysosome; lysosomal hydrolases break down contents → monomers (amino acids, sugars, lipids) released into cytoplasm for recycling. 1 pt per sub-part with correct mechanism.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Secretion blocked (proteins cannot transit Golgi to secretory vesicles); lysosomal delivery impaired (M6P tagging in Golgi cannot occur → enzymes misdirected to secretion, "I-cell" phenotype); ER expands (Golgi membranes retracted into ER → enlarged ER network).
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Predict effects of brefeldin A (Golgi collapse) on secretion, lysosomal delivery, and ER morphology.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Secretion blocked: without COP-I vesicles and functional Golgi, proteins synthesized in RER cannot be transported to Golgi for processing, packaging, and sorting → secretory vesicles cannot form → newly synthesized extracellular proteins accumulate in ER and cannot be secreted. Any proteins already in Golgi would be retrograded to ER. Complete block of constitutive secretion. (ii) Lysosomal delivery blocked: lysosomal enzymes also require Golgi for M6P tagging and packaging into clathrin vesicles → without functional Golgi, lysosomal enzymes are not properly tagged → misdirected to secretory pathway → secreted extracellularly → I-cell disease-like phenotype (lysosomal storage disorder). Cells cannot replenish lysosomal enzyme pool. (iii) ER morphology: Golgi collapses back into ER → ER membrane area increases dramatically; ER becomes enlarged/distended as Golgi lipids and proteins are reabsorbed; the distinct stacked Golgi cisternae disappear; ER may appear as a vastly expanded membrane network by electron microscopy. 1 pt per any two correct predictions with mechanistic explanation.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) The endosymbiotic theory proposes that mitochondria evolved from free-living alpha-proteobacteria engulfed by an ancestral eukaryotic cell.
    (i) Describe FOUR specific lines of evidence that support the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria.
    (ii) Explain why, if mitochondria evolved from bacteria, most mitochondrial proteins are now encoded by the nuclear genome rather than the mitochondrial genome.

(b) Describe the role of the inner mitochondrial membrane in ATP synthesis. In your answer, explain: (i) the source of the proton gradient; (ii) how the proton gradient drives ATP synthesis; and (iii) the specific role of each of the following: Complex I, Complex III, Complex IV, and ATP synthase.

(c) A researcher adds the following compounds to isolated mitochondria respiring aerobically with NADH as the electron donor. For each compound, predict whether O₂ consumption and ATP synthesis will increase, decrease, or be unaffected, and explain your reasoning:
    (i) Rotenone (inhibits Complex I electron transfer)
    (ii) Oligomycin (blocks the F₀ channel of ATP synthase)
    (iii) Dinitrophenol / DNP (uncoupler — makes the inner membrane permeable to H⁺)

(d) Heart muscle cells and neurons both have unusually high numbers of mitochondria. Explain the functional reason for this and describe the specific structural feature of mitochondria that maximizes ATP output. Then explain why a drug that inhibits mitochondrial division (fission) would be especially harmful to neurons compared to rapidly dividing cells like skin fibroblasts.
stimulus:
Mitochondrial structure:
• Outer membrane: permeable to small molecules (porins)
• Intermembrane space: H⁺ accumulates here during electron transport
• Inner membrane: highly folded into cristae; contains electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and ATP synthase; impermeable to ions
• Matrix: contains Krebs cycle enzymes, mtDNA, mitochondrial ribosomes

Electron transport chain complexes (in inner membrane):
• Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase): NADH → NAD⁺; pumps 4H⁺
• Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase): FADH₂ → FAD; does NOT pump H⁺
• Complex III (cytochrome bc1): pumps 4H⁺
• Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase): pumps 2H⁺; O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O
• ATP synthase (Complex V): H⁺ flows back through F₀ rotor → drives F₁ to synthesize ATP
title: APBIO-FRQ-L-014

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Four evidence: (1) size/shape similar to bacteria; (2) double membrane (inner = bacterial membrane with cardiolipin); (3) circular naked mitochondrial DNA; (4) 70S ribosomes (sensitive to bacterial antibiotics). Gene transfer: most mitochondrial genes transferred to nucleus over evolution (endosymbiotic gene transfer) for better regulation, protection, and coordination.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe four lines of evidence for endosymbiosis; explain gene transfer to nucleus.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Four lines of evidence: (1) Size and shape: mitochondria are similar in size (~1-2 μm) and shape to alpha-proteobacteria; (2) Double membrane: mitochondria have two membranes — the outer membrane likely derived from the phagocytic vacuole; the inner membrane is the original bacterial plasma membrane with bacterial-type lipid composition (cardiolipin); (3) Mitochondrial DNA: circular, naked DNA (like bacterial chromosomes) located in the matrix; not associated with histones; encodes rRNA, tRNA, and some proteins; (4) Mitochondrial ribosomes: 70S ribosomes (bacterial type) sensitive to antibiotics that inhibit bacterial ribosomes (chloramphenicol, erythromycin) but not 80S eukaryotic ribosomes; (5) Binary fission: mitochondria divide by binary fission, not mitosis; (6) Phylogenetic similarity: mitochondrial rRNA sequences are closely related to alpha-proteobacteria (specifically Rickettsia-like organisms). Any four with correct explanation. (ii) Gene transfer to nucleus: over evolutionary time, most ancestral bacterial genes were transferred to the host cell nucleus (endosymbiotic gene transfer). This is adaptive because: nuclear genes can be regulated by eukaryotic gene expression machinery; nuclear DNA is protected by repair mechanisms; reduced mtDNA reduces the risk of harmful mutations in the energy-producing organelle; nuclear-encoded proteins are imported post-translationally into mitochondria via TOM/TIM complexes.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: H⁺ pumped from matrix to intermembrane space by Complexes I (4H⁺), III (4H⁺), IV (2H⁺) as electrons flow. Proton gradient (proton-motive force) drives H⁺ back through ATP synthase F₀ channel → F₁ rotation → ATP synthesis from ADP + Pi. Complex IV reduces O₂ to H₂O (final electron acceptor).
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe proton gradient source, ATP synthesis mechanism, and roles of Complexes I, III, IV, and ATP synthase.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Source of proton gradient: NADH and FADH₂ (from glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, Krebs cycle) donate electrons to the ETC. As electrons pass through the complexes, the energy released is used to pump H⁺ from the matrix into the intermembrane space: Complex I pumps 4H⁺, Complex III pumps 4H⁺, Complex IV pumps 2H⁺. This creates an electrochemical proton gradient (high H⁺/low pH in intermembrane space vs. matrix) = proton-motive force. ATP synthesis: H⁺ cannot freely cross the inner membrane (impermeable). H⁺ flows back down its electrochemical gradient through the F₀ channel of ATP synthase (the only route). H⁺ flow drives rotation of the F₀ rotor → mechanical rotation transmitted to F₁ catalytic subunits → conformational changes in F₁ catalyze ATP synthesis from ADP + Pi (rotary catalysis). Specific roles: Complex I — accepts electrons from NADH → passes to ubiquinone, pumps 4H⁺; Complex III — accepts electrons from reduced ubiquinone (QH₂) via Q-cycle → passes to cytochrome c, pumps 4H⁺; Complex IV — accepts electrons from cytochrome c → reduces O₂ to H₂O (final electron acceptor), pumps 2H⁺; ATP synthase — H⁺ gradient drives F₀ rotation → F₁ synthesizes ATP (chemiosmosis).

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Rotenone: O₂ decreases (ETC blocked at Complex I), ATP decreases. Oligomycin: O₂ decreases (back-pressure stops ETC), ATP decreases. DNP: O₂ increases (no back-pressure, ETC runs faster), ATP decreases (gradient dissipated as heat).
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Predict O₂ consumption and ATP synthesis for rotenone, oligomycin, and DNP.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Rotenone (blocks Complex I): electron flow from NADH through Complex I is blocked → electrons cannot enter the ETC from NADH → H⁺ pumping by Complexes I, III, IV stops → proton gradient collapses → ATP synthesis stops. O₂ consumption DECREASES (Complex IV cannot receive electrons; O₂ is not reduced). ATP synthesis DECREASES (no gradient). (ii) Oligomycin (blocks F₀ of ATP synthase): H⁺ cannot flow through ATP synthase → H⁺ accumulates in intermembrane space → proton gradient INCREASES (back-pressure) → this back-pressure slows H⁺ pumping by Complexes → electron flow through ETC slows → O₂ consumption DECREASES. ATP synthesis DECREASES (synthase blocked). Classic observation: oligomycin paradoxically reduces O₂ consumption by back-pressure on the ETC. (iii) DNP (uncoupler): makes inner membrane permeable to H⁺ → H⁺ flows back into matrix bypassing ATP synthase → proton gradient dissipated as heat → no ATP synthesized. But now there is no back-pressure on the ETC → ETC pumps H⁺ as fast as possible to try to maintain gradient → O₂ consumption INCREASES dramatically. ATP synthesis DECREASES (to zero — all gradient dissipated as heat). DNP causes hyperthermia (was used as a diet drug — dangerously). 1 pt per any two correctly predicted and explained.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Heart/neurons have high continuous ATP demand → many mitochondria; cristae (inner membrane folds) increase surface area for ETC/ATP synthase. Fission inhibition: neurons need small mitochondria transported to distant synapses via microtubules; without fission, elongated mitochondria cannot enter axons/dendrites → synapses lack ATP → neurotoxicity. Fibroblasts are small and divide frequently — less dependent on mitochondrial transport.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain why heart/neurons need many mitochondria; describe cristae; explain fission inhibition harm to neurons.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: High energy demand cells: heart muscle and neurons are continuously active and cannot undergo anaerobic metabolism for sustained periods. They require constant high-rate ATP production (heart: ~30 kg ATP/day; neurons: cannot tolerate even brief energy deficits). More mitochondria = more ETC surface area = more ATP. Structural feature: cristae (inner membrane folds) dramatically increase the surface area of the inner membrane → more ETC complexes and ATP synthases per mitochondrion → greater ATP output per organelle. Fission inhibition in neurons vs. fibroblasts: mitochondria must be distributed throughout the cell to local sites of energy demand — in neurons, this means delivering mitochondria to synapses (far from the cell body, up to 1 meter in motor neurons). Mitochondrial fission allows small mitochondria to be transported along microtubules to distant synaptic sites. Without fission: mitochondria become elongated and cannot be transported into dendrites and axons → synapses lack local energy supply → synaptic transmission fails → neurotoxicity. Fibroblasts are small and rapidly dividing; mitochondria can be inherited by daughter cells even without efficient transport; fibroblasts are less dependent on precise organelle localization. 1 pt for heart/neurons high demand + cristae explanation; 1 pt for fission/transport mechanism in neurons.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Trace the carbon atoms from one molecule of glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) through glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, and the Krebs cycle. Account for all six carbon atoms by identifying the carbon-containing molecules produced and the steps at which CO₂ is released.

(b) For one molecule of glucose completely oxidized through aerobic respiration, account for the electron carriers produced. List the number of NADH and FADH₂ produced at each stage (glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, Krebs cycle) and explain where each electron carrier is used in the electron transport chain.

(c) The theoretical maximum ATP yield from one glucose molecule is often stated as ~30-32 ATP. Explain why the actual ATP yield is lower than the theoretical maximum, describing at least THREE specific reasons for this discrepancy.

(d) A cell is shifted from aerobic to anaerobic conditions. Using the data in Table 1, which shows glucose consumption rates, explain the Pasteur effect (why glucose consumption increases dramatically under anaerobic conditions). Your answer should connect glycolytic regulation, the role of NAD⁺ availability, and ATP production efficiency.
stimulus:
Table 1: Glucose consumption in yeast cells
Condition     | Glucose consumed (mmol/hr/g cells)
Aerobic       |        0.5
Anaerobic     |        4.2

ATP yield summary (theoretical):
Glycolysis: 2 ATP (substrate-level), 2 NADH (cytoplasmic)
Pyruvate oxidation: 0 ATP, 2 NADH (mitochondrial)
Krebs cycle (×2 turns): 2 ATP (GTP), 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂

Electron carrier ATP equivalents (approximate):
Mitochondrial NADH: ~2.5 ATP each
Cytoplasmic NADH: ~1.5 ATP each (malate-aspartate shuttle) or ~1.0 (glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle)
FADH₂: ~1.5 ATP each
title: APBIO-FRQ-L-015

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Glycolysis: 6C glucose → 2× 3C pyruvate (no CO₂). Pyruvate oxidation: 2 pyruvate → 2 CO₂ + 2 acetyl-CoA (2C). Krebs ×2: 2 acetyl-CoA → 4 CO₂. Total: 6 CO₂ = all 6 glucose carbons accounted for.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Trace all 6 carbons from glucose through glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, and Krebs cycle; account for CO₂ release.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Glucose (6C): Glycolysis (cytoplasm): 6C glucose → 2× 3C pyruvate. No CO₂ released in glycolysis. All 6 carbons in 2 pyruvate. Pyruvate oxidation (mitochondrial matrix): each 3C pyruvate → 1 CO₂ released + 2C acetyl-CoA (per pyruvate); 2 pyruvate → 2 CO₂ released + 2 acetyl-CoA. Running total: 2 CO₂ out (2 carbons); 4 carbons remain in 2 acetyl-CoA. Krebs cycle (×2 turns per glucose): each acetyl-CoA (2C) + oxaloacetate (4C) → citrate (6C) → 2 CO₂ released per turn → oxaloacetate (4C) regenerated. Per turn: 2 CO₂ released. Two turns: 4 CO₂ released. Running total CO₂: 2 (pyruvate oxidation) + 4 (Krebs) = 6 CO₂ total. All 6 carbons from glucose accounted for as CO₂ released. Oxaloacetate is regenerated (not consumed net) and cycles continuously. 1 pt for correct carbon accounting through pyruvate oxidation; 1 pt for Krebs cycle carbon accounting with correct total CO₂.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Glycolysis: 2 NADH (cytoplasm). Pyruvate oxidation: 2 NADH (matrix). Krebs ×2: 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂ (matrix). Total: 10 NADH + 2 FADH₂. Mitochondrial NADH → Complex I (4H⁺/NADH). FADH₂ → Complex II (no H⁺ pumped). Cytoplasmic NADH: shuttle dependent (2.5 or 1.5 ATP equiv).
accepted_variants: Complex II FADH2 no H+ pumped
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Account for all NADH and FADH₂ produced per glucose; explain where each is used.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Per glucose molecule: Glycolysis: 2 NADH (cytoplasm). Pyruvate oxidation: 2 NADH (mitochondrial matrix). Krebs cycle (×2 turns): 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂ (mitochondrial matrix). Total: 10 NADH (2 cytoplasmic + 8 mitochondrial) + 2 FADH₂. Use in ETC: Mitochondrial NADH → Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase); NADH donates 2 electrons to FMN prosthetic group → electrons passed to ubiquinone (Q); 4 H⁺ pumped per NADH. FADH₂ → Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase, embedded in inner membrane) → electrons enter Q pool directly; no H⁺ pumped by Complex II → fewer ATP per FADH₂. Cytoplasmic NADH: must transfer electrons across inner membrane via shuttles: malate-aspartate shuttle → mitochondrial NADH → ~2.5 ATP; glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle → FADH₂ equivalent → ~1.5 ATP. All electron carriers ultimately deliver electrons to O₂ via Complex IV. 1 pt for complete count of NADH/FADH₂ by stage; 1 pt for correct ETC use with Complex assignments.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Three reasons: (1) proton leak across inner membrane dissipates gradient as heat; (2) ATP-ADP translocase uses part of proton gradient to export ATP; (3) cytoplasmic NADH must use less efficient shuttles (glycerol-3-phosphate gives fewer ATP); (4) non-integer P/O ratio for ATP synthase.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain three reasons actual ATP yield is lower than theoretical maximum.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Three reasons actual < theoretical: (1) Proton leak: the inner mitochondrial membrane is not perfectly impermeable; some H⁺ leaks back across without passing through ATP synthase → energy dissipated as heat rather than captured as ATP → fewer ATP per NADH/FADH₂. (2) ATP transport cost: ATP synthesized in the mitochondrial matrix must be exported by the ATP-ADP translocase (adenine nucleotide translocator, ANT) using a H⁺ cotransport mechanism → importing ADP and exporting ATP consumes some of the proton-motive force that could otherwise drive ATP synthesis. (3) Cytoplasmic NADH shuttle cost: glycolytic NADH cannot directly enter the mitochondria; malate-aspartate or glycerol-3-phosphate shuttles are needed → shuttle type determines effective ATP yield (malate-aspartate shuttle gives ~2.5 ATP per cytoplasmic NADH, but some cells use the less efficient glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle giving ~1.5 ATP). (4) H⁺/ATP ratio uncertainty: the number of H⁺ required to synthesize 1 ATP by ATP synthase (the P/O ratio) is not exactly an integer (~2.7 H⁺/ATP experimentally), creating inherent inefficiency versus theoretical integer assumptions. Accept any three mechanistically correct explanations. 1 pt per 2 explanations, max 2 pts.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Pasteur effect: anaerobic = 8× more glucose consumed. Aerobic: ETC produces ~30 ATP/glucose; high ATP inhibits PFK-1 → glycolysis slows. Anaerobic: no ETC → only 2 ATP/glucose; low ATP → PFK-1 uninhibited → glycolysis runs fast; fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ to keep glycolysis going. Net: must consume much more glucose to maintain ATP.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain the Pasteur effect connecting glycolytic regulation, NAD⁺ availability, and ATP efficiency.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Pasteur effect: aerobic conditions → low glucose consumption; anaerobic → 8× higher glucose consumption to maintain same ATP production rate. Mechanism: Under aerobic conditions: pyruvate enters Krebs/ETC → ~30-32 ATP per glucose; glycolysis is regulated at phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) — allosterically inhibited by high ATP/citrate levels → glycolysis slows when ATP is plentiful → low glucose consumption. Under anaerobic conditions: ETC cannot function (no O₂ as terminal electron acceptor) → no oxidative phosphorylation → only 2 ATP per glucose from glycolysis. To compensate: cell must consume 15-16× more glucose to generate the same ATP. But also: without ETC, NADH (from glycolysis) cannot be oxidized → NAD⁺ becomes depleted → glycolysis would halt at glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step (requires NAD⁺). Fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ (by reducing pyruvate using NADH) → allows glycolysis to continue rapidly. PFK-1 is no longer inhibited (low ATP → low inhibition) → glycolysis runs at maximum rate. Net: high glucose consumption rate required to generate sufficient ATP from inefficient glycolysis alone.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Describe what happens to pyruvate under anaerobic conditions in: (i) yeast (alcoholic fermentation) and (ii) exercising human muscle cells (lactic acid fermentation). For each, write the net reaction for fermentation starting from glucose, identify the enzyme responsible for the final conversion, and explain the primary metabolic purpose of the fermentation reaction.

(b) A student claims: "Fermentation produces ATP from ADP + Pi directly." Evaluate this claim. Clarify which step of the process actually produces ATP and which step is the actual fermentation reaction, and explain why the distinction matters.

(c) Yeast are facultative anaerobes — they switch between aerobic and anaerobic metabolism depending on O₂ availability. Table 1 shows CO₂ production rates in yeast under different conditions. Analyze these data:
    (i) Explain why yeast produce CO₂ under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions.
    (ii) Explain why CO₂ production rate is higher anaerobically despite less ATP production per glucose.
    (iii) Predict what would happen to CO₂ production if you added cyanide (a Complex IV inhibitor) to aerobically respiring yeast.

(d) Long-distance runners sometimes experience muscle fatigue associated with lactate accumulation. A coach claims that "lactic acid burns out the muscle." Evaluate this claim using current understanding of muscle fatigue physiology. Explain what actually causes muscle fatigue during intense exercise and the role (if any) of lactate.
stimulus:
Table 1: CO₂ production by yeast
Condition                    | CO₂ production (mmol/hr/g)
Aerobic (glucose)            |        3.0
Anaerobic (glucose)          |        8.5
Aerobic (glucose + cyanide)  |        ?

Alcoholic fermentation reactions:
Glucose → 2 pyruvate → 2 acetaldehyde + 2 CO₂ (pyruvate decarboxylase)
2 Acetaldehyde + 2 NADH → 2 ethanol + 2 NAD⁺ (alcohol dehydrogenase)

Lactic acid fermentation:
Glucose → 2 pyruvate → 2 lactate (lactate dehydrogenase)
(No CO₂ produced in lactic acid fermentation)
title: APBIO-FRQ-L-016

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Alcoholic: pyruvate → acetaldehyde + CO₂ (pyruvate decarboxylase) → ethanol + NAD⁺ (alcohol dehydrogenase). Lactic acid: pyruvate → lactate + NAD⁺ (LDH). Purpose of both: regenerate NAD⁺ to allow glycolysis to continue producing ATP without O₂.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe alcoholic and lactic acid fermentation pathways; identify enzymes; explain metabolic purpose.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Alcoholic fermentation (yeast): Glucose → 2 pyruvate → 2 acetaldehyde + 2 CO₂ (pyruvate decarboxylase) → 2 ethanol + 2 NAD⁺ (alcohol dehydrogenase). Net: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH + 2 CO₂ + 2 ATP. Key enzyme for final step: alcohol dehydrogenase (reduces acetaldehyde using NADH → ethanol + NAD⁺). Metabolic purpose: regenerate NAD⁺ from NADH so glycolysis can continue producing ATP anaerobically. CO₂ is a byproduct (used in bread leavening, beer carbonation). (ii) Lactic acid fermentation (exercising muscle): Glucose → 2 pyruvate → 2 lactate + 2 NAD⁺ (lactate dehydrogenase). Net: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₃H₆O₃ + 2 ATP. Key enzyme: lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). Metabolic purpose: same — regenerate NAD⁺ to sustain glycolytic ATP production when O₂ is insufficient. No CO₂ produced. Lactate can be exported to liver (Cori cycle) for reconversion to glucose. Purpose of fermentation = regenerate NAD⁺ (not primarily to make lactate/ethanol as products). 1 pt for correct pathway/enzyme for both types; 1 pt for correctly stating metabolic purpose as NAD⁺ regeneration.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Claim is incorrect. ATP is produced by glycolysis (substrate-level phosphorylation), NOT by fermentation reactions. Fermentation (pyruvate → lactate or ethanol) directly regenerates NAD⁺ from NADH — it produces no ATP itself. Fermentation enables glycolysis to continue by preventing NADH accumulation.
accepted_variants: fermentation does not produce ATP directly
enabling glycolysis not directly producing ATP
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Evaluate the claim that fermentation directly produces ATP; clarify which step produces ATP.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: The claim is INCORRECT as stated. ATP is produced by GLYCOLYSIS (substrate-level phosphorylation at phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase steps), NOT by the fermentation reactions themselves. The fermentation reactions (pyruvate → ethanol + CO₂, or pyruvate → lactate) produce NO ATP directly — they are redox reactions that recycle NAD⁺ by oxidizing NADH. The purpose of fermentation is to regenerate NAD⁺ so that glycolysis can continue to operate and produce ATP. Without NAD⁺ regeneration, the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step of glycolysis would halt (requires NAD⁺ as electron acceptor) → glycolysis stops → no more ATP from glycolysis. Distinction matters: the ATP comes from glycolysis; fermentation is a supporting reaction that enables glycolysis to keep running by preventing NADH accumulation. This is why some students confuse fermentation with energy production — it enables energy production (glycolysis) rather than performing it directly.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: (i) Aerobic CO₂: pyruvate oxidation + Krebs. Anaerobic CO₂: pyruvate decarboxylase only (alcoholic fermentation). (ii) Higher anaerobic CO₂: need 4× more glucose to generate ATP → more decarboxylation steps → more CO₂ per hour. (iii) Cyanide: ETC blocked → forced anaerobic → CO₂ increases to anaerobic levels.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain CO₂ under both conditions; explain higher anaerobic rate; predict cyanide effect.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) CO₂ sources: Aerobic — CO₂ released in pyruvate oxidation (1 CO₂ per pyruvate) and Krebs cycle (2 CO₂ per acetyl-CoA × 2 turns = 4 CO₂ total). Anaerobic — CO₂ released only in pyruvate → acetaldehyde step (1 CO₂ per pyruvate; 2 per glucose) by pyruvate decarboxylase. No CO₂ from lactic acid fermentation. Yeast do alcoholic fermentation, so CO₂ is produced anaerobically. (ii) Higher CO₂ anaerobically (8.5 vs. 3.0 mmol/hr/g): despite less ATP per glucose (2 vs. ~30), yeast must consume ~4× more glucose per hour to maintain adequate ATP production → more glucose molecules processed → more total fermentative CO₂ released per hour → higher CO₂ production rate. (iii) Cyanide (Complex IV inhibitor): blocks O₂ from being reduced → ETC halts → aerobic respiration stops → yeast switch to fermentation → CO₂ production would INCREASE toward anaerobic levels (Pasteur effect in reverse); the yeast, now functionally anaerobic, ferment glucose rapidly → high CO₂ output.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Claim outdated: lactate does not cause muscle fatigue. Actual causes: H⁺ accumulation (from ATP hydrolysis, not from lactate) lowers pH → inhibits enzymes, reduces Ca²⁺ sensitivity; inorganic phosphate (Pi) accumulation impairs cross-bridge cycling; phosphocreatine depletion. Lactate itself may buffer acidosis.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Evaluate "lactic acid burns muscle" claim; explain actual cause of muscle fatigue.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: The claim is OUTDATED and largely incorrect. Current understanding: lactate (lactic acid) itself does not cause muscle fatigue or burning sensation. Lactate is a fuel that can be oxidized by heart and oxidative muscle fibers, and the Cori cycle converts lactate to glucose in the liver. Actual causes of muscle fatigue during intense exercise: (1) Inorganic phosphate (Pi) accumulation: Pi released from ATP hydrolysis accumulates in the muscle; Pi inhibits cross-bridge cycling (reduces force per cross-bridge) and may block calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum → reduced force production; (2) Acidosis: excess H⁺ (from ATP hydrolysis: ATP → ADP + Pi + H⁺) lowers intracellular pH → inhibits enzyme activity and reduces calcium sensitivity of troponin → reduced force. The burning sensation is from H⁺ (acid), not lactate per se. (3) Depletion of phosphocreatine and glycogen; (4) ADP accumulation. Lactate correlates with fatigue (produced alongside H⁺ under anaerobic conditions) but does not cause it. Some evidence suggests lactate may actually buffer acidosis by consuming H⁺ in the LDH reaction. 1 pt for correctly identifying the claim as outdated/incorrect; 1 pt for explaining actual fatigue mechanisms (H⁺, Pi accumulation).

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Describe the sequence of molecular events that occurs when insulin binds to its receptor on a liver cell. Begin with receptor binding and end with GLUT4 transporter insertion into the plasma membrane. Include the role of receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) activity, IRS-1, PI3K, and Akt (PKB).

(b) Compare the insulin receptor (RTK) signaling pathway to the epinephrine receptor (GPCR / β-adrenergic receptor) signaling pathway. For each, identify: (i) the receptor type and its location; (ii) the primary intracellular second messenger or signal amplifier; and (iii) one physiological effect in a target cell.

(c) A somatic mutation causes the insulin receptor to remain constitutively active (continuously phosphorylated even in the absence of insulin). Predict THREE distinct cellular consequences of this mutation, including effects on metabolism, cell proliferation, and gene expression.

(d) Many cancer cells overexpress growth factor receptors (RTKs) or carry mutations that make downstream signaling proteins (like Ras or Akt) constitutively active. Explain how each of the following mutations could contribute to uncontrolled cell proliferation:
    (i) Overexpression of EGF receptor (HER2)
    (ii) Ras protein locked in GTP-bound form (cannot hydrolyze GTP)
    (iii) Loss-of-function mutation in PTEN (which converts PIP3 → PIP2)
stimulus:
Insulin signaling pathway:
• Insulin binds → receptor α-subunits change conformation
• β-subunit cytoplasmic tails auto-phosphorylate tyrosines (kinase activation)
• IRS-1 (Insulin Receptor Substrate-1) binds and is phosphorylated by receptor
• PI3K recruited → phosphorylates PIP2 → PIP3
• PIP3 recruits PDK1 and Akt → PDK1 phosphorylates/activates Akt
• Active Akt phosphorylates downstream targets:
  – Phosphorylates AS160 → GLUT4 vesicle fusion with plasma membrane
  – Phosphorylates and inhibits GSK-3 → activates glycogen synthase
  – Activates mTOR → promotes protein synthesis
  – Phosphorylates and inactivates FOXO transcription factors

GPCR comparison:
• β-adrenergic receptor + epinephrine → Gα-GTP → adenylyl cyclase activated
• cAMP produced → PKA activated → multiple downstream phosphorylations
title: APBIO-FRQ-L-017

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Insulin binds receptor → RTK auto-phosphorylation → IRS-1 phosphorylated → PI3K activated → PIP2→PIP3 → Akt (PKB) activated → AS160 phosphorylated → GLUT4 vesicles fuse with plasma membrane → glucose uptake.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe insulin → RTK → IRS-1 → PI3K → Akt → GLUT4 pathway in sequence.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Correct pathway sequence: (1) Insulin binds to the extracellular α-subunit of the insulin receptor → conformational change. (2) β-subunit cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase domains auto-phosphorylate each other (transautophosphorylation) → kinase becomes active. (3) Activated receptor phosphorylates IRS-1 (Insulin Receptor Substrate-1) on multiple tyrosines. (4) Phosphorylated IRS-1 recruits and activates PI3K (phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase). (5) PI3K phosphorylates PIP2 → PIP3 at inner leaflet of plasma membrane. (6) PIP3 recruits PDK1 and Akt (PKB) to the membrane; PDK1 phosphorylates and activates Akt. (7) Active Akt phosphorylates AS160 (a GTPase-activating protein for Rab GTPases) → inactivates AS160 → Rab GTPases remain GTP-bound → GLUT4-containing vesicles traffic to and fuse with plasma membrane → increased glucose uptake. 1 pt for RTK activation mechanism (auto-phosphorylation, IRS-1 phosphorylation); 1 pt for PI3K→PIP3→Akt→GLUT4 mechanism.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: RTK (insulin): intrinsic tyrosine kinase, PIP3/Akt amplification, effect = glucose uptake / glycogen synthesis. GPCR (epinephrine): 7-TM receptor, Gα → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA, effect = glycogenolysis / fight-or-flight response.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Compare RTK (insulin) and GPCR (epinephrine) pathways on receptor type, second messenger, and physiological effect.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Insulin receptor (RTK): (i) Transmembrane receptor with intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity; single-pass (dimer) transmembrane; extracellular ligand-binding domain + intracellular kinase domain. (ii) Primary amplifier: PIP3 (membrane phospholipid second messenger) → activates Akt; no classical second messenger like cAMP; amplification through phosphorylation cascade. (iii) Physiological effect in liver: GLUT4 insertion → increased glucose uptake; glycogen synthase activated → glycogen synthesis; protein synthesis via mTOR. β-adrenergic receptor (GPCR): (i) 7-transmembrane receptor coupled to G-protein; no intrinsic catalytic activity; activates associated Gα protein. (ii) Primary second messenger: cAMP (produced by adenylyl cyclase activated by Gα-GTP) → activates PKA (protein kinase A) → phosphorylates multiple targets. (iii) Physiological effect in skeletal muscle: PKA activates phosphorylase kinase → activates glycogen phosphorylase → glycogenolysis (glycogen breakdown) → glucose-1-phosphate → glycolysis → ATP for fight-or-flight. 1 pt per pathway with all 3 elements correct.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Three consequences: (1) Metabolism: hypoglycemia, excess glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis, lipogenesis even without food. (2) Proliferation: mTOR and Akt constitutively active → cell growth, reduced apoptosis, tumor-like proliferation. (3) Gene expression: FOXO transcription factors constitutively inhibited → reduced gluconeogenesis genes, reduced apoptosis genes.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Predict three consequences of constitutively active insulin receptor.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Three consequences: (1) Metabolism: cells would constitutively import glucose (GLUT4 always at surface in insulin-sensitive cells) → increased glycolysis and glycogen synthesis → hypoglycemia (low blood glucose) as cells deplete blood glucose even in fasting state; excess acetyl-CoA → lipogenesis → excess fat storage. (2) Cell proliferation: Akt constitutively active → phosphorylates and inactivates GSK-3 → β-catenin accumulates → activates Wnt target genes promoting cell division; mTOR constitutively active → enhanced protein synthesis and cell growth; FOXO transcription factors constitutively inactivated → reduced expression of p27 (CDK inhibitor) and other cell cycle brakes → excessive cell proliferation → potential tumor formation. (3) Gene expression: constitutive Akt inactivates FOXO → reduced FOXO-dependent transcription (genes for gluconeogenesis, cell cycle arrest, apoptosis suppressed); mTOR promotes ribosome biogenesis and protein synthesis genes; constitutive growth signals mimic oncogenic transformation. Award 1 pt per two well-explained consequences, max 2 pts.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: (i) HER2 overexpression: spontaneous dimerization → constitutive kinase activity → continuous RAS/MAPK and PI3K/Akt signaling without growth factor. (ii) Ras-GTP locked: cannot hydrolyze GTP → always active → constitutive MAPK → proliferation. (iii) PTEN loss: cannot convert PIP3→PIP2 → PIP3 accumulates → Akt always active → mTOR → proliferation (lost tumor suppressor).
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain how HER2 overexpression, Ras-GTP lock, and PTEN loss each contribute to cancer.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) HER2 overexpression: HER2 (ErbB2) is an RTK that forms dimers with other EGF family receptors; overexpression increases probability of spontaneous dimerization and auto-phosphorylation even without growth factor binding → constitutive downstream signaling (Ras→MAPK, PI3K→Akt) → constant proliferation signal. Also, more receptors means stronger amplified response to any ligand. Targeted by trastuzumab (Herceptin) antibody therapy. (ii) Ras-GTP locked: Ras is a small GTPase; normally GTP-Ras is active and stimulates proliferation (through MAPK cascade); Ras-GAP proteins hydrolyze GTP → GDP to inactivate Ras. A mutation preventing GTP hydrolysis (e.g., G12V mutation in KRAS) locks Ras in the active GTP-bound state → constitutive MAPK activation → continuous proliferation signal regardless of whether growth factor receptor is active. ~30% of human cancers have Ras mutations. (iii) PTEN loss: PTEN is a phosphatase that converts PIP3 back to PIP2 (antagonizes PI3K). Loss-of-function mutation → PIP3 accumulates constitutively → Akt constitutively active → mTOR always on → cell growth, survival, proliferation unchecked → tumor suppressor function lost (PTEN is a tumor suppressor). 1 pt per any two mechanisms with correct molecular detail.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Figure 1 shows cells in various stages of division. For a diploid organism with 2n = 6 chromosomes, state the chromosome number (n) and the DNA content relative to a pre-S phase cell (1C = unreplicated haploid content) for a cell at each of the following stages: (i) G₁ of mitosis; (ii) after Meiosis I (before Meiosis II); (iii) after Meiosis II; (iv) G₂ before mitosis.

(b) Explain THREE distinct mechanisms by which meiosis generates genetic diversity that mitosis does not. For each mechanism, identify when in meiosis it occurs and explain how it increases variation among gametes.

(c) During meiosis I, homologous chromosomes must pair (synapsis) and undergo crossing over before separating. Explain:
    (i) The physical process of crossing over, naming the structure in which it occurs and the enzyme responsible for strand exchange.
    (ii) Why genes that are farther apart on the same chromosome show higher recombination frequencies than genes that are close together.
    (iii) Why the maximum recombination frequency between any two genes on the same chromosome is 50%, regardless of their actual distance.

(d) Nondisjunction can occur in either meiosis I or meiosis II.
    (i) Compare the consequences of nondisjunction in meiosis I vs. meiosis II for the resulting gametes — how does the proportion of aneuploid gametes differ?
    (ii) Down syndrome (trisomy 21) most commonly results from maternal nondisjunction. Explain why maternal age is the strongest risk factor for trisomy 21.
stimulus:
Figure 1 description: cells at G₁, S-phase, G₂, mitotic metaphase, meiosis I metaphase, meiosis II, and post-division.

Organisms used: Diploid (2n = 6); three pairs of homologous chromosomes.

DNA content notation:
• 1C = unreplicated DNA content of one haploid cell
• 2C = diploid unreplicated (G₁ diploid cell)
• 4C = replicated diploid (G₂ or mitotic prophase)
• 2C after Meiosis I = haploid replicated (still has sister chromatids)
• 1C after Meiosis II = haploid unreplicated gamete

Recombination frequency data (hypothetical):
Gene pair | Distance (cM) | Recombination frequency observed
  A–B     |     5 cM      |        5%
  A–C     |    30 cM      |       30%
  A–D     |    80 cM      |       50%
title: APBIO-FRQ-L-018

criteria_json.minimum_fix: G₁: 2n=6, 2C. After Meiosis I: n=3, 2C (sister chromatids still joined). After Meiosis II: n=3, 1C (gamete). G₂ before mitosis: 2n=6, 4C (replicated).
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: State chromosome number and DNA content (C value) at four specified stages.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: For 2n = 6 organism: (i) G₁ of mitosis: chromosome number = 6 (diploid, 2n); DNA content = 2C (unreplicated diploid). Chromosomes are unreplicated single chromatids. (ii) After Meiosis I (before Meiosis II): chromosome number = 3 (haploid, n); DNA content = 2C (each chromosome still consists of 2 sister chromatids joined at centromere → same DNA amount per chromosome as G₁ diploid, but half the number of chromosomes). Actually 2C if we define 1C as unreplicated haploid = genome without replication. After meiosis I: n chromosomes each with 2 chromatids → DNA = 2C. (iii) After Meiosis II: chromosome number = 3; DNA content = 1C (sister chromatids separated, each chromosome now single chromatid, haploid unreplicated). (iv) G₂ before mitosis: chromosome number = 6 (diploid, DNA replicated); DNA content = 4C (all chromosomes replicated → each exists as 2 sister chromatids). 1 pt per two stages correctly identified with both chromosome number AND C value.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Three: (1) Independent assortment (metaphase I): 2^n chromosome combinations. (2) Crossing over (prophase I): recombinant chromosomes with new allele combinations. (3) Random fertilization: any sperm + any egg amplifies diversity.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain three mechanisms by which meiosis generates genetic diversity.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Three mechanisms: (1) Independent assortment (Metaphase I): homologous chromosome pairs (bivalents) align randomly at the metaphase I plate; each pair orients independently → the combination of maternal and paternal chromosomes distributed to each daughter cell is random. For 2n = 6 (3 pairs): 2³ = 8 possible chromosome combinations per gamete. For humans (2n = 46): 2²³ ≈ 8 million combinations. Occurs during meiosis I metaphase/anaphase I. (2) Crossing over / recombination (Prophase I): homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis) and exchange segments at chiasmata (Holliday junctions processed by resolvase) → creates recombinant chromosomes with novel allele combinations not present in either parent. Occurs during prophase I (pachytene stage of meiosis I). Dramatically increases diversity beyond independent assortment alone. (3) Random fertilization: even with only two parents, random fusion of any sperm (one of 8+ million types) with any egg (one of 8+ million types) → ~64 trillion possible combinations in humans. Not within meiosis itself but depends on meiotic diversity being the substrate. Accept if student notes this is a third source. 1 pt per two mechanisms with timing and mechanism correctly explained.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Crossing over occurs in synaptonemal complex (prophase I); Spo11 creates DSBs, Rad51 strand invasion; Holliday junctions resolve at chiasmata. Farther genes = higher chance of crossover between them = higher recombination %. 50% max because each crossover involves only 2 of 4 chromatids; multiple crossovers cancel; equals independent assortment.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain crossing over mechanism; distance-frequency relationship; 50% maximum.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Physical process: crossing over occurs within the synaptonemal complex (a protein scaffold that holds homologous chromosomes together during prophase I / zygotene-pachytene stage). Mechanism: double-strand break (DSB) in one chromatid; DSB processed by resolvase (and RecA/Rad51 homologs) via strand invasion → Holliday junction forms → branch migration → resolution. Each chiasma (visible crossing over point) represents one crossover event. The enzyme primarily responsible for strand exchange is Spo11 (creates DSBs) and Rad51/DMC1 (strand invasion / recombinase). (ii) Distance–frequency: crossing over occurs at roughly random positions along chromosomes. Genes farther apart have a greater length of chromosome between them → higher probability that a crossover will occur between them → higher recombination frequency. 1 cM (centimorgan) = 1% recombination frequency; 30 cM genes = ~30% recombination (for moderate distances). (iii) 50% maximum: if genes are very far apart on the same chromosome, crossovers between them occur so frequently that assortment approaches 50% — the same as if genes were on different chromosomes (independent assortment). When multiple crossovers occur between loci, the combination of crossovers can cancel out each other's effect (double crossover restores parental configuration). The maximum 50% recombination frequency occurs because at any crossover, only 2 of the 4 chromatids are involved → even with 100% crossovers between loci, at most 50% of gametes are recombinant. 1 pt for mechanism with synaptonemal complex; 1 pt for both distance explanation and 50% cap.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Meiosis I nondisjunction: 100% of gametes aneuploid (both homologs in same cell). Meiosis II nondisjunction: 50% aneuploid (only sister chromatids failed). Maternal age: oocytes arrested at prophase I since fetal development → cohesins degrade over decades → chromosomes fail to separate at ovulation → increased trisomy risk with age.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Compare meiosis I vs II nondisjunction outcomes; explain maternal age and trisomy 21.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Nondisjunction in meiosis I: failure of homologous chromosomes to separate properly → both homologs go to same cell → after meiosis II, ALL gametes from this division are aneuploid (2 gametes have n+1, 2 gametes have n-1). Nondisjunction in meiosis II: failure of sister chromatids to separate → only the gametes from the affected meiosis II division are aneuploid → 2 gametes are aneuploid (one n+1, one n-1) and 2 gametes are normal (n) from the unaffected meiosis II division → only 50% of gametes are aneuploid. Key distinction: Meiosis I nondisjunction = 100% aneuploid gametes; Meiosis II nondisjunction = 50% aneuploid gametes. (ii) Maternal age and trisomy 21: human oocytes begin meiosis I during fetal development and arrest at prophase I (the dictyotene stage) until ovulation — this arrest can last 12-50 years. During this prolonged arrest, the cohesins holding homologs together gradually deteriorate/are lost → chromosomes become more likely to fail to separate properly at meiosis I resumption (triggered by LH surge at ovulation). Older oocytes have had longer to lose cohesins → higher risk of nondisjunction → trisomy. Also, the spindle assembly checkpoint may be less stringent in older oocytes. This explains why risk of trisomy 21 rises sharply with maternal age (from <0.1% at 20 to >3% at 45). 1 pt for correct comparison of meiosis I vs II nondisjunction outcomes; 1 pt for cohesin degradation / arrest explanation of maternal age effect.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) The pedigree in Figure 1 shows the inheritance of a trait across three generations. Affected individuals are shaded.
    (i) Determine the most likely mode of inheritance. Justify your answer by identifying at least TWO pedigree observations that support your conclusion.
    (ii) Assign genotypes to individuals I-1, I-2, II-3 (an affected male), and II-4 (an unaffected female who has an affected son).
    (iii) Calculate the probability that a child of II-4 and II-3 will be an affected female.

(b) Males with X-linked recessive conditions are affected at a much higher frequency than females. Explain the molecular and genetic basis for this sex difference, using hemizygosity in your explanation.

(c) Explain X-inactivation (Lyon hypothesis) in female mammals:
    (i) When does X-inactivation occur in development, and how is the choice of which X is inactivated made?
    (ii) Describe the molecular mechanism of X-inactivation, naming the gene responsible and the RNA molecule involved.
    (iii) Explain why X-inactivation is permanent and clonally inherited.

(d) A tortoiseshell cat has patches of orange and black fur. The gene for orange/black fur color is X-linked.
    (i) Explain why tortoiseshell cats are almost always female.
    (ii) Explain why the patches of orange and black fur are large rather than a uniform blended color.
    (iii) Predict the coat color pattern of a female cat that is homozygous for the orange allele.
stimulus:
Pedigree — Figure 1 (described):
Generation I:   I-1 (unaffected male) × I-2 (unaffected female)
Generation II:  II-1 (unaffected female), II-2 (unaffected male),
                II-3 (AFFECTED male), II-4 (unaffected female),
                II-5 (unaffected male)
Generation III: III-1 (AFFECTED male, son of II-4 and II-5)
                III-2 (unaffected female, daughter of II-4 and II-5)

Note: No affected females in pedigree.
Affected: II-3 (male), III-1 (male, son of II-4 and unaffected II-5)

X-linked gene notation:
• X^A = dominant / unaffected allele
• X^a = recessive / affected allele
• Females: X^A X^A (normal), X^A X^a (carrier), X^a X^a (affected)
• Males: X^A Y (normal), X^a Y (affected)
title: APBIO-FRQ-L-019

criteria_json.minimum_fix: X-linked recessive. Evidence: only males affected; skip-generation transmission; unaffected parents have affected sons. Genotypes: I-1 = X^A Y; I-2 = X^A X^a; II-3 = X^a Y; II-4 = X^A X^a. Probability affected female = 1/4 (25%).
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Determine mode of inheritance; assign genotypes; calculate probability of affected female offspring.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) X-linked recessive. Evidence: (1) Only males are affected (II-3, III-1) — X-linked recessive affects males more frequently than females because males are hemizygous; (2) Affected son III-1 was born to two unaffected parents (II-4 and II-5) → trait skipped a generation → characteristic of recessive; (3) Affected II-3 had an unaffected father (I-1) — this rules out Y-linked (which would affect all sons of affected fathers); (4) I-2 must be a carrier (unaffected female with affected son II-3). Also rules out autosomal: autosomal recessive would give equal sex ratios; autosomal dominant would show affected in every generation if parents are affected. (ii) Genotypes: I-1: X^A Y (unaffected male, no allele to give son affected); I-2: X^A X^a (carrier female — must carry X^a to pass to affected son II-3); II-3: X^a Y (affected male); II-4: X^A X^a (carrier — must carry X^a to have affected son III-1, and her husband II-5 is X^A Y unaffected so son must have gotten X^a from her). (iii) Cross II-4 (X^A X^a) × II-3 (X^a Y): Possible offspring: X^A X^a (carrier female), X^a X^a (affected female), X^A Y (normal male), X^a Y (affected male). Probability affected female = X^a X^a = 1/4 = 25%.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Males are hemizygous for X-linked genes (only one X, no second allele on Y). A single recessive allele causes expression in males. Females (XX) need two copies of the recessive allele (homozygous) to be affected. Single-carrier females are unaffected. Therefore males affected much more frequently.
accepted_variants: Y does not carry X-linked alleles
single recessive allele expresses in males
dominant allele masks recessive in heterozygous female
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain molecular basis of higher male frequency for X-linked recessive traits using hemizygosity.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Hemizygosity: males have only one X chromosome and one Y chromosome (XY). The Y chromosome does not carry most genes present on the X chromosome (the non-pseudoautosomal region of Y is distinct). Therefore, for X-linked genes, males have only ONE copy of the allele (hemizygous) — there is no second allele on a homolog to mask the recessive allele's phenotypic effect. For X-linked recessive conditions: a male who inherits even one copy of the recessive allele (X^a Y) will be affected, because there is no corresponding dominant allele on the Y to compensate. For females: they have two X chromosomes (XX), so a female with one recessive allele (X^A X^a) is a heterozygous CARRIER — the dominant X^A allele produces sufficient functional protein to mask the recessive phenotype.
