A female must be homozygous recessive (X^a X^a) to be affected, requiring inheritance of the recessive allele from BOTH parents. This is much less probable than a male inheriting a single recessive allele. Example: red-green color blindness affects ~8% of males but only ~0.5% of females because female frequency ≈ (male frequency)² (Hardy-Weinberg).

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Timing: early embryo (~day 12-16), random choice in each cell (maternal or paternal X). Mechanism: XIST gene transcribes lncRNA that coats inactive X → recruits Polycomb proteins → histone methylation → DNA methylation → Barr body. Clonal: epigenetic marks copied at each cell division → all daughter cells have same inactive X.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain X-inactivation: timing, choice, molecular mechanism, and clonal inheritance.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Timing and choice: X-inactivation occurs early in embryonic development — in placental mammals, around days 12-16 in humans (at the blastocyst → post-implantation stage, around the time of gastrulation; some texts say 100-cell stage). In each somatic cell of the early embryo, ONE X chromosome is randomly inactivated — either the maternal X or the paternal X is chosen with equal probability. (Note: in extra-embryonic cells like trophoblast, the paternal X is preferentially inactivated — imprinted X-inactivation.) After the initial choice is made independently in each cell, it is maintained in all descendants. (ii) Molecular mechanism: the XIST gene (X-Inactive Specific Transcript) on the X chromosome to be inactivated is transcribed and produces a long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) called XIST (or Xist in mice). XIST RNA coats the inactive X chromosome in cis (spreads along the chromosome it is transcribed from). XIST RNA recruits chromatin-remodeling proteins (Polycomb group proteins) → histone modifications (H3K27 methylation, H3K9 methylation, loss of H3 acetylation) → heterochromatin formation → DNA methylation of CpG islands at gene promoters → gene silencing. The inactive X condenses into a dense structure called the Barr body (sex chromatin). (iii) Permanence and clonal inheritance: once X is inactivated, epigenetic marks (DNA methylation and histone modifications) are faithfully copied during DNA replication and cell division → every daughter cell inherits the same inactive X → the inactivation pattern is clonally inherited for the lifetime of the organism. The XIST RNA continues to be expressed from the inactive X to maintain silencing. This is why X-inactivation is an irreversible epigenetic modification in somatic cells. 1 pt per two sub-parts correctly addressed.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: (i) Tortoiseshell = heterozygous female (X^O X^o); males hemizygous cannot have both alleles; rare tortoiseshell males are XXY. (ii) Large patches = clonal expansion from early X-inactivation; each patch descended from one early cell with same inactive X. (iii) Homozygous orange female (X^O X^O) = solid orange; all cells express orange regardless of which X is inactivated.
accepted_variants: X^O X^O solid orange all cells
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain tortoiseshell cat genetics: female only; large patches; homozygous orange prediction.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Tortoiseshell always female: the coat color gene is X-linked (O = orange, o = black). Males (XY) are hemizygous → can only be orange (X^O Y) or black (X^o Y), never both. Females (XX) can be heterozygous (X^O X^o) → carry one orange and one black allele. X-inactivation causes random inactivation of one X in each somatic cell → some cells express orange, others express black → patches of each color. Very rarely, tortoiseshell males occur due to XXY karyotype (Klinefelter syndrome in cats). (ii) Large patches: X-inactivation occurs early in development (small number of cells), and once a cell's X is inactivated, all descendants inherit the same inactive X (clonal inheritance). By the time the cat's coat develops, each early embryonic cell has produced millions of descendants, all with the same X active → large coherent patches of one color. If inactivation were re-randomized at every cell division, colors would be uniformly blended (like a mix of paint) instead of patchy. The large patches are direct evidence of clonal expansion from early X-inactivation events. (iii) Homozygous orange female: X^O X^O → both X chromosomes carry the orange allele. X-inactivation still occurs (one X silenced in each cell), but both X chromosomes carry orange allele → all cells express orange regardless of which X is inactivated → cat is uniformly solid orange (no black patches). 1 pt for (i) with hemizygosity explanation; 1 pt for (ii) + (iii).

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Human height shows a continuous, bell-shaped (normal) distribution rather than discrete phenotypic classes.
    (i) Explain why polygenic inheritance produces a continuous distribution rather than discrete classes. Use the concept of additive alleles in your explanation.
    (ii) If height were controlled by only 3 genes, each with two alleles (A/a, B/b, C/c), where each uppercase allele adds 5 cm to a baseline height of 155 cm: calculate the height of a person with genotype AaBbCc. Then state the tallest and shortest possible heights and their genotypes.

(b) Twin studies compare concordance rates (both twins sharing a trait) between monozygotic (MZ, identical) and dizygotic (DZ, fraternal) twins. The table shows concordance data for three traits.
    (i) Calculate the heritability of height using the formula: H² ≈ 2(MZ concordance − DZ concordance).
    (ii) Explain what the heritability value for schizophrenia tells you about the relative contributions of genes and environment to that condition.
    (iii) Explain why MZ twins can sometimes have different phenotypes despite identical genotypes.

(c) The norm of reaction for a genotype is the range of phenotypes that genotype can produce across a range of environments. Figure 2 shows norm-of-reaction curves for three wheat genotypes grown at low, medium, and high nitrogen levels.
    (i) Define phenotypic plasticity and explain how the norm-of-reaction graph demonstrates it.
    (ii) Which genotype shows the greatest phenotypic plasticity? Justify using data.
    (iii) Which genotype would you recommend planting if you did not know the nitrogen level of the field? Justify your choice.

(d) Distinguish between phenotypic plasticity and genetic adaptation as mechanisms by which a population can respond to environmental change. Describe one scenario in which natural selection could convert phenotypic plasticity into a genetically fixed trait (genetic assimilation).
stimulus:
Table 1: Twin concordance rates
Trait          | MZ concordance | DZ concordance
Height         |      90%       |      45%
Blood type     |     100%       |      50%
Schizophrenia  |      48%       |      17%

Figure 2: Norm of reaction for wheat yield (kg/plot)
Nitrogen level:      Low    Medium   High
Genotype X:          20      25       30
Genotype Y:          15      25       35
Genotype Z:          28      28       28

Heritability formula: H² ≈ 2(r_MZ − r_DZ)
H² = 1.0 means entirely genetic; H² = 0 means entirely environmental.
title: APBIO-FRQ-L-020

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Additive alleles: each uppercase allele adds 5 cm; many genes × many allele combinations → continuous range of phenotypes; environmental variation widens distribution → bell curve. AaBbCc = 155 + 15 = 170 cm. Tallest AABBCC = 185 cm. Shortest aabbcc = 155 cm.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain continuous distribution from additive alleles; calculate AaBbCc height; state extremes.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Polygenic inheritance + additive alleles → continuous distribution: when multiple genes each contribute small additive effects to a phenotype, the number of possible phenotypic values increases greatly. With each gene adding independent small increments, the distribution of phenotypic values in a population approaches a normal (bell-shaped) curve by the Central Limit Theorem. Each gene may have two or more alleles, each adding or not adding to the phenotype. The many possible combinations of additive alleles (plus environmental variation) produce a continuous gradient of phenotypes rather than 2–3 distinct classes seen in single-gene Mendelian traits. Discrete classes are expected only when a single locus with complete dominance controls the trait; with 3+ loci, phenotypic classes overlap and blend. (ii) AaBbCc calculation: Each uppercase allele adds 5 cm. AaBbCc has 3 uppercase alleles (A, B, C from heterozygous pairs contribute 1 uppercase each). Height = 155 + (3 × 5) = 155 + 15 = 170 cm. Tallest: AABBCC (6 uppercase alleles) = 155 + 30 = 185 cm. Shortest: aabbcc (0 uppercase alleles) = 155 + 0 = 155 cm. 1 pt for correct explanation of additive alleles → continuous distribution; 1 pt for correct calculations (170 cm, 185 cm, 155 cm with correct genotypes).

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Height heritability: H² = 2(0.90-0.45) = 0.90 (90% of variation genetic). Schizophrenia H² = 0.62: 62% genetic, 38% environmental; 48% MZ concordance proves environment matters significantly. MZ twins differ due to: epigenetic differences, somatic mutations, environmental exposures, gene expression noise.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Calculate heritability of height; interpret schizophrenia heritability; explain MZ differences.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Heritability of height: H² ≈ 2(0.90 − 0.45) = 2(0.45) = 0.90. Height is highly heritable — about 90% of the variation in height in this population is attributable to genetic differences. (ii) Schizophrenia interpretation: H² ≈ 2(0.48 − 0.17) = 2(0.31) = 0.62. This means approximately 62% of schizophrenia risk variation is attributable to genetic differences; the remaining ~38% is due to environmental factors. This does NOT mean schizophrenia is 62% genetic — it means 62% of the variance in risk in this population has genetic sources. The MZ concordance of only 48% (not 100%) proves that environment plays a substantial role — if schizophrenia were purely genetic, MZ twins would have 100% concordance. Both genetic predisposition AND environmental triggers (stress, prenatal factors, drug use) are required. (iii) MZ twins can differ despite identical DNA due to: epigenetic differences (different patterns of DNA methylation and histone modification that accumulate with age and different experiences); stochastic gene expression noise during development; somatic mutations acquired post-zygotically; different environmental exposures (prenatal position, diet, infections, stress); X-inactivation differences in female MZ twins. 1 pt for correct H² calculation and interpretation; 1 pt for MZ phenotypic differences with at least 2 mechanisms.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Phenotypic plasticity = one genotype → different phenotypes in different environments. Most plastic: Genotype Y (range 15-35 = 20 kg/plot variation). Recommend for unknown N: Genotype Z (flat norm of reaction, 28 kg/plot regardless of N = most predictable).
accepted_variants: phenotypic plasticity one genotype multiple phenotypes
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Define phenotypic plasticity; identify most plastic genotype from data; recommend genotype for unknown environment.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Phenotypic plasticity: the ability of a single genotype to produce different phenotypes in different environments. The norm-of-reaction graph demonstrates this by showing that the same genotype (same line in the graph) produces different yields depending on nitrogen level → the phenotype changes without any change in genotype → this is plasticity. The steeper the slope of the norm-of-reaction line, the greater the plasticity. (ii) Most plastic genotype: Genotype Y. Data: Genotype Y yield ranges from 15 (low N) to 35 (high N) = range of 20 kg/plot. Genotype X: 20 to 30 = range of 10 kg/plot. Genotype Z: 28 to 28 = range of 0 kg/plot (no plasticity). Genotype Y shows the greatest phenotypic change across environments. (iii) Recommendation for unknown nitrogen level: Genotype Z is best for an unknown environment. Data justification: Genotype Z yields 28 kg/plot regardless of nitrogen level (flat norm of reaction = no plasticity) → predictable performance across all conditions; Genotype Z is the most reliable (lowest variance). Genotype Y would be best in high nitrogen but worst in low nitrogen; Genotype X is intermediate but still variable. Planting Z minimizes risk when nitrogen level is uncertain. 1 pt for plasticity definition + graph interpretation; 1 pt for correct genotype selection with data justification.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Plasticity: single genotype responds to environment, no heritable change, within lifetime. Genetic adaptation: allele frequencies change over generations via natural selection, requires multiple generations, heritable. Genetic assimilation: selection favors constitutive expression of a previously plastic trait → alleles that always produce the adaptive phenotype increase in frequency → plastic response becomes genetically fixed.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Distinguish phenotypic plasticity from genetic adaptation; describe genetic assimilation scenario.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Phenotypic plasticity: a single genotype responds to environmental variation by producing different phenotypes; the genetic makeup is unchanged; no heritable genetic change in the population; rapid response within an organism's lifetime. Examples: leaves growing larger in shade, animals developing thicker fur in cold climates during their lifetime. Genetic adaptation: allele frequencies change in the population over generations due to natural selection; individuals do not change — genetically different individuals survive and reproduce differentially → the genetic composition of the population shifts; requires multiple generations; results in a heritable change. Genetic assimilation scenario: a population has phenotypic plasticity for a stress response (e.g., plants can induce thorn production when grazed). Initially, thorns are only produced when herbivores are present (plastic response). In an environment with constant herbivore pressure: (1) Plants that happen to have alleles causing constitutive (always-on) thorn production are at an advantage even without the inductive trigger; (2) Natural selection favors constitutive thorn genotypes → allele frequency for constitutive thorns increases; (3) Over generations, the population becomes genetically fixed for thorn production — even without herbivores, all plants make thorns; (4) The formerly plastic response is now genetically canalized (Waddington's genetic assimilation). The key insight: selection acts on the genetic variation underlying plasticity to fix the most adaptive phenotype permanently.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Eukaryotic gene expression requires the coordinated action of transcription factors, RNA polymerase II, and chromatin remodeling.
    (i) Describe the sequence of events that leads to the assembly of the pre-initiation complex (PIC) at a eukaryotic promoter. Name TWO general transcription factors and their roles.
    (ii) Explain how an enhancer element located 10,000 base pairs upstream of a gene can stimulate transcription at the gene's promoter. Include the role of activator proteins and Mediator in your explanation.

(b) Chromatin structure regulates access to DNA. Using Figure 1 (which shows the same gene in euchromatin vs. heterochromatin states):
    (i) Describe the structural difference between euchromatin and heterochromatin at the level of histone modification.
    (ii) Explain how histone acetyltransferases (HATs) and histone deacetylases (HDACs) have opposite effects on transcription. Include the mechanism by which acetylation opens chromatin.
    (iii) A researcher adds trichostatin A (an HDAC inhibitor) to cells. Predict and explain the effect on global gene expression.

(c) Experiment: The researcher fuses the DNA-binding domain of a transcription factor to different activation domains and measures target gene expression. Results are shown in Table 1. Interpret these results:
    (i) What does the DNA-binding domain alone demonstrate about gene activation?
    (ii) What do the activation domain results reveal about how transcription is activated?
    (iii) The researcher finds that activation domain 3 interacts physically with the Mediator complex. Explain how this interaction could lead to increased transcription.

(d) Explain how the following two mechanisms contribute to cell-type-specific gene expression in a multicellular organism that has one genome but hundreds of distinct cell types:
    (i) Combinatorial control by transcription factors
    (ii) Epigenetic inheritance of chromatin states
stimulus:
Figure 1 (described):
• Euchromatin: beads-on-a-string appearance; histones visible as individual nucleosomes; 30nm fiber partially unfolded; gene accessible to RNA polymerase → gene ON
• Heterochromatin: highly compact; 300nm fiber; DNA wound tightly; gene inaccessible → gene OFF

Table 1: Transcription factor domain fusion experiment
Construct                    | Target gene expression (relative units)
DBD alone                    |         1 (baseline)
DBD + Activation Domain 1    |        45
DBD + Activation Domain 2    |        12
DBD + Activation Domain 3    |        87
DBD + AD1 + AD3              |       203

Note: DBD = DNA-binding domain; all constructs bind the same promoter sequence.
title: APBIO-FRQ-L-021

criteria_json.minimum_fix: TFIID (TBP binds TATA box) and TFIIH (helicase opens DNA, CTD kinase activates RNA pol II) assemble PIC. Enhancer: activators bind → DNA loops (cohesin/CTCF) → enhancer contacts promoter → Mediator bridges activators and RNA pol II → increased transcription.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe PIC assembly at eukaryotic promoter naming two GTFs; explain enhancer-Mediator mechanism.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) PIC assembly: (1) A pioneer transcription factor or general factor recognizes the TATA box (core promoter element ~25 bp upstream of TSS) → TFIID (containing TBP, TATA-Binding Protein) binds the TATA box; TBP bends DNA. (2) TFIIA and TFIIB are recruited → TFIIB positions RNA pol II. (3) TFIIF enters with RNA pol II → stabilizes RNA pol II at promoter. (4) TFIIE and TFIIH join → TFIIH has helicase activity to unwind DNA at TSS (open complex formation) and kinase activity to phosphorylate the C-terminal domain (CTD) of RNA pol II → triggers elongation. Two GTFs to name: TFIID (TBP subunit recognizes TATA box), TFIIH (helicase opens DNA and CTD kinase activates polymerase). (ii) Enhancer mechanism: activator proteins bind the enhancer element via their DNA-binding domains. The activation domains of activators recruit coactivators and Mediator complex. The chromatin between enhancer and promoter loops around (enhancer-promoter looping, mediated by cohesin and CTCF proteins) → brings the activator-Mediator complex into contact with the PIC at the promoter → Mediator bridges activators and RNA pol II → stimulates transcription initiation rate. This looping explains action at a distance (10 kb away). 1 pt for PIC assembly with two GTFs and roles; 1 pt for enhancer-looping-Mediator mechanism.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Euchromatin: hyperacetylated histones (H3K4me3), loose chromatin. Heterochromatin: deacetylated histones (H3K9me3, H3K27me3), compact. HATs acetylate lysines → neutralize charge → looser chromatin → more transcription. HDACs remove acetyl → compact. HDAC inhibitor → all histones remain acetylated → global gene upregulation → silenced genes de-repressed.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe euchromatin/heterochromatin histone modifications; HAT/HDAC mechanisms; predict HDAC inhibitor effect.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Euchromatin vs. heterochromatin at histone level: Euchromatin — histones are hyperacetylated (acetyl groups on lysine residues of H3 and H4 N-terminal tails) and have active histone methylation marks (H3K4me3 at promoters); chromatin is loose and accessible. Heterochromatin — histones are hypoacetylated (deacetylated), have repressive methylation marks (H3K9me3, H3K27me3); histone H1 (linker histone) compacts chromatin further; chromatin is condensed, DNA inaccessible. (ii) HAT/HDAC mechanism: HATs (histone acetyltransferases) add acetyl groups to histone lysine residues → neutralizes positive charge of lysine → reduces attraction between histones and negatively charged DNA → chromatin loosens (nucleosome-DNA interaction weakened) → DNA more accessible to transcription machinery → transcription increases. HDACs (histone deacetylases) remove acetyl groups → lysines revert to positive charge → stronger histone-DNA interactions → chromatin compacts → transcription decreases. (iii) Trichostatin A (HDAC inhibitor) effect: HDACs cannot remove acetyl groups → histones remain hyperacetylated → chromatin stays loose/open → global increase in transcription of many genes, including genes normally kept silenced. Genes under active repression via deacetylation would be de-repressed. Effect: widespread upregulation of gene expression; some previously silenced genes (tumor suppressors, differentiation genes) may be reactivated. This is why HDAC inhibitors are investigated as cancer therapies. 1 pt for euchromatin/heterochromatin marks with mechanism; 1 pt for correct HDAC inhibitor prediction with reasoning.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: DBD alone: binding DNA insufficient for activation. ADs differ in strength; AD3 > AD1 > AD2. AD1+AD3 synergistic (203 > 132) = combinatorial activation. AD3-Mediator interaction: recruits Mediator to promoter → bridges activator to RNA pol II → stimulates PIC assembly or CTD phosphorylation → increased transcription.
accepted_variants: Mediator bridges activator to RNA pol II
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Interpret domain fusion experiment data; explain Mediator interaction mechanism.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) DBD alone (expression = 1, baseline): the DNA-binding domain alone can bind the promoter but does NOT activate transcription — it shows that DNA binding is necessary but not sufficient for transcription activation. Simply recruiting a protein to the DNA does not stimulate RNA pol II. Transcriptional activation requires a separate activation domain. (ii) Activation domain results: activation domains differ in strength (AD3 > AD1 > AD2); the activation domain is the functional module responsible for stimulating transcription, independent of what DNA it is bound to (domain swap experiment works). Combining AD1 + AD3 gives superadditive (synergistic) activation (203 > 45+87 = 132) — demonstrates that multiple activation domains can work cooperatively (combinatorial activation), perhaps by recruiting different coactivators simultaneously. (iii) Mediator interaction of AD3: if AD3 physically contacts the Mediator complex, AD3 recruits Mediator to the promoter → Mediator acts as a bridge between activators and the general transcription machinery → Mediator interacts with RNA pol II CTD → stimulates assembly of the PIC or transition from initiation to productive elongation (CTD phosphorylation) → increased transcription. AD3's stronger activation could be because it makes particularly favorable contacts with Mediator subunits. 1 pt for correct interpretations of DBD alone + AD results; 1 pt for Mediator mechanism.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Combinatorial TF control: different cell types have different TF combinations; each gene requires a specific TF combination; same genome interpreted differently per cell type. Epigenetic inheritance: chromatin marks (DNA methylation, H3K27me3) copied at each division; liver cell daughters remain liver cells; self-perpetuating chromatin states stabilize cell identity.
accepted_variants: different TF combinations per cell type
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain cell-type-specific expression via combinatorial TF control and epigenetic inheritance.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Combinatorial control by transcription factors: different cell types express different subsets of transcription factors; the combination of TFs present in a cell determines which genes are active. Gene A may require TF1 + TF2 + TF3 to be activated; Gene B requires TF1 + TF4. A neuron expresses TF1+TF2+TF3 (→ Gene A on, Gene B off); a muscle cell expresses TF1+TF4 (→ Gene A off, Gene B on). With as few as 10 different TFs, the combinatorial possibilities (2^10 = 1024 combinations) can specify hundreds of distinct cell identities. The same promoter is interpreted differently depending on which TFs are present → same genome, different expression profiles. (ii) Epigenetic inheritance of chromatin states: once a cell commits to a lineage, its chromatin state (which regions are euchromatic vs. heterochromatic, DNA methylation at CpG islands, Polycomb/Trithorax marks on histones) is faithfully copied at each cell division. Maintenance methyltransferases (DNMT1) re-methylate hemimethylated DNA after replication. Histone modifications are self-perpetuating (Polycomb group proteins recognize their own mark → spread to newly deposited histones). This ensures that a liver cell's daughter cells remain liver cells and do not become neurons — the gene expression program is inherited epigenetically without changes in DNA sequence. 1 pt per mechanism correctly explained with cellular specificity logic.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression post-transcriptionally.
    (i) Describe the biogenesis of a miRNA, beginning with the miRNA gene and ending with the functional RISC (RNA-Induced Silencing Complex). Name the two key enzymes involved in miRNA processing.
    (ii) Explain the TWO molecular mechanisms by which miRNA-RISC can silence target mRNA expression. Specify the condition under which each mechanism predominates.

(b) Table 1 shows the results of an experiment in which a miRNA was introduced into cells expressing a reporter gene (luciferase). Cells were transfected with either a wild-type 3'UTR sequence or a mutant 3'UTR lacking the miRNA binding site.
    (i) Interpret the results. What do the data demonstrate about the role of the 3'UTR in miRNA-mediated silencing?
    (ii) The researcher observes that luciferase mRNA levels decrease by only 30% in wild-type cells, but luciferase protein decreases by 80%. Explain this discrepancy.

(c) Explain the role of the 5' cap (7-methylguanosine) and the 3' poly-A tail in mRNA stability and translation efficiency. For each, describe what happens to an mRNA that lacks that feature.

(d) Alternative splicing of pre-mRNA is a key mechanism for generating proteome diversity from a limited genome.
    (i) Explain how alternative splicing can generate multiple protein isoforms from a single gene. Describe one mechanism (exon skipping, alternative splice sites, or intron retention) and give a biological example.
    (ii) The gene DSCAM in Drosophila can produce more than 38,000 different protein isoforms through alternative splicing. Explain why this exceeds the number of genes in the entire Drosophila genome and what this reveals about the relationship between gene number and proteome complexity.
stimulus:
Table 1: miRNA reporter assay
Condition                        | Luciferase activity (relative units)
No miRNA, wild-type 3'UTR        |        100
miRNA added, wild-type 3'UTR     |         20
No miRNA, mutant 3'UTR           |        100
miRNA added, mutant 3'UTR        |         98

miRNA biogenesis summary:
• miRNA gene transcribed by RNA pol II → primary miRNA (pri-miRNA, hairpin structure)
• Drosha (nuclear RNase III) + DGCR8 → cleaves to ~70-nt pre-miRNA
• Exportin-5 → exported to cytoplasm
• Dicer (cytoplasmic RNase III) → cleaves pre-miRNA duplex → ~22-nt miRNA duplex
• One strand loaded into Argonaute (AGO) protein → RISC formed
• Guide strand targets complementary mRNA sequences (usually in 3'UTR)
title: APBIO-FRQ-L-022

criteria_json.minimum_fix: miRNA gene → Drosha/DGCR8 → pre-miRNA → exported → Dicer → ~22nt duplex → guide strand loaded into AGO → RISC. Two mechanisms: (1) perfect complementarity → AGO Slicer cleavage; (2) imperfect complementarity → translational repression + deadenylation/decay in P-bodies.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe miRNA biogenesis from gene to RISC; name Drosha and Dicer; explain two silencing mechanisms.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Biogenesis: (1) miRNA gene transcribed by RNA polymerase II → primary miRNA (pri-miRNA) with hairpin stem-loop structure; (2) Drosha (nuclear RNase III enzyme) + cofactor DGCR8/Pasha recognizes and cleaves the hairpin → releases ~70-nucleotide precursor miRNA (pre-miRNA) hairpin; (3) Exportin-5 exports pre-miRNA to cytoplasm; (4) Dicer (cytoplasmic RNase III enzyme) cleaves the loop → generates ~22-bp miRNA duplex; (5) One strand of the duplex (guide strand) is loaded into Argonaute (AGO) protein → forms RISC (RNA-Induced Silencing Complex); passenger strand is degraded. Two key enzymes: Drosha (nuclear processing) and Dicer (cytoplasmic duplex cleavage). (ii) Two silencing mechanisms: (A) mRNA cleavage: when miRNA has PERFECT or near-perfect complementarity to the target mRNA (common in plants; also in animal siRNA) → AGO's endonuclease (Slicer) activity cleaves the mRNA at the complementary site → mRNA degraded → no protein made. (B) Translational repression + mRNA destabilization: when miRNA has IMPERFECT complementarity (bulges, mismatches, typical for animal miRNAs) → RISC blocks ribosome translation without immediately cleaving → mRNA is also recruited to P-bodies (processing bodies) where it is deadenylated (poly-A tail removed), decapped, and degraded over time. 1 pt for biogenesis with Drosha/Dicer; 1 pt for both mechanisms with complementarity condition.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: 3'UTR required for silencing: miRNA binding site in 3'UTR necessary (mutant with no site shows no silencing); silencing is sequence-specific. Discrepancy: 30% mRNA reduction + 50% additional protein reduction = miRNA acts via both mRNA degradation AND translational repression simultaneously.
accepted_variants: both mRNA degradation and translational repression
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Interpret reporter assay data; explain mRNA vs protein level discrepancy.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Data interpretation: Wild-type 3'UTR + miRNA → 80% reduction in luciferase activity (100→20). Mutant 3'UTR + miRNA → no reduction (100→98; 2% variation is noise). Conclusion: the 3'UTR is required for miRNA-mediated silencing. The miRNA must bind to a complementary sequence in the 3'UTR to suppress translation or destabilize the mRNA. Removing the 3'UTR binding site (mutant) completely abolishes silencing → the 3'UTR sequence is the functional target of miRNA silencing. This demonstrates that miRNA silencing is sequence-specific (the miRNA must base-pair with the target 3'UTR) and that the 3'UTR is the cis-regulatory element mediating repression. (ii) mRNA decreases 30%, protein decreases 80% — discrepancy: miRNAs act by BOTH mRNA destabilization AND translational repression simultaneously. The 30% reduction in mRNA accounts for the mRNA degradation component. The additional 50% reduction in protein (beyond what the mRNA reduction would predict) reflects translational repression — ribosomes are blocked from efficiently translating the remaining mRNA. This demonstrates that translational repression is a major silencing mechanism independent of mRNA degradation. If silencing were purely through mRNA degradation, protein reduction would equal mRNA reduction. 1 pt for 3'UTR interpretation with mechanistic explanation; 1 pt for mRNA/protein discrepancy with translational repression.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: 5' cap: protects from 5'→3' exonuclease; recognized by eIF4E → ribosome recruitment; absence = rapid decay + no translation. Poly-A tail: PABP protects from 3'→5' exonuclease; interacts with eIF4G for mRNA circularization and ribosome recycling; absence = rapid deadenylation decay + reduced translation efficiency.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain roles of 5' cap and poly-A tail in mRNA stability and translation; predict consequences of absence.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: 5' cap (7-methylguanosine, m7G): Role in stability: the 5' cap protects the mRNA from 5'→3' exonuclease degradation; without the cap, 5'→3' exonucleases rapidly degrade the mRNA from the 5' end. Role in translation: the 5' cap is recognized by eIF4E (eukaryotic initiation factor 4E), which is part of the eIF4F cap-binding complex; eIF4E recruits the 43S ribosomal pre-initiation complex → ribosome scanning begins. Without 5' cap: mRNA is rapidly degraded; ribosomes cannot initiate translation efficiently → both stability and translation are severely impaired → essentially no protein produced. 3' poly-A tail (stretch of 100-250 adenine residues): Role in stability: poly-A tail + PABP (poly-A binding protein) protect the mRNA from 3'→5' exonuclease degradation. Deadenylation (removal of poly-A tail) is the first step in mRNA decay (deadenylation → decapping → degradation). Role in translation: PABP on the poly-A tail interacts with eIF4G at the 5' cap (circularization of mRNA) → promotes ribosome recycling and re-initiation → increases translation efficiency. Without poly-A tail: mRNA is rapidly degraded by exonucleases; translation efficiency reduced; reduced ribosome recycling. 1 pt per feature (5' cap + poly-A tail) with both stability AND translation roles + absence consequence.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Alternative splicing: different exon combinations → different protein isoforms from one gene. Exon skipping: spliceosome skips exons → shorter protein. Example: tropomyosin, DSCAM. DSCAM: 38,016 isoforms from 1 gene; Drosophila has 13,600 genes; more isoforms from one gene than total gene count; gene number ≠ proteome complexity.
accepted_variants: gene number does not equal proteome complexity
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain alternative splicing; describe one mechanism with example; interpret DSCAM numbers.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Alternative splicing: the same pre-mRNA can be spliced in different ways in different cell types or conditions → different exon combinations are included in the mature mRNA → different polypeptide sequences (isoforms) are produced from the same gene. Mechanism — exon skipping: the spliceosome can be directed (by SR proteins and other splicing regulators) to skip over certain exons → they are spliced out with the introns rather than retained → shorter mRNA with different protein sequence. Example: the human DSCAM gene (neuronal adhesion); or tropomyosin gene in muscle vs. non-muscle cells — same pre-mRNA, different exons included → tissue-specific protein isoforms with different functional properties. Alternative splice sites: a splice donor (5' splice site) or acceptor (3' splice site) can be used at one of multiple positions → variable-length exons included. Intron retention: an intron is retained in the mature mRNA → produces a protein with the intron-encoded sequence, if it does not contain a premature stop codon. (ii) DSCAM and proteome complexity: Drosophila has ~13,600 genes total; DSCAM alone can produce >38,000 protein isoforms through combinatorial alternative splicing of multiple variable exon clusters (exon 4: 12 variants, exon 6: 48 variants, exon 9: 33 variants, exon 17: 2 variants → 12×48×33×2 = 38,016 combinations). This single gene produces more protein variants than the entire gene count of the organism. This reveals that gene number does not equal proteome complexity — alternative splicing dramatically amplifies the coding capacity of a genome beyond what gene counting alone would suggest. The "one gene, one polypeptide" model is an oversimplification. 1 pt for alternative splicing mechanism with example; 1 pt for DSCAM interpretation with numbers and conclusion.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Epigenetic modifications alter gene expression without changing the DNA sequence.
    (i) Define epigenetic inheritance and explain how it differs from sequence-based genetic inheritance.
    (ii) Describe the two major classes of epigenetic modification (DNA methylation and histone modification), identifying a specific mark associated with gene silencing for each.
    (iii) Explain how DNA methylation at CpG island promoters causes gene silencing at the molecular level — describe the chain of events from methyl-CpG to transcriptional repression.

(b) Genomic imprinting results in the expression of only one parental allele for certain genes.
    (i) Using the Igf2/H19 imprinting locus as an example, explain how differential DNA methylation of the imprinting control region (ICR) leads to monoallelic expression.
    (ii) Explain why imprinting defects (such as loss of imprinting) can cause developmental disorders. Use Prader-Willi syndrome or Angelman syndrome as a specific example.
    (iii) Explain why most imprinted genes are involved in fetal growth and nutrient acquisition, citing the parental conflict hypothesis.

(c) Identical twins (MZ twins) are born with nearly identical genomes, yet they can develop different diseases as they age. Table 1 shows methylation data at four CpG sites in young (age 3) vs. older (age 50) MZ twin pairs.
    (i) Interpret the data: what trend do you observe in epigenetic similarity with age?
    (ii) Propose TWO mechanisms that could explain why MZ twins's epigenomes diverge over time.
    (iii) Explain whether these epigenetic differences would be passed to the twins' children.

(d) Environmental factors can alter epigenetic marks and potentially affect offspring. Describe ONE specific example of environmentally induced epigenetic change and its consequences, and explain the concept of transgenerational epigenetic inheritance — the mechanism by which epigenetic marks acquired in one generation can affect the next.
stimulus:
Table 1: Epigenome similarity (methylation correlation, r) in MZ twin pairs
CpG site | Similarity (r) at age 3 | Similarity (r) at age 50
    1    |         0.97            |          0.54
    2    |         0.95            |          0.61
    3    |         0.98            |          0.79
    4    |         0.94            |          0.42

Note: r = 1.0 means twins have identical methylation; r = 0 means no correlation.

Igf2/H19 locus:
• Maternal chromosome: ICR is UNMETHYLATED → CTCF insulator protein binds → blocks Igf2 enhancer from reaching Igf2 gene → Igf2 OFF; H19 is expressed
• Paternal chromosome: ICR is METHYLATED → CTCF cannot bind → Igf2 enhancer freely activates Igf2 → Igf2 ON; H19 is silenced by methylation
title: APBIO-FRQ-L-023

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Epigenetic: heritable gene expression changes without DNA sequence change. DNA methylation at CpG islands (5mC) silences; H3K9me3 or H3K27me3 histone marks silence. Chain: 5mC → MeCP2 binds → recruits HDACs → histone deacetylation → chromatin compact → transcription blocked.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Define epigenetic inheritance; describe DNA methylation and histone modification silencing marks; explain CpG → repression chain.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Epigenetic inheritance: heritable changes in gene expression that do not involve changes in the DNA sequence. Marks are on the chromatin (DNA or histones) rather than in the base sequence itself. Unlike mutations (sequence changes), epigenetic marks can in principle be reversed. They are passed from parent cell to daughter cells during mitosis; some cross generational boundaries. (ii) Two major classes + silencing marks: DNA methylation — addition of methyl group to cytosine at CpG dinucleotides, catalyzed by DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs). Mark associated with silencing: methylated CpG (5-methylcytosine, 5mC) at promoter CpG islands → gene repression. Histone modification — covalent modifications to N-terminal histone tails (methylation, acetylation, phosphorylation, ubiquitination). Mark associated with silencing: H3K9me3 (trimethylation of lysine 9 on histone H3) or H3K27me3 (added by Polycomb group proteins). (iii) Chain of events — DNA methylation → transcriptional repression: CpG islands are methylated (5mC) → methyl-binding proteins (MBDs, e.g., MeCP2) recognize and bind methylated CpG → MeCP2 recruits HDAC complexes → histone deacetylation → chromatin compaction → transcription factor binding inhibited OR DNA methylation directly blocks transcription factor binding (if TF binding site overlaps with CpG) → RNA pol II cannot be recruited → gene silenced. 1 pt for definition + two marks; 1 pt for methylation → repression chain.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: ICR unmethylated (maternal): CTCF binds → blocks Igf2 enhancer → Igf2 OFF, H19 ON. ICR methylated (paternal): CTCF absent → enhancer activates Igf2 → Igf2 ON. PWS: paternal 15q11 lost → paternal-expressed genes absent. Parental conflict: paternal alleles promote growth (Igf2); maternal alleles restrain (H19).
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain ICR/Igf2 imprinting mechanism; describe imprinting disorder; explain parental conflict hypothesis.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Igf2/H19 imprinting via ICR: Maternal chromosome: ICR is unmethylated → CTCF insulator protein binds the ICR → CTCF acts as a chromatin insulator/loop domain boundary → blocks the downstream enhancers from activating the upstream Igf2 gene → Igf2 is SILENCED on maternal chromosome. The enhancers instead activate H19 → H19 is expressed maternally. Paternal chromosome: ICR is methylated → CTCF cannot bind → insulator function abolished → downstream enhancers freely loop to and activate Igf2 → Igf2 is EXPRESSED paternally. H19 is also silenced on paternal chromosome (methylation spreads). Result: Igf2 is only expressed from the paternal copy (paternal imprinting). (ii) Imprinting disorder: Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS): caused by loss of paternally expressed genes on chromosome 15q11-q13 (typically deletion of paternal 15q11-q13 OR maternal uniparental disomy where both copies of 15 come from mother → only maternal-imprinted [silenced] copies present → critical paternal genes not expressed). Features: hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity, intellectual disability. The genes affected include SNRPN (paternally expressed). OR: Angelman syndrome: loss of maternally expressed UBE3A in the same region. (iii) Parental conflict hypothesis (David Haig): in species where offspring of one female can have different fathers, each parent's genes are "in conflict." Paternal genes maximize growth of current offspring (extracts maximum resources from mother) → paternal alleles promote growth factors (Igf2). Maternal genes favor restraint (protect mother's ability to have future offspring with other mates) → maternal alleles suppress growth or act via growth inhibitors. This predicts that paternally imprinted genes (maternally expressed) tend to limit growth; maternally imprinted genes (paternally expressed) tend to promote growth — matches Igf2 (paternal, growth promoter) and H19 (maternal, growth inhibitor). 1 pt for ICR mechanism; 1 pt for disorder or parental conflict.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Trend: high similarity at age 3 (r ~0.96), lower at age 50 (r ~0.59 average) — epigenomes diverge with age. Mechanisms: (1) different environmental exposures; (2) stochastic replication errors in DNMT1 copying. Transgenerational: most epigenetic marks erased during gametogenesis/early embryo (demethylation); most somatic marks not inherited; exceptions: imprinted regions, some transposons.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Interpret MZ twin methylation divergence data; propose mechanisms; explain transgenerational transmission.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Trend: at age 3, MZ twins have very high epigenetic similarity (r = 0.94–0.98, nearly identical methylation patterns). At age 50, similarity has decreased substantially (r = 0.42–0.79). The twins' epigenomes diverge progressively with age — epigenetic differences accumulate over a lifetime despite identical DNA sequences. This demonstrates that epigenetic marks are influenced by environmental and stochastic factors, not solely genotype. (ii) Two mechanisms for divergence: (1) Different environmental exposures: different diets, smoking, stress, exercise, toxin exposure → different signals reaching cells → different DNMT or TET enzyme activity → different methylation patterns acquired at specific CpG sites. (2) Stochastic (random) epigenetic errors during DNA replication: during each cell division, maintenance methyltransferase (DNMT1) copies methylation patterns onto daughter strands, but errors occur at low frequency (~1/1000 CpGs per division); over millions of cell divisions across 50 years, these errors accumulate differently in each twin → diverging epigenomes. (iii) Transgenerational transmission: epigenetic marks are largely RESET (erased) during gametogenesis and early embryogenesis (global demethylation waves). Most methylation is cleared in primordial germ cells and re-established based on sex. For most loci: no, these somatic epigenetic differences would NOT be inherited by children. However, imprinted regions and certain transposable element-associated loci escape demethylation and can be transmitted. Examples of true transgenerational epigenetic inheritance in mammals remain controversial but include agouti mouse coat color via methylation of an IAP element. 1 pt for data trend interpretation; 1 pt for two mechanisms OR transgenerational explanation.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Dutch Hunger Winter: prenatal famine → altered IGF2 methylation in offspring → increased disease risk in adulthood (obesity, CVD, schizophrenia). Transgenerational inheritance: marks must escape two demethylation waves (PGC reprogramming + post-fertilization). Escape mechanisms: IAP transposons retain methylation; imprinted loci protected; histone marks re-established.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe one environmental epigenetic change; explain transgenerational epigenetic inheritance mechanism.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Environmental example: Dutch Hunger Winter (1944-45): Dutch women pregnant during Nazi food blockade (severe caloric restriction ~500 cal/day for months) gave birth to children who, as adults, had altered methylation at the IGF2 imprinting control region, higher rates of obesity, cardiovascular disease, schizophrenia, and type 2 diabetes compared to siblings conceived before or after the famine. The prenatal nutrient restriction altered DNMT activity during critical developmental windows → different methylation patterns established at key metabolic loci → these patterns influenced lifelong gene expression and metabolism. Other acceptable examples: maternal stress → glucocorticoid receptor methylation changes in offspring; cigarette smoke → specific methylation changes. Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance mechanism: For epigenetic marks to be inherited across generations, they must escape the two waves of epigenetic reprogramming: (1) in the primordial germ cells (PGC reprogramming — demethylation of most of the genome); (2) after fertilization (post-fertilization demethylation and re-methylation). A mark that survives both waves in the germline will be transmitted to offspring. Mechanisms of escape: (A) Certain transposable elements (like IAP retrotransposons in mice) retain methylation through reprogramming; (B) Imprinted loci have protected methylation marks; (C) Histone modifications (H3K9me3, H3K27me3) on some loci are reestablished post-fertilization using residual histone information. Consequence: offspring of stressed/nutrition-deprived parents can inherit altered metabolic programming without any DNA sequence change. 1 pt for specific environmental example with mechanism; 1 pt for transgenerational mechanism with at least one escape mechanism named.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) The Galápagos Islands are home to 14 species of Darwin's finches, all descended from a common South American ancestor that colonized the islands about 2–3 million years ago.
    (i) Explain allopatric speciation and apply it to the adaptive radiation of Galápagos finches. Describe the sequence of events from the original colonization to the presence of multiple species on the same island.
    (ii) Explain the role of natural selection in shaping beak morphology across finch species. Use the concept of character displacement to explain why sympatric species on the same island tend to have more different beak sizes than allopatric populations of the same species on different islands.

(b) Reproductive isolating mechanisms prevent gene flow between species. Classify each of the following as prezygotic or postzygotic and give the specific mechanism name:
    (i) Two species of frogs breed in the same pond but one breeds in early spring and one in late spring.
    (ii) A horse and a donkey can mate and produce a mule, but mules are sterile.
    (iii) Eastern and western meadowlarks look nearly identical but have different songs — females only respond to their own species' song.
    (iv) Two species of plants have flowers adapted to different pollinators (bumblebees vs. hummingbirds).

(c) Sympatric speciation can occur without geographic isolation.
    (i) Explain how polyploidy can cause sympatric speciation in plants. Give a specific type (allopolyploidy or autopolyploidy) and describe how it creates immediate reproductive isolation.
    (ii) Explain why polyploid speciation is much more common in plants than in animals.
    (iii) Modern bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) is a hexaploid (6n = 42). Explain how it likely arose from hybridization events between ancestral diploid (2n=14) species.

(d) The biological species concept (BSC) defines species as groups of actually or potentially interbreeding populations that are reproductively isolated from other groups. Describe TWO limitations of the BSC and explain which alternative species concept (morphological, phylogenetic, or ecological) best addresses each limitation.
stimulus:
Darwin's finch diversity on the Galápagos:
• Ground finches (Geospiza): thick beaks, crush seeds of varying hardness
• Tree finches (Camarhynchus): grip-and-pry beaks, eat insects in woody vegetation
• Warbler finch (Certhidea): slender beak, glean tiny insects
• Woodpecker finch (Camarhynchus pallidus): uses cactus spine as tool to extract insects

Character displacement data:
Beak depth (mm) of Geospiza species:
Island type              | G. fortis | G. fuliginosa
Allopatric (each alone)  |  11.0 mm  |   10.5 mm
Sympatric (together)     |  13.5 mm  |    8.0 mm

Polyploidy examples:
• Allopolyploidy: two different species hybridize → combine both genome sets → new species
• Bread wheat = T. urartu (AA, 2n=14) × Aegilops speltoides (BB, 2n=14) → T. turgidum (AABB, 4n=28, emmer wheat) × Aegilops tauschii (DD, 2n=14) → T. aestivum (AABBDD, 6n=42, bread wheat)
title: APBIO-FRQ-L-024

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Allopatric speciation: geographic isolation → independent evolution → reproductive isolation. Finches: South American ancestor → colonized different islands → different selection pressures → beak divergence → new species → secondary sympatry. Character displacement: sympatric species diverge in beak size due to competition; data shows beak depths more different when together (13.5 vs 8.0 mm) than when apart (11.0 vs 10.5 mm).
accepted_variants: beak size data sympatric vs allopatric
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain allopatric speciation and Galápagos finch adaptive radiation; explain character displacement.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Allopatric speciation: speciation driven by geographic isolation. Population split by a physical barrier → separated populations cannot interbreed → genetic drift, mutation, and differential natural selection act independently on each population → populations diverge genetically → after sufficient time, populations are reproductively isolated even if geographic barrier is removed. Applied to Galápagos finches: (1) Original founder population from South America colonized one island; (2) Some individuals dispersed (over-water colonization) to other islands → geographic isolation on different islands; (3) Different island environments (food types, competitors, predators) applied different natural selection pressures → beaks and body size diverged on each island; (4) Eventually, sufficient genetic divergence → speciation; (5) Secondary colonization events brought different species back to same island (sympatry) → by this time, reproductive isolation had evolved → no interbreeding. This radiation produced multiple ecological niches occupied by different finch species (adaptive radiation). (ii) Character displacement: when two species co-occur (sympatry), competition for the same resource (e.g., medium seeds) intensifies. Natural selection favors individuals in each species that specialize on DIFFERENT resources → divergent selection → beak sizes diverge. Data: G. fortis and G. fuliginosa have almost identical beak depths when alone (11.0 vs. 10.5 mm) but diverge dramatically when co-occurring (13.5 vs. 8.0 mm). This competitive release of niche differentiation is character displacement. 1 pt for allopatric speciation sequence applied to finches; 1 pt for character displacement with data.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: (i) Temporal isolation (prezygotic). (ii) Hybrid sterility (postzygotic). (iii) Behavioral/ethological isolation (prezygotic). (iv) Mechanical or ecological isolation (prezygotic).
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Classify four isolation mechanisms as prezygotic or postzygotic with specific names.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Frogs breeding at different times: PREZYGOTIC — temporal isolation. Gametes of the two species never meet because they breed at different times. (ii) Horse × donkey → sterile mule: POSTZYGOTIC — hybrid sterility. The species can mate and produce viable offspring but the offspring (mule) are sterile (2n = 63, cannot complete meiosis due to unequal chromosome number → no viable gametes). (iii) Meadowlarks with species-specific songs: PREZYGOTIC — behavioral (ethological) isolation. Female only responds to conspecific male song → mating behavior does not occur between species → gametes never meet. (iv) Plants with different pollinators: PREZYGOTIC — mechanical isolation (some texts: ecological isolation). If pollinators are the vector for pollen transfer and each species uses a different pollinator, pollen cannot be transferred between species → no fertilization possible. Alternatively classified as ecological isolation if the mechanism is broader than just flower morphology. Accept either classification with justification. Award 0.5 pt per correct classification and mechanism name, max 2 pts.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Allopolyploidy: hybrid of two species → sterile (no homologs) → chromosome doubling → homologs present → fertile polyploid; cannot mate with parental diploids (different ploidy) → immediate reproductive isolation without geographic separation. Plants: can self-fertilize, vegetative propagation, tolerant of ploidy changes. Bread wheat: T. urartu (AA) × Aegilops (BB) → AABB emmer × Aegilops (DD) → AABBDD hexaploid (6n=42).
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain polyploid sympatric speciation; explain plant-animal difference; explain bread wheat hexaploidy.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Allopolyploidy: two different species hybridize → hybrid inherits one genome set from each parent species → hybrid is typically sterile because chromosomes cannot pair at meiosis. If chromosome doubling occurs (spontaneously or induced) → the allopolyploid has homologs for all chromosomes and can produce viable gametes. Immediate reproductive isolation: the new allopolyploid can mate only with itself or other same-ploidy individuals; it cannot successfully mate with either parent species. (ii) More common in plants: plants can self-fertilize and often reproduce asexually or vegetatively, so a rare polyploid can persist. Animals are less tolerant of ploidy changes. (iii) Bread wheat likely arose through two successive hybridization-and-doubling events: a diploid AA species hybridized with a diploid BB species to form a sterile AB hybrid; chromosome doubling produced fertile AABB emmer wheat; later, AABB emmer hybridized with a DD species; another chromosome-doubling event produced AABBDD hexaploid bread wheat.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Limitation 1: does not apply to asexual organisms (bacteria) or fossils. Alternative: Phylogenetic species concept — uses synapomorphies and monophyly; applies to any organism regardless of reproduction. Limitation 2: cannot handle occasional hybridization between distinct species. Alternative: Ecological species concept — species = distinct ecological niche; hybridization allowed as long as ecological roles remain separate.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe two BSC limitations and best alternative concepts.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Limitation 1: The BSC cannot be applied to asexual (clonal) organisms or fossil species. Bacteria reproduce asexually and undergo horizontal gene transfer — the concept of interbreeding populations does not apply. Fossils cannot be observed to interbreed. Best alternative: Phylogenetic (evolutionary) species concept — defines a species as the smallest monophyletic group diagnosable by shared derived characters (synapomorphies). Can be applied to asexual organisms and fossils using molecular or morphological data; based on evolutionary history rather than mating. Limitation 2: The BSC cannot handle situations where two populations can occasionally interbreed (hybridize) but remain distinct. Many plant species (e.g., oaks) hybridize frequently yet remain recognizable species. Also, ring species (like Ensatina salamanders in California) produce chains where adjacent populations interbreed but terminal populations do not. Best alternative: Ecological species concept — defines a species as a lineage occupying a distinct ecological niche (adaptive zone). Species remain distinct because they occupy different ecological roles; limited hybridization does not dissolve species boundaries as long as they maintain distinct ecological niches. This works for hybridizing plant species that occupy different habitats. 1 pt per limitation + matching alternative concept with reasoning.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Figure 1 shows the results of a morphological analysis of five species (A–E). Shared derived characters (synapomorphies) are listed in the matrix.
    (i) Define synapomorphy and explain why it is more informative for constructing phylogenies than symplesiomorphy (a shared ancestral character).
    (ii) Using the character matrix data, construct the most parsimonious cladogram for species A–E. Identify the outgroup and explain your reasoning.
    (iii) Explain what "most parsimonious" means in phylogenetic analysis, and why parsimony is preferred when building cladograms.

(b) The molecular clock hypothesis proposes that DNA sequences accumulate mutations at an approximately constant rate over time.
    (i) Explain the molecular basis for the molecular clock — why do neutral mutations accumulate at a relatively constant rate?
    (ii) Cytochrome b is commonly used as a molecular clock gene. Table 1 shows the percentage sequence differences in cytochrome b between pairs of primate species, and known fossil divergence dates for two of the pairs. Use the data to estimate the divergence time for the third pair (Human–Gorilla) and show your work.
    (iii) Describe TWO reasons why the molecular clock is not perfectly constant and can give inaccurate divergence estimates.

(c) Convergent evolution can mislead phylogenetic analysis based on morphology.
    (i) Explain how analogous structures (homoplasy) can cause morphological phylogenies to incorrectly group unrelated organisms together.
    (ii) Explain why molecular phylogenies are generally considered more reliable than morphological phylogenies for resolving deep evolutionary relationships. Give a specific example of a case where molecular data overturned a morphologically derived phylogeny.

(d) A researcher wants to determine whether two geographically isolated populations of mice are separate species or subspecies. Describe THREE lines of evidence the researcher could collect and explain how each line of evidence would contribute to a decision.
stimulus:
Character matrix (1 = character present, 0 = absent):
               | Char 1 | Char 2 | Char 3 | Char 4
Species A      |   0    |   0    |   0    |   0    (outgroup)
Species B      |   1    |   0    |   0    |   0
Species C      |   1    |   1    |   0    |   0
Species D      |   1    |   1    |   1    |   0
Species E      |   1    |   1    |   1    |   1

Table 1: Molecular clock data — Cytochrome b sequence divergence
Species pair         | % sequence difference | Known divergence (Mya)
Human–Chimpanzee     |       2.5%            |      5-7 Mya
Rhesus–Baboon        |       5.4%            |     10-12 Mya
Human–Gorilla        |       2.1%            |      ?

Calculation setup: Assume 1% cytochrome b divergence ≈ 2 Mya
(calibrated from the known pairs above)
title: APBIO-FRQ-L-025

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Synapomorphy = shared derived character at a node. More informative than symplesiomorphy (ancestral, too broadly shared). Cladogram: A=outgroup; (B,(C,(D,E))). Each character evolved once → 4 total steps → most parsimonious. Parsimony: fewest evolutionary changes = most likely tree; minimizes ad hoc convergences.
accepted_variants: cladogram B C D E nested
B sister to C D E
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Define synapomorphy; construct cladogram from matrix; explain parsimony.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Synapomorphy: a shared derived character state that evolved in the common ancestor of a clade and is present in all members of that clade but not in the outgroup. It is more informative than symplesiomorphy because a symplesiomorphy is a character inherited from a remote common ancestor shared by many taxa (e.g., vertebral column in all vertebrates does not help distinguish mammals from reptiles). A synapomorphy is diagnostic for a specific node (clade) in the tree — it unites only the taxa that inherited it from their most recent common ancestor. (ii) Cladogram from matrix: Species A has no derived characters → outgroup (the ancestral state reference). Character 1 is shared by B, C, D, E → groups B+C+D+E as a clade (sister to A). Character 2 shared by C, D, E → groups C+D+E as a nested clade. Character 3 shared by D, E → groups D+E as sister. Character 4 only in E → autapomorphy of E. Cladogram: A is outgroup; sister group = (B + (C + (D + E))). Most parsimonious tree requires 4 evolutionary events (one for each character, each evolving once). (iii) Most parsimonious means the tree that requires the fewest evolutionary changes (fewest independent gains or losses of characters) to explain the data. Parsimony is preferred because it minimizes ad hoc hypotheses; Occam's razor — the simplest explanation (fewest events) is the best starting hypothesis; convergent evolution (homoplasy) is relatively rare, so the tree requiring the fewest evolutionary steps is most likely to reflect true evolutionary history. 1 pt for synapomorphy definition + cladogram topology; 1 pt for parsimony explanation.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Clock mechanism: neutral mutations accumulate by drift at rate = neutral mutation rate; constant per unit time because no selection acts. Human-Gorilla: 2.1% × 2 Mya/% = ~4.2 Mya. Limitations: (1) generation time effect (short-generation organisms run clock faster); (2) purifying selection slows rate in conserved genes; positive selection speeds it locally.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain molecular clock mechanism; calculate Human-Gorilla divergence; describe two limitations.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Molecular basis of clock: the molecular clock reflects the accumulation of neutral mutations (mutations that do not affect fitness) at a rate determined by the mutation rate of DNA replication. Because neutral mutations are not subject to natural selection (neither advantageous nor deleterious), their accumulation rate is primarily determined by the neutral mutation rate (errors per nucleotide per generation) × generation time, both of which are relatively stable within a lineage. Genetic drift is the primary force fixing neutral alleles; fixation rate of neutral alleles = neutral mutation rate (by drift theory). Therefore sequences diverge at an approximately constant rate per unit time for neutral sites. (ii) Human-Gorilla calculation: Calibration from known pairs: Human-Chimp: 2.5% / 6 Mya midpoint = ~0.42%/Mya; Rhesus-Baboon: 5.4% / 11 Mya midpoint = ~0.49%/Mya. Using the provided conversion: 1% divergence ≈ 2 Mya. Human-Gorilla: 2.1% × 2 Mya/1% = 4.2 Mya. Estimated divergence: ~4.2 million years ago. (Actual data supports ~6-8 Mya; students should use the provided calibration, not outside knowledge.) (iii) Two limitations: (1) Generation time effect: organisms with shorter generation times have higher absolute mutation rates per year (more cell divisions per year → more replication errors). A mouse molecular clock runs faster than an elephant's. (2) Natural selection affects rate: protein-coding regions under strong purifying selection accumulate synonymous mutations faster than nonsynonymous → clock rates vary by functional constraint. Genes under positive selection accumulate changes faster in some lineages than others. Also: variation in DNA repair efficiency, metabolic rate (oxidative damage), and substitution rate heterogeneity among sites. Any two valid reasons accepted. 1 pt for neutral mutation rate explanation; 1 pt for calculation + 2 limitations.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Homoplasy: analogous structures evolve independently (wings in birds/bats/insects); morphological analysis treats as synapomorphy → incorrect grouping. Molecular more reliable: many more characters; statistical models; neutral sites. Example: birds (Aves) are nested within Reptilia with crocodilians as sister — molecular overturned the traditional bird/reptile division. Or: whales sister to hippos.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain how homoplasy misleads morphological phylogenies; explain molecular reliability; give example of overturned phylogeny.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Homoplasy: analogous structures evolve independently in unrelated lineages due to similar selective pressures (convergent evolution) or can be lost in parallel. In morphological phylogenetics, if two unrelated species share an analogous structure (not inherited from common ancestor), a morphological analysis treating it as a synapomorphy would incorrectly group them together. Example: wings evolved independently in birds, bats, and insects — a morphological analysis using "wings" as a character would incorrectly cluster these groups as close relatives. Streamlined body shape evolved independently in dolphins, sharks, and ichthyosaurs. (ii) Molecular phylogenies more reliable: DNA sequences have far more characters (billions of nucleotide positions) than morphological characters (dozens to hundreds), reducing the impact of any single homoplastic character; synonymous nucleotide changes at 3rd codon positions are nearly neutral and abundant → better molecular clock; molecular data allows statistical methods (maximum likelihood, Bayesian) that model the probability of change at each site and correct for multiple hits (saturation). Specific example: traditional morphology grouped birds with reptiles (classifying them separately as "Reptilia" + "Aves"); molecular phylogenetics conclusively showed birds ARE reptiles — specifically the sister group to crocodilians (archosaurs). Another example: traditional morphology placed whales with other aquatic animals; molecular data shows whales are most closely related to even-toed ungulates (hippopotamus is the closest living relative). 1 pt for homoplasy misleading mechanism; 1 pt for molecular reliability + specific example.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Three evidence types: (1) Genetic: FST, fixed allele differences, phylogenetic monophyly; (2) Morphological: diagnostic fixed morphological characters; (3) Behavioral/reproductive isolation: mate preference experiments or contact zone interbreeding. Higher divergence and isolation → species; partial divergence → subspecies.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe three lines of evidence for species vs. subspecies determination.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Three lines of evidence: (1) Genetic/molecular: sequence DNA from both populations (multiple loci — mitochondrial DNA, nuclear microsatellites, or whole-genome SNPs). Calculate FST (genetic differentiation index) between populations. High FST (>0.25) suggests strong genetic isolation; distinct alleles fixed in each population → distinct evolutionary lineages. Species-level divergence may show fixed differences at multiple loci; subspecies would show partial differentiation. Phylogenetic species concept: if populations are monophyletic (each is a clade with respect to the other), they qualify as separate species. (2) Morphological: measure multiple quantitative morphological traits (body size, skull dimensions, pelage color/pattern). Test for statistical differences between populations. Greater and more consistent morphological divergence supports species status; slight average differences support subspecies. Identify diagnostic characters (characters that are 100% fixed as different between populations). (3) Behavioral/reproductive isolation (common garden or contact zone): if the populations are allopatric, identify contact zones where the ranges meet (or create in the lab). Test whether individuals recognize, court, and mate with individuals from the other population. Use acoustic, chemical, and visual cue experiments. If females show significant mate preference for conspecifics, reproductive isolation is evolving → species. If free interbreeding occurs in contact zones, they are likely subspecies. 1 pt per two evidence types with correct reasoning, max 2 pts.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Genetic drift is a random change in allele frequencies due to chance events.
    (i) Explain the bottleneck effect and how it differs mechanistically from natural selection as a cause of reduced genetic diversity.
    (ii) A cheetah population experienced a severe bottleneck ~10,000 years ago. Today, all cheetahs are nearly genetically identical and can accept skin grafts from any other cheetah without rejection. Explain why this is remarkable and what it reveals about the level of genetic diversity in the cheetah population.
    (iii) The northern elephant seal population dropped to ~20 individuals in the 1890s due to hunting and has since recovered to ~170,000 individuals. Despite this large census size, genetic diversity remains very low. Explain this paradox using the concept of effective population size (Ne).

(b) Inbreeding is common in small populations and can lead to inbreeding depression.
    (i) Explain the molecular mechanism of inbreeding depression. Include the roles of heterozygosity, recessive deleterious alleles, and the purging hypothesis.
    (ii) Table 1 shows genetic data for two Florida panther populations. Explain what the data indicate about genetic diversity and predict the fitness consequences for Population B.

(c) A conservation manager introduces 8 Texas pumas (a different subspecies) into the Florida panther population as a genetic rescue strategy.
    (i) Explain the mechanism by which genetic rescue increases fitness in an inbred population.
    (ii) Predict TWO risks of this genetic rescue strategy and explain why each is a concern.
    (iii) Five years after the introduction, the manager measures the heterozygosity and cub survival rate of offspring of puma-panther crosses versus pure panther offspring. Predict the outcome and the mechanism.

(d) Conservation biologists use the concept of minimum viable population (MVP) to determine the minimum population size needed to maintain a population long-term.
    (i) Define the effective population size (Ne) and explain why Ne is almost always much smaller than census size (N).
    (ii) Describe TWO genetic risks that threaten populations below the MVP threshold.
    (iii) Explain why maintaining genetic diversity is important for a species' long-term survival in a changing environment.
stimulus:
Table 1: Florida panther genetic data
                      | Population A (1994, before rescue) | Population B (captive, inbred)
Mean heterozygosity   |         0.04                       |         0.01
Allelic richness      |         3.2 alleles/locus          |         1.8 alleles/locus
Major histocompatibility complex (MHC) alleles | 2 | 1
Kinked tail frequency |         50%                        |         85%
Cryptic testes freq.  |         55%                        |         90%

Cheetah fact: In lab skin graft experiments, cheetah-to-cheetah skin grafts survive indefinitely. Human-to-human grafts from unrelated donors are rejected within days.

Genetic rescue context: 8 Texas pumas released into Florida in 1995; subsequent panther population showed:
• Increased heterozygosity
• Increased cub survival from 20% to 50%
• Reduced frequency of morphological defects (kinked tails, cryptic testes)
title: APBIO-FRQ-L-026

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Bottleneck = random loss of alleles regardless of fitness (not directional). Selection = directional loss/gain based on fitness. Cheetah skin grafts: MHC diversity near zero → all cheetahs same MHC → no immune rejection. Elephant seal Ne paradox: current Ne still reflects the ~20 bottleneck founders; census size recovery does not restore genetic diversity lost during bottleneck.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain bottleneck vs. selection; interpret cheetah skin grafts; explain elephant seal paradox with Ne.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Bottleneck vs. selection: Bottleneck = random sampling event; when a population is dramatically reduced, only a small random sample of the original gene pool survives. Rare alleles are lost by chance regardless of their fitness value — loss is not based on phenotypic benefit/cost. Natural selection, by contrast, changes allele frequencies in a direction determined by fitness — it increases frequency of beneficial alleles and decreases frequency of harmful alleles. Bottleneck reduces diversity non-directionally (random alleles fixed or lost); selection changes diversity directionally (adaptive alleles favored). Result: a post-bottleneck population has low diversity across the genome, including at immune loci; post-selection population has adaptive alleles at high frequency but may retain diversity at neutral loci. (ii) Cheetah skin grafts: MHC (Major Histocompatibility Complex) genes determine self/non-self recognition in the immune system. Normally, unrelated individuals of the same species differ at MHC loci → immune cells detect MHC mismatch → reject transplanted tissue. Cheetahs can accept grafts from any other cheetah because the bottleneck reduced MHC diversity to near-zero — all cheetahs carry essentially the same MHC alleles → no immune mismatch → graft accepted. This reveals extreme genetic homogeneity; cheetahs are nearly as similar to each other as identical twins. This makes them vulnerable to epidemics. (iii) Elephant seal Ne paradox: Census size N = 170,000, but effective population size Ne was ~20 during the bottleneck. Ne is based on the breeding individuals and variance in reproductive success; the genetic diversity in the current population reflects the diversity that existed when Ne was at its minimum (~20 breeders). A population recovered from a recent bottleneck retains the low diversity of its bottleneck founders regardless of census size — recovery of numbers does not restore genetic variation lost during the bottleneck; only mutation over generations and gene flow can restore it. 1 pt per two sub-points correctly explained.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Inbreeding depression: increased homozygosity exposes recessive deleterious alleles → reduced fitness. Purging removes most severe alleles. Population B: lower heterozygosity, fewer alleles, 1 MHC allele, 85-90% morphological defects → predicted reduced fertility (cryptic testes), possible locomotion issues, severe disease susceptibility from single MHC allele.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain inbreeding depression mechanism; interpret panther data; predict fitness consequences.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Inbreeding depression mechanism: inbreeding (mating between relatives) increases the probability that an individual inherits the same allele from both parents (identity by descent) → increased homozygosity genome-wide. Most deleterious alleles are recessive and rare in outbred populations — they are mostly present in heterozygous individuals where the dominant allele masks the effect. In inbred individuals, probability of homozygosity for recessive deleterious alleles increases dramatically → deleterious alleles exposed → reduced fitness (growth, fertility, survival, immunity). Purging hypothesis: in populations with prolonged inbreeding, the most severely deleterious recessive alleles may be "purged" — exposed in homozygotes and eliminated by natural selection. Mildly deleterious alleles are less efficiently purged because they have small fitness effects. (ii) Data interpretation for Population B: Population B has lower heterozygosity (0.01 vs. 0.04), fewer alleles/locus (1.8 vs. 3.2), only 1 MHC allele (vs. 2), and higher frequency of morphological defects (kinked tail 85% vs. 50%; cryptic testes 90% vs. 55%). This indicates severe inbreeding. Predicted fitness consequences: high frequency of cryptic (undescended) testes → reduced male fertility → lower reproductive success; kinked tails (morphological defect, possibly spinal) → possible locomotion impairment in a predatory species; only 1 MHC allele → cannot recognize a diverse pathogen array → high susceptibility to infectious disease; low MHC diversity → poor immune response → epidemic vulnerability. Overall: inbreeding depression → low cub survival, poor reproductive performance, disease susceptibility.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Rescue mechanism: outbred immigrants → heterozygosity → recessive alleles masked → heterosis/hybrid vigor; new MHC alleles → better immunity. Risks: (1) outbreeding depression (maladapted Texas alleles in Florida); (2) genetic swamping (Florida genome replaced). Hybrid offspring: higher heterozygosity → heterosis → better survival, fewer defects; complementation masks deleterious recessive alleles.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain genetic rescue mechanism; predict two risks; predict outcome of hybrid vs. pure offspring.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Genetic rescue mechanism: introducing individuals from an outbred population provides new alleles not present in the inbred population.
