Crosses between inbred resident and outbred immigrant → offspring are heterozygous at many loci where residents are homozygous → dominant alleles mask previously exposed recessive deleterious alleles → fitness increases (heterosis/hybrid vigor). Also restores functional diversity at immune loci (MHC) → improved pathogen resistance. Effectively reverses inbreeding depression without changing the genome. (ii) Two risks: (1) Outbreeding depression: the introduced subspecies may carry alleles adapted to different Texas environments (different climate, prey, pathogens) that are maladaptive in Florida conditions; co-adapted gene complexes may be disrupted by hybridization → offspring less adapted to local environment than pure residents. (2) Genetic swamping: if Texas pumas are introduced in large numbers and have higher fitness (due to heterosis), their alleles could eventually replace the Florida panther genome entirely → the unique local adaptations and genetic identity of the Florida subspecies could be lost → "genetic extinction" even if population persists. (iii) Hybrid vs. pure offspring prediction: Hybrid offspring (puma × panther) will have higher heterozygosity than pure panther offspring → expect higher cub survival, fewer morphological defects (kinked tails, cryptic testes), better immune function. This is heterosis (hybrid vigor) — the mechanism is complementation: the Texas puma alleles complement the Florida panther's recessive deleterious alleles, so the harmful homozygous recessive phenotypes are not expressed. Data from the 1995 introduction confirms: cub survival increased from 20% to 50%; defects declined dramatically. 1 pt for rescue mechanism; 1 pt for two risks OR hybrid prediction.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Ne = effective population size (ideal population with same genetic drift rate). Ne < N due to: unequal sex ratio, variance in reproductive success, past bottlenecks (harmonic mean). Two genetic risks: inbreeding depression + genetic erosion (drift removes adaptive variation). Diversity for future: provides variation for selection to act on new challenges (disease, climate) → adaptation and survival.
accepted_variants: Ne ideal population genetic drift rate
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Define Ne; explain why Ne < N; describe two genetic risks below MVP; explain diversity for future change.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Effective population size (Ne): the size of an ideal panmictic population (random mating, equal sex ratio, equal reproductive success, no migration) that would experience the same rate of genetic drift (allele frequency change) as the actual population. Ne is almost always much smaller than census size N because: unequal sex ratio (e.g., 1 breeding male + 99 females → Ne ≈ 4, not 100); variance in reproductive success (dominant individuals breed much more than others → many individuals contribute no offspring → only a fraction effectively breed); fluctuating population sizes (Ne is dominated by the lowest N across generations — harmonic mean of past Ns); overlapping generations and age structure; geographic subdivision reducing effective breeding population. Typical Ne/N ratio in wildlife: 0.10–0.11. (ii) Two genetic risks below MVP: (1) Inbreeding depression: small populations have high relatedness → mating between relatives → homozygosity → recessive deleterious alleles exposed → reduced fitness (fertility, immunity, survival). (2) Loss of adaptive potential (genetic erosion): genetic drift is strongest in small populations → neutral and mildly beneficial alleles lost by chance → allelic diversity decreases → population has fewer alleles available to respond to new selection pressures (disease outbreaks, climate change, new predators) → extinction risk increases. (iii) Genetic diversity for future change: a population with high genetic diversity has more heritable variation → when the environment changes (new pathogen, climate shift, habitat alteration), some individuals may already carry pre-existing alleles that confer survival advantage → natural selection can rapidly increase frequency of those alleles → population adapts and survives. A genetically uniform population (after bottleneck) has no variation for selection to act on → cannot adapt → high extinction risk. Genetic diversity = evolutionary raw material for adaptation. 1 pt per two of the four sub-parts correctly explained.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Trace the pathway of a single carbon atom as it cycles through the major components of the carbon cycle. Begin with CO₂ in the atmosphere and describe at least FOUR steps in the cycle, identifying the biological processes and organisms involved at each step. Include both the fast (biological) and slow (geological) components of the carbon cycle.

(b) Atmospheric CO₂ concentration has increased from ~280 ppm (pre-industrial) to over 420 ppm today, largely due to burning fossil fuels.
    (i) Using Figure 1 data (atmospheric CO₂ and global temperature, 1850–2024), describe the relationship between CO₂ and global temperature. Explain the greenhouse effect mechanism at the molecular level.
    (ii) Explain why burning fossil fuels disrupts the carbon cycle at both short-term (decades) and geological-time (millions of years) timescales.
    (iii) Explain a positive feedback loop involving the carbon cycle and climate change. Use a specific example (permafrost thaw, ocean warming, or deforestation) and explain why positive feedback makes climate change self-reinforcing.

(c) When CO₂ dissolves in seawater, it forms carbonic acid.
    (i) Write the complete chemical reaction sequence from CO₂ dissolution to hydrogen ion release. Explain how this leads to ocean acidification.
    (ii) Describe TWO specific consequences of ocean acidification for marine organisms, explaining the biological mechanism of each effect.
    (iii) Predict the effect of ocean acidification on the ocean's ability to absorb future CO₂ emissions, and explain the feedback mechanism.

(d) A land manager must choose between three strategies to maximize long-term carbon storage in a 1000-hectare forest. Evaluate each strategy using your knowledge of carbon cycling:
    Strategy 1: Clear-cut the forest and plant fast-growing tree monocultures
    Strategy 2: Selectively harvest mature trees and maintain diverse natural forest structure
    Strategy 3: Protect old-growth forest as a carbon reserve and never harvest
    Recommend one strategy and justify your recommendation with biological reasoning.
stimulus:
Figure 1 (described): Keeling Curve overlaid with global mean surface temperature anomaly
• Atmospheric CO₂: 1850 = 280 ppm; 2024 = 421 ppm; rate of increase accelerating (currently ~2.4 ppm/yr)
• Global temperature anomaly: 1850 baseline ≈ 0°C; 2024 ≈ +1.4°C above pre-industrial
• Strong positive correlation (r ≈ 0.97) between CO₂ and temperature over 170-year record
• Seasonal oscillation in CO₂ (±4 ppm) from Northern Hemisphere vegetation cycles

Ocean acidification chemistry:
CO₂ (atm) + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid)
H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ (bicarbonate ion)
HCO₃⁻ ⇌ H⁺ + CO₃²⁻ (carbonate ion)
Ocean pH: 1750 ≈ 8.25; today ≈ 8.10 (0.15 pH unit decrease = 40% increase in H⁺ concentration)

Carbon stocks (Pg C = petagrams carbon):
Atmosphere: ~880 Pg C
Terrestrial biosphere: ~550 Pg C (plants) + ~1,500 Pg C (soil)
Oceans: ~38,000 Pg C
Fossil fuel reserves: ~3,700 Pg C
title: APBIO-FRQ-L-027

criteria_json.minimum_fix: At least 4 steps: CO₂ → photosynthesis (plants) → carbon in organic molecules → consumed by animals → respiration releases CO₂; or death → decomposers → CO₂. Slow component: burial → fossil fuels → millions of years; or limestone formation. Both fast (biological) and slow (geological) named.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Trace carbon atom through at least four cycle steps including both fast and slow components.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Pathway trace (multiple acceptable routes): (1) Atmosphere → Plants: CO₂ in atmosphere fixed by photosynthesis in autotrophs (plants, algae, cyanobacteria); CO₂ incorporated into organic molecules (glucose → starch, cellulose, proteins, lipids) in chloroplasts using light energy. Process: photosynthesis (Calvin cycle). (2) Plants → Consumers: plant tissue eaten by primary consumers (herbivores) → carbon in organic molecules transferred through food chain → passes to secondary consumers, etc. Process: consumption / ecological transfer. (3) Consumers/Plants → Atmosphere: cellular respiration in plants, animals, fungi, bacteria releases CO₂ back to atmosphere as organisms oxidize organic molecules for energy. Process: aerobic respiration, CO₂ released in Krebs cycle. (4) Dead organisms → Soil: dead organisms and waste decomposed by decomposers (bacteria, fungi) → CO₂ released to atmosphere (decomposition/mineralization); some carbon stored in soil organic matter (SOM) / humus. (5) Slow geological component: carbon buried in sediments → compressed over millions of years → fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas); or marine organisms with calcium carbonate shells die → shells accumulate → limestone (CaCO₃) rock. This takes millions of years and represents the slow geological carbon cycle. (6) Geological → Atmosphere: volcanic outgassing releases CO₂ from carbonate rock metamorphism; weathering of silicate rocks consumes CO₂. Human burning of fossil fuels short-circuits the slow geological cycle. 1 pt for at least 4 steps with organisms and processes named; 1 pt for including both fast biological and slow geological components.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: CO₂-temperature strong positive correlation. Greenhouse: CO₂ absorbs infrared (IR) re-emitted by Earth → re-emits back → traps heat. Fossil fuels: release millions of years of sequestered carbon in centuries → faster than removal; reverses Carboniferous carbon burial. Positive feedback: warming → permafrost thaws → CO₂/CH₄ released → more warming (self-reinforcing).
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe CO₂-temperature relationship and greenhouse mechanism; explain fossil fuel disruption; describe positive feedback.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) CO₂-temperature relationship: strong positive correlation — as CO₂ increased from 280 to 421 ppm (+50%), global temperature increased ~1.4°C. Greenhouse mechanism at molecular level: solar radiation (short wavelength visible light) passes through atmosphere → absorbed by Earth's surface → Earth re-emits longer wavelength infrared radiation (heat). CO₂ molecules (and CH₄, H₂O, N₂O) have molecular vibration modes (bending and stretching of C=O bonds) that absorb specific infrared wavelengths (CO₂ absorbs IR at ~15 μm) → CO₂ molecules re-emit IR in all directions, including back toward Earth → reduces energy escaping to space → atmospheric temperature increases (blanket effect). (ii) Fossil fuel disruption: Short-term (decades): burning releases CO₂ sequestered over millions of years → rapid spike in atmospheric CO₂ on timescale shorter than natural removal processes (ocean absorption, silicate weathering) → CO₂ builds up faster than it is removed. Geological timescale: fossil fuels represent carbon removed from the atmosphere during the Carboniferous Period (~360-300 Mya) by photosynthesis → reducing atmospheric CO₂ from >1000 ppm to present-day levels over millions of years. Burning reverses this in centuries. (iii) Positive feedback example: Permafrost thaw — Arctic permafrost contains ~1,500-1,600 Pg C (frozen organic matter from thousands of years). As global temperature rises: permafrost thaws → previously frozen organic matter exposed to microbial decomposition → decomposers release CO₂ and CH₄ (methane, 25× more potent greenhouse gas than CO₂ over 100 years) → atmospheric greenhouse gases increase → more warming → more permafrost thaws → more CH₄/CO₂ released. This is self-reinforcing (positive feedback) because the output (warming) amplifies the input (warming). Positive feedback: initial warming → more permafrost thaw → more CH₄/CO₂ → more warming. 1 pt for greenhouse mechanism; 1 pt for positive feedback with mechanism.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Chemistry: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → H⁺ + CO₃²⁻; H⁺ increases → pH drops. Consequences: (1) calcification impaired (less CO₃²⁻ → thinner shells in corals, mollusks); (2) respiratory acidosis in fish (CO₂ in body fluids, altered behavior). Feedback: acidification weakens biological pump → less CO₂ absorbed → positive feedback.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Write ocean acidification chemistry; describe two organism consequences; predict CO₂ absorption feedback.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Chemistry sequence: CO₂(aq) + H₂O → H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid); H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ (bicarbonate); HCO₃⁻ → H⁺ + CO₃²⁻ (carbonate). Net result: dissolving CO₂ releases H⁺ ions → ocean pH decreases. The pH has dropped from 8.25 to 8.10 (40% increase in H⁺, since pH is logarithmic). Acidification also drives the equilibrium: CO₃²⁻ + H⁺ → HCO₃⁻ → carbonate ions consumed → less carbonate available. (ii) Two consequences: (A) Calcification impairment: corals, mollusks, sea urchins, pteropods, and calcareous plankton (coccolithophores, foraminifera) build shells/skeletons from calcium carbonate (CaCO₃). Lower pH = lower CO₃²⁻ concentration (consumed by H⁺) → aragonite and calcite saturation state decreases → organisms cannot precipitate CaCO₃ fast enough → thinner shells, dissolution of existing shells → impaired structural integrity, growth, and survival. Coral bleaching is exacerbated by acidification. (B) CO₂ narcosis / physiological acid-base disruption: marine fish and invertebrates regulate blood pH for enzyme function; excess CO₂ dissolving in body fluids = respiratory acidosis → disrupts acid-base balance → neurological effects (altered behavior, impaired predator avoidance) → reduced survival; disrupted fertilization and larval development. (iii) Feedback on CO₂ absorption: as ocean acidifies: CO₃²⁻ → HCO₃⁻ shift reduces the ocean's buffering capacity; also, if calcifying organisms decline or die → less biogenic CaCO₃ sedimentation → less carbon buried in sediments (biological pump weakened) → less carbon removed from upper ocean → reduced capacity to absorb atmospheric CO₂. Positive feedback: more CO₂ → acidification → impaired biological pump → less CO₂ absorbed → more CO₂ in atmosphere → more warming. 1 pt per two sub-points correctly addressed.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Strategy 1: clear-cut releases stored carbon, monocultures low diversity/resilience — NOT recommended. Strategy 2: selective harvest maintains structure, soil carbon, continuous uptake — moderate. Strategy 3: old-growth has highest carbon stocks (large trees, deep soils, dead wood), continues to sequester, no emissions — BEST for long-term storage. Recommendation: protect old-growth; alternatives take centuries to match old-growth carbon density.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Evaluate three forest carbon strategies and recommend one with biological justification.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Evaluation of strategies: Strategy 1 (Clear-cut + monoculture): Clear-cutting releases stored carbon immediately as debris decomposes and soil carbon is lost → large pulse of CO₂ emissions. Monocultures have low structural diversity → low carbon density in understory, soil, and woody debris; fast-growing trees fix carbon quickly but store less total carbon (smaller trees, less belowground carbon); monocultures are vulnerable to disease and pests → risk of catastrophic carbon release. NOT recommended for maximum long-term carbon storage. Strategy 2 (Selective harvest + diverse natural forest): maintains forest structure and continuous canopy cover → minimizes soil disturbance and carbon loss; selective harvest creates gaps that stimulate new growth → continuous carbon uptake; diverse structure supports high soil carbon (diverse root systems and litter inputs); more resilient to disturbance. Moderate carbon storage per hectare, but sustainable long-term. Strategy 3 (Protect old-growth as carbon reserve): old-growth forests have the highest carbon stocks per hectare — large-diameter trees have enormous woody biomass; dead wood (snags, fallen logs) stores carbon for decades; deep organic soils with high carbon content; carbon continues to accrue slowly even in old-growth (contrary to the misconception that mature forests are carbon neutral). Old-growth also has co-benefits (biodiversity, water regulation, climate buffering). Recommendation: Strategy 3 (old-growth protection) maximizes long-term carbon storage because: old-growth forests store more carbon per hectare than younger forests; protecting them avoids catastrophic emissions from disturbance; regeneration after clear-cutting takes decades to centuries to restore equivalent carbon stocks. Strategy 2 is a reasonable alternative if sustainable yield is required. 1 pt for evaluation of all three; 1 pt for recommendation with biological justification.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Mount St. Helens erupted in 1980, destroying 600 km² of forest and depositing meters of volcanic ash and rock. Ecologists have monitored species recovery in this area since 1980.
    (i) Classify the ecological succession occurring at Mount St. Helens as primary or secondary, and justify your classification.
    (ii) Describe the facilitiation model of succession and apply it to the Mount St. Helens recovery. Name a specific type of early colonist (pioneer species) and explain how it modifies the environment to make it suitable for later species.
    (iii) Describe how species diversity (as measured by the Shannon diversity index or species richness) would change over succession time from year 0 to year 50 at Mount St. Helens. Explain the mechanism.
stimulus:
(b) The intermediate disturbance hypothesis (IDH) predicts that species diversity is highest at intermediate levels of disturbance frequency and intensity.
    (i) Explain why diversity is lower in undisturbed communities. What process dominates in the absence of disturbance?
    (ii) Explain why diversity is also lower in highly disturbed communities. What types of species persist?
    (iii) Explain why intermediate disturbance maximizes diversity. Use the concept of competitive exclusion in your answer.
    (iv) Predict how the IDH applies to coral reefs, where wave disturbance creates patches of open substrate.

(c) Keystone species have a disproportionately large effect on community structure relative to their abundance. Robert Paine's classic experiment with sea stars (Pisaster ochraceus) in Pacific tidepools demonstrated this.
    (i) Explain what happened to species diversity when Paine removed Pisaster from the tidal zone.
    (ii) Define keystone species and explain the trophic cascade mechanism by which losing a keystone predator causes loss of biodiversity.
    (iii) Give ONE example of a keystone species in a terrestrial ecosystem (not Pisaster) and explain its role.

(d) Invasive species are a leading cause of native species extinction. The invasive zebra mussel (Dreissena polymorpha) was introduced into the Great Lakes in 1988 via ballast water.
    (i) Describe THREE ecological impacts of zebra mussels on the Great Lakes ecosystem.
    (ii) Explain why invasive species often succeed so dramatically in their introduced environment.
    (iii) Propose ONE ecologically sound management strategy for zebra mussels and explain its mechanism.
title: APBIO-FRQ-L-028

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Primary succession: bare substrate, no soil, no biological legacy. Facilitation: pioneer species (cyanobacteria/lichens or lupines) → fix N, add organic matter → enable later species. Diversity: low at first, increases as facilitation builds soil, then may slow as late-successional dominants compete. Lupines or N-fixing pioneers named.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Classify Mt. St. Helens succession; describe facilitation model; explain diversity change over time.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Primary succession. Justification: the eruption created entirely new substrate (volcanic rock, ash) devoid of any organisms or soil — there is no pre-existing biological legacy (no seedbank, no soil organic matter, no residual plant roots). Primary succession begins on bare, lifeless substrate; secondary succession begins where an existing community was disturbed but biological remnants remain (soil, seeds, roots). (ii) Facilitation model: early colonist species (pioneer species) arrive first, establish, modify the abiotic environment in ways that make it more hospitable for other species, and are eventually replaced by later-successional species they facilitated. At Mt. St. Helens: pioneer species include cyanobacteria and lichens (which fix atmospheric nitrogen → add N to bare substrate) and lupines (Lupinus lepidus — a nitrogen-fixing legume that colonized the pumice plain). Lupines: fix N₂ via Rhizobium symbiosis → add organic matter to barren substrate → create pockets of nutrient-rich soil → enable grasses and later shrubs to establish. Over time: accumulated organic matter → soil formation → more species can establish. Each wave of species facilitates the next. (iii) Diversity change: Years 0-5: very low species richness (only pioneer species tolerate bare substrate — cyanobacteria, lichens, specialized plants). Years 5-20: rising diversity as pioneer species modify substrate; mid-successional species colonize (grasses, forbs, early shrubs); overall diversity increases. Years 20-50: continued increase in diversity as forest species establish; eventually slowing as competitive exclusion and dominance by late-successional species begins to reduce diversity. IDH prediction: diversity may peak at intermediate stages before late-successional dominance reduces it. 1 pt for primary succession with correct justification; 1 pt for facilitation with pioneer species example.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Undisturbed: competitive exclusion → dominants reduce diversity. Highly disturbed: only stress-tolerators/r-selected persist → low diversity. Intermediate: competitive dominants eliminated periodically → patch renewal → fugitive species coexist → highest diversity. Coral reefs: intermediate wave disturbance creates diverse patch mosaic; prevents coral competitive exclusion.
accepted_variants: intermediate wave energy highest coral diversity
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain IDH: why undisturbed is low diversity, disturbed is low, and intermediate is high; apply to coral reefs.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Low diversity in undisturbed communities: without disturbance, competitive dominants monopolize resources over time → competitive exclusion drives inferior competitors to local extinction → the community becomes dominated by one or a few superior competitors → diversity declines. This is the expected endpoint of community succession toward climax (competitive equilibrium). Competitive exclusion: one species can drive another extinct if they compete for the same limited resource. (ii) Low diversity in highly disturbed communities: frequent or intense disturbance eliminates most species that cannot tolerate or recover from disturbance → only stress-tolerators or r-selected species (high dispersal, fast reproduction) can persist → few species → low diversity. Many species cannot complete life cycles before the next disturbance kills them. (iii) Intermediate disturbance maximizes diversity: intermediate disturbance creates patches where competitive dominants are eliminated → freed habitat colonized by new colonists including poor competitors → diversity high. Two processes coexist: competitive exclusion (favors late-successional specialists) and disturbance-mediated patch renewal (maintains space for early colonists and intermediate species). Disturbance prevents any single dominant from monopolizing → diverse "fugitive species" coexist with competitive dominants. Diversity is maximized because no single competitive dominant has time to exclude all others, but disturbance is not so frequent that only stress-tolerators persist. (iv) Coral reefs: intermediate wave disturbance (storms, wave action) creates open patches on the reef → pioneer coral species colonize → before competitive dominant corals (massive corals) can overgrow, another disturbance opens new patches → diverse coral species coexist at different patch ages. Reefs with intermediate wave energy → highest coral diversity. 1 pt for undisturbed + highly disturbed explanation; 1 pt for intermediate mechanism + reef application.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Pisaster removal: mussels dominate → competitive exclusion of 15 species → diversity collapses to monoculture. Keystone species: disproportionate community effect relative to abundance; trophic cascade: predator controls dominant competitor → diversity maintained; remove predator → dominant explodes → exclusion. Terrestrial example: wolves in Yellowstone (control elk → allow riparian vegetation recovery).
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain Pisaster removal effect; define keystone and trophic cascade; give terrestrial example.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Paine's Pisaster removal: when Paine removed all sea stars (Pisaster) from the experimental plot, mussels (Mytilus) — the primary prey of Pisaster and the competitive dominant — rapidly spread and covered all available rock surface → mussels competitively excluded barnacles, limpets, chitons, whelks, and other intertidal species → species richness declined dramatically from ~15 to ~1 species (mussel monoculture). Control plots (with Pisaster) maintained ~15 species. (ii) Keystone species definition: a species that has a disproportionately large effect on its community relative to its abundance — removing it causes dramatic changes in community structure (diversity, composition). Pisaster represented only a small fraction of intertidal biomass but controlled the dominant competitor. Trophic cascade mechanism: keystone predator (Pisaster) preys on dominant competitor (mussels) → keeps mussel population in check → prevents competitive exclusion of inferior species → multiple inferior competitors coexist. Remove predator → dominant competitor released from top-down control → exponential growth of dominant → competitive exclusion of all other species → diversity collapses. The cascade flows down from the top predator through the food web. (iii) Terrestrial example: wolves in Yellowstone National Park are keystone species. Wolves prey on elk → regulate elk numbers and behavior (elk avoid certain habitats when wolves present) → reduced elk browsing → recovery of willows, aspens, cottonwoods in riparian areas → beavers return → beaver dams create wetlands → increased bird species, fish, amphibians. This is a trophic cascade triggered by reintroduction of wolves in 1995. 1 pt for Pisaster experiment interpretation; 1 pt for keystone + trophic cascade + terrestrial example.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Three impacts: (1) filter feeding depletes phytoplankton → food web disruption; (2) native unionid mussel competition/smothering; (3) biofouling infrastructure. Invasive success: no natural enemies, reduced competition, high reproduction. Management: biological control (native-range predator/parasite) for long-term suppression without chemical harm.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe three zebra mussel impacts; explain invasive success; propose management strategy.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Three ecological impacts of zebra mussels: (1) Filter feeding and phytoplankton depletion: zebra mussels are extremely efficient filter feeders (one mussel can filter up to 1 liter/day); dense populations (up to 700,000/m²) filter massive quantities of phytoplankton → water clarity increases dramatically but phytoplankton community collapses → zooplankton that depend on phytoplankton decline → food web base disrupted → native fish (whitefish, cisco) that eat zooplankton decline. (2) Competition with native bivalves: native unionid mussels (clams) cannot compete with zebra mussel density; zebra mussels attach to native clam shells, physically smothering and competing for food → native freshwater mussel species (many endangered) dramatically decline → 37+ species of unionid mussels in Great Lakes threatened. (3) Biofouling and infrastructure damage: zebra mussels attach to boat hulls, water intake pipes, underwater structures → clog municipal water intakes → cost billions of dollars; alter substrate availability for other benthic organisms. (ii) Invasive success reasons: released from natural enemies (predators, pathogens, parasites that controlled population in native range); novel ecosystem lacks co-evolved competitors → reduced interspecific competition; high reproductive rate (r-selected); high phenotypic plasticity → adapt to wide range of conditions; accidental or intentional introduction provides propagule pressure. (iii) Ecologically sound management: biological control — identify and introduce a specialist predator or parasite from the native Eurasian range that targets zebra mussels without harming native species. Example: the diving duck Aythya ferina (common pochard) preferentially eats Dreissena in Europe; or research into native crayfish that may prey on juveniles. Mechanism: natural enemy → top-down population control → long-term suppression without chemicals. Chemical control (e.g., chlorine, potassium chloride) is ecologically harmful to non-target species. Accept any biologically sound strategy with mechanism. 1 pt for three impacts; 1 pt for invasive success + management strategy.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Symbiosis describes close ecological relationships between two species. Compare mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism using the following framework for each: (i) effect on each partner (+ or −); (ii) specific biological example; (iii) whether the relationship is obligate or facultative; and (iv) one evolutionary implication of the relationship.

(b) Mycorrhizal fungi form mutualistic associations with the roots of over 90% of plant species.
    (i) Describe the mechanism of the mycorrhizal mutualism — explain specifically what each partner contributes to and receives from the relationship.
    (ii) The data in Table 1 show plant growth with and without mycorrhizal fungi at different phosphorus soil levels. Analyze these data and explain why the mutualistic benefit is greatest under low phosphorus conditions.
    (iii) Explain whether mycorrhizal associations are truly mutualistic or whether they lie on a mutualism-parasitism continuum. Describe the conditions under which mycorrhizal fungi might become "cheaters" (gaining resources without providing benefit).

(c) Coevolution occurs when two species exert reciprocal selective pressure on each other, each evolving in response to the other.
    (i) The Red Queen hypothesis proposes that parasites drive ongoing coevolution with their hosts. Explain this hypothesis, using the concept of frequency-dependent selection. Include why sexual reproduction may be advantageous in coevolving host-parasite systems.
    (ii) Describe the coevolutionary arms race between the rough-skinned newt (Taricha granulosa) and its predator, the common garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis). Explain the molecular mechanism involved and the geographic variation observed.

(d) Describe a plausible evolutionary pathway by which a mutualistic symbiosis could have originated from a parasitic or antagonistic relationship. Your answer should include: the ancestral interaction, the selective pressures acting on both species, specific genetic/phenotypic changes, and the evolutionary transition from antagonism to mutualism. You may use any pair of organisms as your example.
stimulus:
Table 1: Plant growth (dry mass, grams) with and without mycorrhizal fungi (MF)
Soil phosphorus level | Without MF | With MF | Benefit (% increase)
    Very low           |    0.8 g   |  4.5 g  |       +463%
    Low                |    1.4 g   |  5.2 g  |       +271%
    Medium             |    3.0 g   |  4.8 g  |        +60%
    High               |    4.5 g   |  4.6 g  |         +2%

Rough-skinned newt (Taricha granulosa) toxicity:
• Newts produce tetrodotoxin (TTX) — a potent sodium channel blocker
• TTX blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels → prevents action potential propagation → paralysis, death
• Some garter snake populations have evolved Na⁺ channel mutations (in SCN4A gene) that reduce TTX binding
• Population variation: Oregon coastal garter snakes (high TTX resistance) vs. inland snakes (low resistance)
title: APBIO-FRQ-L-029

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Mutualism (+/+): mycorrhizae or bee-flower; both benefit; can be obligate; coevolve mutual dependence. Commensalism (+/0): barnacles on whale; one benefits, other unaffected; usually facultative; commensal may drift to parasitism. Parasitism (+/−): Plasmodium in human; parasite benefits, host harmed; often obligate; Red Queen arms race.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Compare mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism with effects, examples, obligate/facultative, and evolutionary implication.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Mutualism (+/+): both partners benefit. Example: mycorrhizal fungi + plant roots (fungus gets photosynthate/sugars; plant gets water/phosphorus via extended hyphal network). Or: nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium in legume root nodules; pollinator-flower (bee gets nectar/pollen; flower gets pollination). Obligate in many cases (neither partner survives or reproduces as well without the other); some are facultative. Evolutionary implication: reciprocal positive selection pressure → coevolution of mutual dependence; both species' fitness increases with the other's presence → selection favors stronger partnership → can lead to irreversible co-dependence. Commensalism (+/0): one benefits, the other is neither helped nor harmed. Example: barnacles on whale skin (barnacles get transport and access to food; whale unaffected). Or: cattle egrets following grazing cattle (egrets benefit from insects disturbed by cattle; cattle unaffected). Usually facultative. Evolutionary implication: commensal may evolve traits that better exploit the host; if the host eventually bears a cost, commensalism slides toward parasitism. Parasitism (+/−): parasite benefits, host harmed. Example: Plasmodium (malaria parasite) in human host; tapeworms in vertebrate gut; mistletoe on trees. Obligate for many. Evolutionary implication: coevolutionary arms race — host evolves defenses (immune recognition), parasite evolves countermeasures (immune evasion) → Red Queen dynamics. Award 1 pt for two symbiosis types with all four elements; 1 pt for the third.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Mechanism: plant gives sugars; fungus gives phosphorus and water via extensive hyphae inaccessible to roots. Data: greatest benefit at low P (fungus essential for P uptake); minimal benefit at high P (plant absorbs P directly). Cheating: at high P, fungus gains carbon but delivers little P → shifts toward parasitism; some fungal strains become net negative cheaters.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain mycorrhizal mechanism; analyze phosphorus data; explain cheater conditions.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Mycorrhizal mutualism mechanism: The plant contributes: photosynthetically produced carbohydrates (sugars, sucrose) transported to fungal partner via phloem to root, then across the symbiotic interface to the fungus. The fungus contributes: extensive hyphal network that extends far beyond the plant's root system → vastly increases the effective soil volume explored for water and mineral nutrients, especially phosphorus (P) and nitrogen (N). Fungal hyphae are much thinner than roots → can penetrate soil pores inaccessible to roots → access P bound to soil particles; hyphae secrete phosphatases to mineralize organic P. The fungus delivers P and water to the plant via the symbiotic interface (periarbuscular membrane in arbuscular mycorrhizae) in exchange for sugars. (ii) Data analysis: Benefit is greatest at very low P (463% increase) and decreases as soil P increases until at high P only 2% benefit. Explanation: when soil P is scarce, the plant cannot absorb sufficient P through its own roots → severely P-limited → fungal hyphae provide essential P access → huge growth benefit. At high soil P: plant can absorb P directly through roots without fungal help → fungal phosphorus delivery is redundant → plant gains little from the relationship, but still pays cost in photosynthate → net benefit minimal. (iii) Mutualism-parasitism continuum / cheaters: under high nutrient conditions (high P, high N), the plant has little to gain from mycorrhizae but still pays carbon to the fungus → relationship shifts toward parasitism (fungus benefits more than plant, plant bears net cost). Cheating fungi: some fungal strains fail to deliver adequate P to the plant while still receiving carbon → "parasitic" cheater strategies; in lab, some Glomus strains become net negative in high P soils. The relationship is context-dependent; not a fixed mutualism. 1 pt for mechanism; 1 pt for data analysis and cheater explanation.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Red Queen: ongoing arms race; parasites evolve to infect common host → common genotype declines → rare escapes → becomes common → cycle. Sexual reproduction advantage: produces new genotypes faster than asexual clones → harder for parasites to keep up. Newt-snake: newt TTX blocks sodium channels; snake SCN4A mutations reduce TTX binding → resistance; higher TTX newts → more resistance snakes → arms race; coastal Oregon highest co-evolution.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain Red Queen hypothesis with frequency-dependent selection and sexual reproduction; describe newt-snake arms race.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Red Queen hypothesis: parasites co-evolve with hosts in an ongoing arms race where neither side "wins" — both must constantly evolve just to maintain their relative fitness (like the Red Queen in Alice in Wonderland who runs constantly just to stay in place). Frequency-dependent selection: parasites evolve to infect the most COMMON host genotype (because infecting rare genotypes is not adaptively favored); when a common host genotype is heavily parasitized → fitness decreases → its frequency declines; a rare genotype that parasites cannot yet infect → escapes parasitism → increases in frequency → eventually becomes common → parasites evolve to infect it → cycle continues. Advantage of sexual reproduction: sexual reproduction continuously generates new genotype combinations (through recombination and independent assortment) → rare genotypes continuously produced → one step ahead of parasites. Asexual populations produce clonal offspring (identical genotype) → once parasite evolves to infect the common clone, all offspring are vulnerable → high susceptibility. This "tangled bank" hypothesis predicts sexual reproduction is adaptive in environments with abundant coevolving parasites. Empirical support: New Zealand snail (Potamopyrgus antipodarum) populations with heavy parasite loads have higher rates of sexual reproduction than populations in low-parasite environments. (ii) Newt-snake arms race: Newts produce TTX (tetrodotoxin) → blocks voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav) → prevents action potential conduction → paralysis and death of most predators. Garter snakes that eat newts have evolved resistance alleles in the SCN4A gene (encodes Nav1.4 sodium channel subunit) → point mutations change the TTX-binding site on the channel → TTX cannot bind effectively → channels remain functional → snake survives eating newt. Arms race: populations with higher newt TTX → selection for snakes with higher Nav resistance → snakes develop resistance → newts face selection for higher TTX production → escalation cycle. Geographic variation: coastal Oregon populations co-occur with highly toxic newts → snakes have highest TTX resistance allele frequencies; inland populations rarely encounter toxic newts → low resistance allele frequency → "geographic mosaic of coevolution." 1 pt for Red Queen + frequency-dependent selection + sexual reproduction; 1 pt for newt-snake molecular mechanism + geographic variation.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Ancestral antagonism: intracellular parasite (α-proteobacterium) in proto-eukaryote. Selection: host tolerates bacterium if gains ATP; bacterium less virulent if host survives longer. Genetic changes: bacterial genome reduced, host import machinery (TOM/TIM) evolved, protein transfer to nucleus. Transition: parasite → commensal → mutualist (mitochondria) as mutual dependence increased. Endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe evolutionary pathway from antagonism to mutualism with ancestral interaction, selection, genetic changes, and transition.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Example: Wolbachia bacteria → mitochondria (endosymbiosis evolution): Ancestral interaction: ancient alpha-proteobacterium was initially an intracellular parasite/pathogen of a proto-eukaryotic cell — extracting energy and nutrients from the host cell → parasitic antagonistic relationship (bacterium +, host −). Selective pressures on the host: selection favored host cells that could tolerate the intracellular bacterium without dying, or that extracted metabolic benefit from bacterial energy production (oxidative phosphorylation capacity). Selective pressures on the bacterium: selection favored less virulent strains that did not kill their host too quickly (enhanced transmission if host survives longer; vertical transmission through cell division). Genetic and phenotypic changes: (1) Bacterium → reduced genome (non-essential genes lost; genes transferred to host nucleus); (2) Host → evolved protein import machinery (TOM/TIM complexes) to import nuclear-encoded proteins into bacterium; (3) Both → evolved complementary metabolite exchange (bacterium exports ATP; host exports substrates). Evolutionary transition: as bacteria became increasingly dependent on host-imported proteins and less able to survive outside the cell, and as host became dependent on bacterial ATP, the relationship shifted from parasitism → commensalism (bacterium neutral effect) → mutualism (both benefit → mitochondria/chloroplasts). This is endosymbiotic theory. Other examples: cleaning stations (cleaner wrasse originally eat skin parasites off fish → possible mutualism from kleptoparasitism); fig-fig wasp mutualism (from parasite that laid eggs in flowers). Accept any well-reasoned pathway. 1 pt for ancestral antagonistic relationship + selective pressures; 1 pt for genetic changes + evolutionary transition with mechanism.

stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) The MacArthur-Wilson theory of island biogeography predicts that species richness on an island represents a dynamic equilibrium between immigration and extinction rates.
    (i) Explain how island SIZE affects species richness. Describe the mechanism connecting island size to extinction rate.
    (ii) Explain how island DISTANCE from a mainland source pool affects species richness. Describe the mechanism connecting distance to immigration rate.
    (iii) Using the species-area relationship (S = CA^z, where S = number of species, A = area, C and z are constants), predict what happens to species richness if an island's effective area is halved. Use z = 0.25 in your calculation and express your answer as a percentage of the original species richness.

(b) Habitat fragmentation effectively converts contiguous habitat into island-like patches.
    (i) Explain THREE ways in which habitat fragmentation reduces biodiversity beyond simply reducing total habitat area.
    (ii) The SLOSS debate asks whether conservation managers should prefer a Single Large (SL) or Several Small (SS) reserves of equivalent total area.
    Describe the ecological arguments for EACH side of the debate. Then state which side the empirical evidence most often supports and explain why.
    (iii) Explain the biological mechanism by which wildlife corridors connecting habitat patches maintain or increase biodiversity.

(c) A conservation biologist tracks the reintroduction of a locally extinct species (the black-footed ferret) into a fragmented prairie landscape. Three years after reintroduction into Patch A (large, connected to Patch B by a corridor), the ferret population is thriving. In Patch C (same size as A but isolated), the reintroduction failed. Explain the likely reasons for the difference in outcomes, using concepts from island biogeography, metapopulation theory, and inbreeding depression.

(d) Climate change is shifting species' geographic ranges poleward and to higher elevations.
    (i) Explain why mountaintop species face a greater extinction risk from climate change than lowland species, using island biogeography theory as a framework.
    (ii) A plant species currently has its range between 800–1200 m elevation. As temperatures warm, the suitable thermal range shifts to 1000–1400 m. Predict the demographic consequences for this population and explain whether the population can respond.
    (iii) Describe TWO conservation strategies that explicitly account for climate change in protecting biodiversity.
stimulus:
Species-area relationship data:
Island area (km²) | Number of bird species
     1             |          11
    10             |          20
   100             |          36
  1,000            |          64
 10,000            |         112

From log-log plot: z ≈ 0.25, consistent with MacArthur-Wilson predictions
(z = 0.13-0.18 for mainland habitat patches; z = 0.25-0.35 for true oceanic islands)

SLOSS background:
• Species-area relationship: SL may contain more species (especially area-sensitive and interior species)
• Rescue effect: Several small patches may protect against catastrophic single-event extinction
• Edge effects: fragmented habitat has high perimeter-to-area ratio → more edge, less interior
• Minimum viable area: some species (large carnivores, area-sensitive forest birds) require a minimum patch size to persist

Black-footed ferret facts:
• North America's most endangered mammal; dependent on prairie dog colonies for food and burrows
• Current population: ~300 individuals in the wild from reintroduction programs beginning 1991
• Highly sensitive to sylvatic plague (Yersinia pestis) — can kill entire ferret and prairie dog colonies
title: APBIO-FRQ-L-030

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Size → larger populations → lower extinction rate → more species. Distance → lower immigration rate → fewer colonists → fewer species. Calculation: S_new = S × (1/2)^0.25 = S × 0.841; species richness drops to ~84% (≈16% loss) when area is halved — NOT proportional because z < 1.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain island size → extinction rate; distance → immigration rate; calculate effect of halving area.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Island size and extinction rate: larger islands support larger population sizes for each species → larger populations have lower extinction probability (lower demographic stochasticity, lower genetic drift, can absorb environmental fluctuation). Smaller islands → smaller populations → higher extinction rate per species → fewer species at equilibrium. Also, larger islands offer more habitat types/niches → support more species. Mechanism: extinction rate decreases with increasing island area; immigration rate is roughly independent of island size → larger island has lower extinction rate relative to immigration rate → higher equilibrium species richness. (ii) Island distance and immigration rate: more distant islands are reached by fewer colonists from mainland because dispersal probability decreases with distance (many organisms cannot travel far; propagule survival declines with distance). Lower immigration rate on distant islands → fewer new species arrive per year → fewer new arrivals to replace extinct species → lower equilibrium species richness. Near islands: higher immigration → more arrivals → more colonizations per year → higher equilibrium. Mechanism: immigration rate decreases with increasing distance; extinction rate is distance-independent → near islands achieve higher equilibrium than far islands. (iii) Species-area calculation: S = CA^z. If area is halved: S_new = C(A/2)^z = CA^z × (1/2)^z = S_original × (1/2)^0.25. (1/2)^0.25 = 2^(-0.25) = 1/2^0.25 ≈ 1/1.189 ≈ 0.841. New S ≈ 84.1% of original. Halving the area reduces species richness to ~84% (a ~16% reduction in species) — not 50%, because the species-area relationship is sublinear (z < 1). 1 pt per correct mechanism (size + distance); 1 pt for calculation.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Three effects: (1) edge effects (interior habitat loss, edge-adapted invaders); (2) reduced gene flow and inbreeding in isolated patches; (3) no recolonization after local extinction (rescue effect lost). SLOSS: SL → more interior species, larger populations; SS → insurance against catastrophe, geographic spread. Empirical: usually SL wins for species richness. Corridors: restore gene flow, rescue effect (recolonization), expand effective metapopulation size.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain three fragmentation effects beyond area loss; argue SLOSS; explain corridor mechanism.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Three fragmentation effects beyond area: (1) Edge effects: fragmentation increases the ratio of edge habitat to interior habitat; edge habitat has altered abiotic conditions (higher light, temperature, wind, drying) and is invaded by edge-tolerant and invasive species → interior species cannot survive in edge zones → effective interior habitat much smaller than total patch area → loss of area-sensitive species (many forest birds nest only in deep interior). (2) Reduced connectivity and gene flow: isolated patches → no immigration between patches → populations cannot receive new alleles → inbreeding within isolated populations → inbreeding depression + loss of adaptive variation → higher local extinction risk. (3) Barrier to movement and dispersal: organisms cannot move between isolated patches → recolonization of a patch after local extinction is impossible (rescue effect eliminated) → once a species goes locally extinct in a patch, it is permanently lost from that patch. Also, migration for seasonal resources prevented. (ii) SLOSS debate: Arguments for Single Large (SL): large reserves contain more interior habitat → fewer edge effects; support larger populations per species → lower extinction rates; can accommodate species with large home ranges (large carnivores, wide-ranging birds); can harbor more total species due to species-area relationship; contain complete ecological communities including rare interior-specialist species. Arguments for Several Small (SS): multiple reserves hedge against catastrophic single events (disease, fire, pollution, invasive species) — if all individuals are in one reserve, a single event can cause total extinction; several reserves can protect species with different habitat requirements; can cover more geographic area and therefore more habitat types; provide redundancy. Empirical evidence: generally favors SL for maximizing species richness, especially for large, area-sensitive species; however, SS may be superior in practice for population viability (insurance against catastrophe). No universal winner — landscape context matters. (iii) Wildlife corridor mechanism: corridors allow individuals to move between otherwise isolated patches → restores gene flow between patches → prevents inbreeding depression; allows recolonization after local extinction (rescue effect) → population can recover from disease or stochastic events in one patch; allows seasonal migration; expands effective population size (Ne) by connecting subpopulations into a metapopulation → reduces individual patch extinction probability. Functionally, corridors convert an "island" landscape into a metapopulation network. 1 pt for three edge/connectivity/barrier effects; 1 pt for SLOSS arguments; 1 pt for corridor mechanism.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Patch A success: corridor provides rescue effect (recolonization from B if population declines), gene flow (prevents inbreeding, maintains fitness), metapopulation dynamics. Patch C failure: no immigration possible → no rescue effect; inbreeding → fitness decline; demographic stochasticity + sylvatic plague → extinction with no recovery.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain why Patch A (connected) succeeded and Patch C (isolated) failed using island biogeography, metapopulation, and inbreeding.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Patch A + corridor: (1) Island biogeography rescue effect: corridor to Patch B allows immigration of new individuals → if ferret population in A declines, individuals from B can recolonize/supplement (rescue effect) → lower extinction probability; (2) Metapopulation dynamics: A and B are connected subpopulations within a metapopulation; recolonization maintains each patch population above minimum viable population threshold; (3) Gene flow: corridor allows exchange of individuals and alleles between A and B → prevents inbreeding; heterozygosity maintained → inbreeding depression avoided → cubs survive, reproduction high. Patch C isolated: (1) No rescue effect: if local extinction or severe decline occurs, no immigration possible → population cannot recover; stochastic events (disease outbreak: sylvatic plague from Yersinia could wipe out all prairie dogs → ferrets starve) → no recolonization; (2) Small isolated population → genetic drift + inbreeding → loss of MHC diversity → poor immune function → disease susceptibility → population crash; (3) Demographic stochasticity: with few founding individuals in isolated patch, sex ratio imbalance, loss of breeding individuals to accidents, etc., → population cannot sustain itself. The corridor provides the rescue effect, gene flow, and connectivity that Patch C lacks entirely → Patch C functions as a true ecological island with no immigration → expected outcome: eventual extinction following any perturbation. 1 pt for Patch A connectivity advantages (rescue effect + gene flow); 1 pt for Patch C isolation failure mechanisms.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Mountaintops: suitable habitat shrinks as thermal zone shifts up → species-area → fewer species; no habitat beyond summit → extinction. Plant: lower range contracts (conditions unsuitable below 1000 m); upper range may expand if seeds can disperse to 1400 m; if dispersal too slow → range shrinks → decline. Strategies: (1) assisted migration; (2) elevation and latitudinal corridors for natural range tracking.
accepted_variants: mountaintop island shrinks as temperature rises
no higher to go extinction risk
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain mountaintop extinction risk from climate; predict demographic consequences; describe two climate-aware conservation strategies.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: (i) Mountaintop species and island biogeography: as temperatures warm, suitable habitat shifts upslope → high-elevation species must track their thermal niche by moving upslope. Mountaintops are like true islands of suitable habitat surrounded by unsuitable warm lowland "sea." As the suitable thermal zone shifts up: the area of suitable habitat SHRINKS (mountain width decreases toward the summit → species-area relationship predicts fewer species can be supported → extinction risk increases). Eventually, the suitable zone disappears off the top of the mountain → complete habitat loss → extinction. Unlike lowland species, mountaintop species cannot move further north or to higher elevations without running out of mountain → climate-tracked range contraction leads to island shrinkage and eventual extinction. (ii) Demographic consequences for plant (800-1200 m → 1000-1400 m shift): Lower boundary shifts up to 1000 m → plants below 1000 m experience unsuitable thermal conditions → lower population declines as plants die or fail to reproduce at the trailing edge. Upper boundary shifts to 1400 m → plants above 1200 m (assuming they can disperse there) find new suitable habitat at leading edge. Net effect: if seeds can disperse upslope fast enough → population may shift range (but plants have limited dispersal). If dispersal insufficient → range shrinks as lower end contracts faster than upper end expands → population decline → extinction risk. Many plants cannot disperse 200 m in elevation fast enough to track a shifting thermal zone under rapid climate change. (iii) Two climate-aware conservation strategies: (1) Assisted migration (assisted colonization): deliberately translocate individuals to suitable habitats outside their current range that will be climatically suitable in the future. Moves species faster than they can disperse naturally; pre-emptively establishes populations in future range. Risk: potential invasive effects in recipient community. (2) Climate-adaptive reserve networks: identify and protect corridors along elevation gradients and latitudinal gradients → allow species to naturally migrate to track their climate niche; connect reserves from low to high elevation and south to north → functional corridors enable range shifts. Design reserves to include diverse elevation gradients within each reserve. 1 pt for mountaintop island biogeography explanation; 1 pt for demographic consequences OR two strategies.

stem: A researcher studying cell volume regulation places human red blood cells in solutions of different solute concentrations and observes changes in cell size.
stimulus: A student places a red blood cell in a hypotonic solution and records that the cell swells and eventually lyses.
canonical_answer_1: Water moves by osmosis from the lower-solute side to the higher-solute side, so red blood cells swell in hypotonic solution and shrink in hypertonic solution.
canonical_answer_2: The phospholipid bilayer's hydrophobic core limits water movement, so only small amounts of water cross directly and osmosis is slower than in pure water.
canonical_answers: Water moves by osmosis from the lower-solute side to the higher-solute side, so red blood cells swell in hypotonic solution and shrink in hypertonic solution.
The phospholipid bilayer's hydrophobic core limits water movement, so only small amounts of water cross directly and osmosis is slower than in pure water.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-001

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Water moves into the cell because the solution has a lower solute concentration than the cytoplasm.
accepted_variants: osmosis drives water into the cell
net movement of water is into the cell
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Predict the direction of water movement when a cell is placed in a hypotonic solution and explain why.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: States water moves INTO the cell; explains water moves from low solute concentration (high water potential) to high solute concentration (low water potential) by osmosis.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: The hydrophobic core of the bilayer repels polar water molecules, slowing osmosis through the membrane lipids.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe one structural feature of the plasma membrane that limits the rate of water movement through the lipid bilayer itself (not through aquaporins).
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Identifies the hydrophobic interior (nonpolar fatty acid tails) of the phospholipid bilayer as a barrier to polar water molecules.

stem: An experiment measures the rate of a catalase-catalyzed reaction at temperatures from 10 degrees C to 70 degrees C.
stimulus: A graph shows reaction rate peaking near 37 degrees C and declining sharply above 50 degrees C, approaching zero by 65 degrees C.
canonical_answer_1: Catalase activity increases up to its optimum temperature because warmer molecules move faster, so collisions with the active site become more frequent.
canonical_answer_2: Above the optimum, catalase denatures as weak bonds break, changing the active site so substrate can no longer bind properly.
canonical_answers: Catalase activity increases up to its optimum temperature because warmer molecules move faster, so collisions with the active site become more frequent.
Above the optimum, catalase denatures as weak bonds break, changing the active site so substrate can no longer bind properly.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-002

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Higher temperature gives molecules more kinetic energy, increasing collision frequency with the active site.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain why enzyme-catalyzed reaction rate increases as temperature rises from 10 degrees C to the optimum temperature.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Higher temperature increases kinetic energy of substrate molecules, leading to more frequent collisions with the enzyme active site and a higher reaction rate.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Heat breaks hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions that maintain the enzyme tertiary structure; denaturation distorts the active site so substrate cannot bind.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain the molecular basis for the sharp decline in enzyme activity above 50 degrees C.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: High temperatures disrupt weak bonds (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions) that maintain enzyme tertiary structure, causing denaturation and loss of active site shape so substrate cannot bind.

stem: Light energy absorbed by chlorophyll in the thylakoid membrane drives production of ATP and NADPH during the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.
stimulus: A diagram shows the thylakoid membrane with Photosystem II, the electron transport chain, Photosystem I, and ATP synthase.
canonical_answer_1: Water is split at PSII, and the released electrons move through PSII, cytochrome b6f, and PSI before reducing NADP+ to NADPH.
canonical_answer_2: As electrons pass through the thylakoid membrane, proton pumping builds a gradient that powers ATP synthase to make ATP and reduces NADP+ to NADPH.
canonical_answers: Water is split at PSII, and the released electrons move through PSII, cytochrome b6f, and PSI before reducing NADP+ to NADPH.
As electrons pass through the thylakoid membrane, proton pumping builds a gradient that powers ATP synthase to make ATP and reduces NADP+ to NADPH.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-003

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Electrons from water oxidation at PSII flow through the electron transport chain to PSI, then reduce NADP+ to NADPH.
accepted_variants: water to PSII to ETC to PSI to NADPH
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Trace the path of electrons from water to NADP+ during the light-dependent reactions, naming at least two electron carriers or complexes.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Water is split at PSII releasing electrons; electrons flow through plastoquinone, cytochrome b6f complex, plastocyanin; reach PSI; re-energized; transferred via ferredoxin to NADP+ reductase to reduce NADP+ to NADPH.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Electron transfer pumps H+ into the thylakoid lumen; the resulting concentration gradient drives H+ through ATP synthase, powering ATP synthesis by chemiosmosis.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain how the proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane is established and how it drives ATP synthesis.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: H+ accumulates in thylakoid lumen from water splitting and ETC proton pumping; electrochemical gradient drives H+ through ATP synthase back into stroma; flow powers phosphorylation of ADP to ATP (chemiosmosis).

stem: A cell lacking functional mitochondria can still generate ATP through glycolysis in the cytoplasm.
stimulus: A researcher treats yeast cells with a drug that destroys mitochondrial function and measures ATP production with and without oxygen.
canonical_answer_1: Glycolysis in the cytoplasm produces a net 2 ATP per glucose by substrate-level phosphorylation: one ATP is made at phosphoglycerate kinase and one at pyruvate kinase.
canonical_answer_2: Without mitochondria, the cell cannot run the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, so ATP production stays low and fermentation may be needed to regenerate NAD+
canonical_answers: Glycolysis in the cytoplasm produces a net 2 ATP per glucose by substrate-level phosphorylation: one ATP is made at phosphoglycerate kinase and one at pyruvate kinase.
Without mitochondria, the cell cannot run the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, so ATP production stays low and fermentation may be needed to regenerate NAD+
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-004

criteria_json.minimum_fix: 2 net ATP per glucose are produced by substrate-level phosphorylation during glycolysis.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Identify the net ATP yield from glycolysis per molecule of glucose and explain how this ATP is produced.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Net yield is 2 ATP per glucose; produced by substrate-level phosphorylation at the phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase steps.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Fermentation regenerates NAD+ from NADH, allowing glycolysis to continue producing ATP when oxygen (and the ETC) is unavailable.
accepted_variants: NAD+ is required for glycolysis to continue
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain why fermentation is necessary to sustain glycolysis in the absence of oxygen.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Glycolysis requires NAD+ to accept electrons; NADH produced during glycolysis must be re-oxidized to NAD+ for glycolysis to continue; fermentation regenerates NAD+ from NADH without oxygen.

stem: A signaling molecule binds to a G protein-coupled receptor on the cell surface and triggers a phosphorylation cascade inside the cell.
stimulus: A diagram shows: signal molecule to GPCR, G protein activation, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP production, protein kinase A activation, and multiple phosphorylated downstream targets.
canonical_answer_1: A single signaling molecule can cause a large response because one activated receptor starts a cascade that activates many G proteins and many downstream enzymes.
canonical_answer_2: The cascade stops when the G protein hydrolyzes GTP or cAMP is broken down by phosphodiesterase, shutting off the signal.
canonical_answers: A single signaling molecule can cause a large response because one activated receptor starts a cascade that activates many G proteins and many downstream enzymes.
The cascade stops when the G protein hydrolyzes GTP or cAMP is broken down by phosphodiesterase, shutting off the signal.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-005

criteria_json.minimum_fix: At each step in the cascade, one activated molecule activates many downstream molecules, exponentially amplifying the original signal.
accepted_variants: one receptor activates many G proteins
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain how a single signaling molecule binding one receptor can produce a large amplified cellular response.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Each activated receptor activates multiple G proteins; each G protein activates adenylyl cyclase; each adenylyl cyclase produces many cAMP molecules; each PKA phosphorylates many substrates — the signal is amplified at each step of the cascade.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Phosphodiesterase degrades cAMP, ending protein kinase A activation when the signaling molecule is no longer bound.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Identify one mechanism by which a cell terminates a signal transduction cascade after the signaling molecule is removed.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Any one of: phosphodiesterase degrades cAMP to AMP; protein phosphatases remove phosphate groups from substrates; receptor undergoes endocytosis (internalization); GTPase activity of G protein hydrolyzes GTP to GDP, inactivating G protein.

stem: A diploid organism with chromosome number 2n = 6 undergoes cell division under different conditions.
stimulus: A table compares the number of divisions, ploidy of resulting cells, and occurrence of crossing over in mitosis versus meiosis.
canonical_answer_1: Mitosis produces two diploid daughter cells with 2n = 6, while meiosis produces four haploid cells with n = 3.
canonical_answer_2: Crossing over during prophase I exchanges DNA between homologous chromosomes, creating new allele combinations in the gametes.
canonical_answers: Mitosis produces two diploid daughter cells with 2n = 6, while meiosis produces four haploid cells with n = 3.
Crossing over during prophase I exchanges DNA between homologous chromosomes, creating new allele combinations in the gametes.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-006

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Mitosis yields cells with 6 chromosomes (2n = 6); meiosis II yields cells with 3 chromosomes (n = 3).
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Compare the chromosome number of cells produced by mitosis to the chromosome number of cells produced at the end of meiosis II for this organism.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Mitosis produces 2 diploid cells each with 6 chromosomes (2n = 6). Meiosis II produces 4 haploid cells each with 3 chromosomes (n = 3).

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Crossing over exchanges segments between homologous chromosomes during prophase I, creating new combinations of alleles on chromatids that differ from either parental chromosome.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain how crossing over during meiosis I increases genetic variation among offspring.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: During prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair and exchange chromosome segments at chiasmata; new combinations of alleles on chromatids are created that were not present in either parent, increasing allele diversity in gametes and offspring.

stem: In a hypothetical plant species, purple flower color (allele A) is dominant over white flower color (allele a). Two heterozygous plants are crossed.
stimulus: Parental cross: Aa x Aa. Students predict offspring phenotypes and genotypes.
canonical_answer_1: Aa x Aa gives a 3 purple : 1 white phenotype ratio, so 25% of offspring are white.
canonical_answer_2: This follows the law of segregation: during meiosis I the two alleles separate so each gamete gets only one allele of the gene.
canonical_answers: Aa x Aa gives a 3 purple : 1 white phenotype ratio, so 25% of offspring are white.
This follows the law of segregation: during meiosis I the two alleles separate so each gamete gets only one allele of the gene.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-007

criteria_json.minimum_fix: The Punnett square gives a 1:2:1 genotypic ratio (AA:Aa:aa) and a 3:1 phenotypic ratio (purple:white).
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Construct a Punnett square for the Aa x Aa cross and predict the expected phenotypic ratio in the offspring.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Correct 2x2 Punnett square showing AA, Aa, Aa, aa. Phenotypic ratio: 3 purple : 1 white (or 75% purple, 25% white).

criteria_json.minimum_fix: The principle of segregation states alleles separate during gamete formation; homologous chromosomes separate at meiosis I, delivering one allele to each gamete.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: State the principle of segregation and explain how meiosis accounts for it at the cellular level.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Principle of Segregation: the two alleles for a gene separate during gamete formation so each gamete carries one allele. Meiosis accounts for this because homologous chromosomes (each carrying one allele) separate during meiosis I, placing one allele into each gamete.

stem: During DNA replication, both strands of the parental double helix serve as templates for synthesis of two new daughter strands.
stimulus: A diagram of a replication fork shows the parental DNA being unwound, with arrows indicating the leading and lagging strands and the locations of helicase and DNA polymerase.
canonical_answer_1: Helicase unwinds the parental DNA at the replication fork, and DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides to build new strands.
canonical_answer_2: Because DNA polymerase can only build 5' to 3', the lagging strand is made in Okazaki fragments that DNA ligase joins into a continuous strand.
canonical_answers: Helicase unwinds the parental DNA at the replication fork, and DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides to build new strands.
Because DNA polymerase can only build 5' to 3', the lagging strand is made in Okazaki fragments that DNA ligase joins into a continuous strand.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-008

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Helicase unwinds the double helix; DNA polymerase adds nucleotides in the 5-prime to 3-prime direction using the template strand.
accepted_variants: helicase unwinds DNA at replication fork
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe the roles of helicase and DNA polymerase at the replication fork.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Helicase unwinds the double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds between base pairs. DNA polymerase adds complementary deoxyribonucleotides to the 3-prime end of the growing strand, synthesizing new DNA in the 5-prime to 3-prime direction using each parental strand as a template.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: DNA polymerase only synthesizes 5 to 3; the lagging strand template runs away from the fork, requiring discontinuous synthesis as Okazaki fragments; DNA ligase seals the nicks between fragments after primer removal.
accepted_variants: synthesized away from fork in fragments
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain why the lagging strand is synthesized in short fragments and describe how these fragments are joined into a continuous strand.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides in the 5-prime to 3-prime direction; the lagging strand template runs antiparallel (3-prime to 5-prime) away from the fork, so synthesis must proceed in short Okazaki fragments, each primed by an RNA primer. Primers are later replaced with DNA by DNA polymerase and gaps are sealed by DNA ligase.

stem: In eukaryotic cells, the primary RNA transcript undergoes several modifications in the nucleus before export to the cytoplasm for translation.
stimulus: A diagram shows a pre-mRNA with labeled exons (E1, E2, E3) and introns (I1, I2) before processing, and two alternative mature mRNA products after splicing.
canonical_answer_1: The pre-mRNA is capped, spliced, and polyadenylated before export from the nucleus.
canonical_answer_2: Alternative splicing joins different combinations of exons from the same pre-mRNA, so one gene can produce multiple proteins with different amino acid sequences.
canonical_answers: The pre-mRNA is capped, spliced, and polyadenylated before export from the nucleus.
Alternative splicing joins different combinations of exons from the same pre-mRNA, so one gene can produce multiple proteins with different amino acid sequences.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-009

criteria_json.minimum_fix: A 5-prime methylguanosine cap is added to protect the mRNA and aid ribosome attachment; a poly-A tail is added to the 3-prime end to protect from degradation.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Identify two modifications made to pre-mRNA during RNA processing in eukaryotes other than splicing.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Any two of: (1) a 5-prime 7-methylguanosine cap is added to the 5-prime end; (2) a poly-A tail of adenine nucleotides is added to the 3-prime end.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Alternative splicing joins different combinations of exons to produce different mRNAs from the same gene; each mRNA encodes a different protein.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain how alternative splicing of a single gene can produce multiple different proteins.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Different exons can be included or excluded from the mature mRNA in different cell types or at different developmental stages; each combination of exons produces a different mRNA, which is translated into a different polypeptide with a different amino acid sequence and potentially different function.

stem: In a forest ecosystem, bark-colored beetles survive predation by insectivorous birds at a higher rate than green-colored beetles resting on tree bark.
stimulus: Over 10 generations, the proportion of bark-colored beetles in the population increases from 20 percent to 75 percent.
canonical_answer_1: Bark-colored beetles survive predation at a higher rate, reproduce more, and pass the bark-color alleles to more offspring; over generations the frequency of those alleles increases in the population.
canonical_answer_2: It is measured by comparing the number of viable, fertile offspring produced by each phenotype or genotype.
canonical_answers: Bark-colored beetles survive predation at a higher rate, reproduce more, and pass the bark-color alleles to more offspring; over generations the frequency of those alleles increases in the population.
It is measured by comparing the number of viable, fertile offspring produced by each phenotype or genotype.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-010

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Bark-colored beetles survive and reproduce at higher rates; alleles producing bark color are passed to more offspring each generation, increasing allele frequency over time.
accepted_variants: alleles for bark color increase in frequency
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain how natural selection acting on phenotypic variation in beetle color changes allele frequencies over generations.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Bark-colored phenotype confers higher survival and reproduction rate; individuals with alleles for bark color contribute more offspring to each generation; over many generations the allele frequency for bark color increases in the population.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Relative fitness is reproductive success compared to the most fit phenotype; measured by comparing the number of surviving offspring produced by bark-colored versus green-colored beetles.
accepted_variants: relative fitness = reproductive success compared to most fit
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Define relative fitness and explain how it would be measured in the beetle population described above.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Relative fitness is the reproductive success of a genotype or phenotype compared to the most reproductively successful phenotype in the population. Measured by comparing survival rate to reproductive age and number of viable offspring produced by bark-colored vs. green-colored beetles per generation.

stem: A botanist surveys a large, randomly mating population of 500 plants for flower color. Red flower (rr, homozygous recessive) plants number 80; all others have white flowers.
stimulus: Students must use Hardy-Weinberg equations (p + q = 1 and p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1) to calculate genotype frequencies.
canonical_answer_1: q^2 = 80/500 = 0.16, so q = 0.40 and p = 0.60; the expected counts are 180 RR, 240 Rr, and 80 rr.
canonical_answer_2: Two Hardy-Weinberg conditions are random mating and a large population; random mating prevents allele choice bias, and a large population reduces genetic drift.
canonical_answers: q^2 = 80/500 = 0.16, so q = 0.40 and p = 0.60; the expected counts are 180 RR, 240 Rr, and 80 rr.
Two Hardy-Weinberg conditions are random mating and a large population; random mating prevents allele choice bias, and a large population reduces genetic drift.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-011

criteria_json.minimum_fix: q^2 = 0.16, so q = 0.4; p = 0.6; 2pq = 0.48; expected heterozygote frequency is 48 percent.
