criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Calculate the expected frequency of heterozygotes (Rr) in this population assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Show your work.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Large population size prevents genetic drift from randomly changing allele frequencies; random mating ensures allele frequencies combine according to probability.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Identify two conditions required for a population to remain in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and explain why each is necessary.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Any two of: large population size (prevents genetic drift); random mating (ensures random allele combination); no mutation (allele frequencies unchanged); no gene flow (no alleles entering or leaving); no natural selection (all genotypes equally fit). Each condition explained mechanistically.

stem: A rabbit population colonizes an island with limited food and space resources. Its growth is tracked over 50 years.
stimulus: A graph shows logistic growth: rapid initial increase, then a leveling off as the population approaches carrying capacity K.
canonical_answer_1: The rabbit population should show logistic growth because resources are limited, so growth slows as it approaches carrying capacity.
canonical_answer_2: Food competition is a density-dependent factor, while drought or fire is density-independent and can reduce population size regardless of density.
canonical_answers: The rabbit population should show logistic growth because resources are limited, so growth slows as it approaches carrying capacity.
Food competition is a density-dependent factor, while drought or fire is density-independent and can reduce population size regardless of density.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-012

criteria_json.minimum_fix: As N approaches K, limited resources increase competition among individuals, reducing birth rates and/or increasing death rates until growth rate approaches zero.
accepted_variants: birth rate falls or death rate rises near K
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain why the rabbit population growth rate slows as the population size approaches the carrying capacity K.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: As population size approaches K, resources per individual (food, space, nesting sites) decrease; competition intensifies; birth rate falls and/or death rate rises; the (K - N)/K term in the logistic equation approaches zero, reducing growth rate.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Density-dependent: predation increases as rabbits become more concentrated, removing more individuals at higher densities. Density-independent: a drought reduces food availability for all rabbits regardless of population size.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Identify one density-dependent factor and one density-independent factor that could limit the rabbit population and explain how each acts.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Density-dependent: e.g., food competition, predation, disease — effect increases as population density increases. Density-independent: e.g., drought, hurricane, wildfire — effect is unrelated to population density; kills individuals regardless of how crowded the population is.

stem: A plant scientist soaks potato cubes of known mass in salt solutions of varying concentration and measures mass change after 24 hours.
stimulus: Data show that cubes gain mass in dilute solutions, lose mass in concentrated solutions, and show no change at an intermediate concentration.
canonical_answer_1: Water potential (Ψ) is the free energy of water relative to pure water; adding solute lowers the solute potential and makes Ψ more negative.
canonical_answer_2: Because the solution has higher water potential (-0.3 MPa) than the cell (-0.5 MPa), water moves into the cell, so the cell gains water.
canonical_answers: Water potential (Ψ) is the free energy of water relative to pure water; adding solute lowers the solute potential and makes Ψ more negative.
Because the solution has higher water potential (-0.3 MPa) than the cell (-0.5 MPa), water moves into the cell, so the cell gains water.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-013

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Water potential is the free energy of water per unit volume; higher solute concentration lowers (makes more negative) water potential by reducing solute potential.
accepted_variants: water potential = solute potential + pressure potential
water moves from high to low water potential
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Define water potential and explain how increasing solute concentration in a solution affects its water potential.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Water potential (psi) is the tendency of water to move from one area to another; measured in megapascals (MPa). Adding solute decreases (makes more negative) the solute potential component (psi-s), thereby decreasing overall water potential — water is less likely to leave a region with high solute concentration.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: The cell will GAIN water because the solution (-0.3 MPa) has a higher water potential than the cell (-0.5 MPa); water moves from higher to lower water potential, so water enters the cell.
accepted_variants: water moves from solution into cell
water moves high to low water potential
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Predict whether a plant cell with a water potential of negative 0.5 MPa placed in a solution with a water potential of negative 0.3 MPa will gain or lose water, and justify your prediction.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: The cell will GAIN water. Water moves from high (less negative) to low (more negative) water potential. The solution has higher water potential (-0.3 MPa) than the cell (-0.5 MPa), so water moves from the solution into the cell.

stem: Most ATP produced during aerobic respiration is generated at the inner mitochondrial membrane through the electron transport chain and ATP synthase.
stimulus: A diagram shows the inner mitochondrial membrane with Complexes I, II, III, and IV, plus ATP synthase, and arrows indicating electron flow and proton pumping.
canonical_answer_1: At the inner mitochondrial membrane, the electron transport chain pumps protons and ATP synthase uses the gradient to make ATP by chemiosmosis.
canonical_answer_2: If Complex IV is inhibited, electron flow stops, the proton gradient collapses, ATP synthase cannot run, and oxidative phosphorylation stops.
canonical_answers: At the inner mitochondrial membrane, the electron transport chain pumps protons and ATP synthase uses the gradient to make ATP by chemiosmosis.
If Complex IV is inhibited, electron flow stops, the proton gradient collapses, ATP synthase cannot run, and oxidative phosphorylation stops.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-014

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Electrons from NADH and FADH2 flow through ETC complexes to oxygen; energy released pumps H+ into the intermembrane space; H+ gradient drives ATP synthesis through ATP synthase by chemiosmosis.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe how electrons move through the electron transport chain and explain what drives ATP synthesis.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: NADH and FADH2 donate electrons to the ETC; electrons pass through protein complexes (I, III, IV), releasing energy that pumps H+ from matrix to intermembrane space; H+ gradient (electrochemical) drives H+ back through ATP synthase; flow of H+ powers phosphorylation of ADP to ATP by chemiosmosis.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Blocking Complex IV halts electron flow through the entire ETC; proton pumping stops; the proton gradient is not maintained; ATP synthase cannot produce ATP; aerobic respiration nearly ceases.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Predict what would happen to ATP production if a chemical inhibitor blocked Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) and explain why.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: ETC would halt because electrons cannot be transferred to oxygen (final acceptor); H+ pumping stops; proton gradient dissipates; ATP synthase cannot make ATP; NADH and FADH2 cannot be re-oxidized; Krebs cycle and glycolysis would slow. Net result: ATP synthesis drops dramatically.

stem: In E. coli, genes that encode lactose-metabolizing enzymes are controlled by the lac operon, a cluster of genes with shared regulatory sequences.
stimulus: A diagram shows the lac operon with the regulatory gene (lacI), promoter, operator, and structural genes (lacZ, lacY, lacA), plus the repressor protein and allolactose.
canonical_answer_1: When lactose is absent, the lac repressor binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase from transcribing the lac structural genes, so the operon is off.
canonical_answer_2: When glucose is scarce, adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP; CAP-cAMP binds near the lac promoter and increases RNA polymerase binding, boosting transcription.
canonical_answers: When lactose is absent, the lac repressor binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase from transcribing the lac structural genes, so the operon is off.
When glucose is scarce, adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP; CAP-cAMP binds near the lac promoter and increases RNA polymerase binding, boosting transcription.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-015

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Without lactose, the lac repressor binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase, so the structural genes are not transcribed.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe what happens to lac operon transcription when lactose is absent from the environment.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: When lactose is absent, the lac repressor (lacI gene product) binds to the operator sequence, physically blocking RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes; lacZ, lacY, and lacA are not transcribed and lactase enzymes are not produced.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Low glucose raises cAMP levels; cAMP-CAP complex binds upstream of the promoter and enhances RNA polymerase binding, increasing transcription of the lac structural genes.
accepted_variants: high cAMP when glucose is low
catabolite activator protein binds promoter region
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain why glucose deprivation also increases lac operon expression (catabolite repression / positive control).
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: When glucose is absent, adenylyl cyclase is active and cAMP levels rise; cAMP binds to CAP (catabolite activator protein); CAP-cAMP complex binds to the CAP site upstream of the lac promoter and stimulates RNA polymerase binding, increasing transcription of the structural genes — this is positive control on top of negative (repressor) control.

stem: A mountain range formed 2 million years ago divided a formerly continuous lizard population into two geographically isolated groups.
stimulus: Present-day descendants of the two groups have morphological and behavioral differences. When brought into contact in the lab, they rarely interbreed and hybrids have reduced survival.
canonical_answer_1: Geographic isolation stops gene flow, so the lizard populations diverge by mutation, natural selection, and drift.
canonical_answer_2: A prezygotic barrier like behavioral isolation prevents mating, and a postzygotic barrier like hybrid sterility reduces the reproductive success of any offspring that do form.
canonical_answers: Geographic isolation stops gene flow, so the lizard populations diverge by mutation, natural selection, and drift.
A prezygotic barrier like behavioral isolation prevents mating, and a postzygotic barrier like hybrid sterility reduces the reproductive success of any offspring that do form.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-016

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Physical separation prevented gene flow; each population independently accumulated genetic differences through mutation and natural selection; eventually reproductive isolation arose, producing two distinct species.
accepted_variants: independent evolution via mutation and selection
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain how allopatric speciation could produce two distinct species from a single ancestral population.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Geographic isolation (mountain range) prevents gene flow between populations; each population accumulates different mutations and evolves under different selection pressures; over time genetic differences accumulate to the point where the two groups can no longer interbreed successfully even if barriers were removed.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Prezygotic: behavioral isolation — the two groups do not recognize each other as potential mates, preventing mating attempts. Postzygotic: hybrid inviability — offspring from mixed-group matings have reduced survival or fertility.
accepted_variants: prezygotic: behavioral, temporal, or mechanical isolation
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe one prezygotic and one postzygotic reproductive isolating mechanism that could prevent interbreeding between the two lizard groups if they came back into contact.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Prezygotic: behavioral isolation (different mating displays or pheromones prevent courtship); or temporal isolation (different mating seasons); or mechanical isolation (incompatible genitalia). Postzygotic: hybrid inviability (hybrid offspring die before reproducing); or hybrid sterility (hybrids are sterile, as in the scenario).

stem: Ecologists studying a meadow ecosystem measure biomass and energy at each trophic level of the food chain: grass to grasshopper to frog to hawk.
stimulus: A pyramid of energy shows: grass 10,000 kcal, grasshoppers 1,000 kcal, frogs 100 kcal, hawks 10 kcal.
canonical_answer_1: Most energy at each trophic level is lost as heat during cellular respiration and used in metabolism; only the energy stored in new biomass is available to the next level.
canonical_answer_2: If grasshoppers decline, frogs get less food and hawks then get less energy, so the hawk population would decrease.
canonical_answers: Most energy at each trophic level is lost as heat during cellular respiration and used in metabolism; only the energy stored in new biomass is available to the next level.
If grasshoppers decline, frogs get less food and hawks then get less energy, so the hawk population would decrease.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-017

criteria_json.minimum_fix: About 90 percent of energy is lost as heat through cellular respiration and metabolic processes at each trophic level; only about 10 percent is stored in new biomass available to the next level.
accepted_variants: energy not stored is lost as heat
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain why only approximately 10 percent of the energy at one trophic level is available to the next trophic level.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Most energy consumed at each trophic level is lost as heat during cellular respiration; some is used for metabolism, growth, and reproduction; some is excreted as waste; only the energy stored in new biomass (approximately 10%) is available to the next trophic level.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Fewer grasshoppers reduces energy available to frogs; frog population declines; reduced frog population provides less energy to hawks; hawk population decreases due to reduced food supply.
accepted_variants: less energy to frogs then to hawks
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Predict how the hawk population would be affected if the grasshopper population declined sharply, and explain using energy flow principles.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Hawk population would decrease. Fewer grasshoppers means less energy available to frogs (the trophic level below hawks); frog population declines; less energy available to hawks; hawk birth rate falls and/or death rate rises; hawk population shrinks. Loss of energy at one trophic level cascades up the food chain.

stem: Cells in multicellular organisms communicate and exchange materials through direct cell-to-cell connections.
stimulus: A diagram shows two animal cells joined by gap junctions (connexin channels) and two plant cells joined by plasmodesmata passing through the cell wall.
canonical_answer_1: Gap junctions are clusters of connexin channels spanning neighboring animal cell membranes, while plasmodesmata are cytoplasmic channels through plant cell walls, often with a desmotubule.
canonical_answer_2: In cardiac muscle, gap junctions let ions and electrical signals spread directly from cell to cell, synchronizing depolarization and contraction.
canonical_answers: Gap junctions are clusters of connexin channels spanning neighboring animal cell membranes, while plasmodesmata are cytoplasmic channels through plant cell walls, often with a desmotubule.
In cardiac muscle, gap junctions let ions and electrical signals spread directly from cell to cell, synchronizing depolarization and contraction.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-018

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Gap junctions are protein-lined channels through adjacent animal cell plasma membranes; plasmodesmata are channels through plant cell walls lined with plasma membrane, directly connecting plant cell cytoplasm.
accepted_variants: gap junctions: connexin proteins, no cell wall
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Compare the structure of gap junctions in animal cells to plasmodesmata in plant cells.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Gap junctions: protein channels (connexins) span both plasma membranes of adjacent animal cells, forming a direct cytoplasmic connection; no cell wall involved. Plasmodesmata: channels lined with plasma membrane that pass through the cell walls of adjacent plant cells, connecting cytoplasm; may contain desmotubule (ER strand).

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Gap junctions allow ions to pass directly between cardiac muscle cells; an electrical signal in one cell spreads to adjacent cells through gap junctions, causing coordinated depolarization and contraction across the heart tissue.
accepted_variants: action potential propagates cell to cell
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain how gap junctions allow cardiac muscle cells to contract in a coordinated wave.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Gap junctions allow ions (Na+, Ca2+, K+) and small molecules to pass directly between cardiac muscle cells; an electrical signal (action potential) depolarizes one cell and ions flow through gap junctions to the next cell, triggering its depolarization; the signal propagates cell-to-cell as a wave without requiring neuromuscular junctions at each cell.

stem: The endosymbiotic theory proposes that mitochondria and chloroplasts evolved from free-living prokaryotes that were engulfed by a host cell and eventually became permanent organelles.
stimulus: No additional stimulus provided. Students answer based on knowledge of mitochondrial structure, genetics, and biochemistry.
canonical_answer_1: Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own circular DNA and divide by binary fission, consistent with endosymbiosis.
canonical_answer_2: Their double membranes fit engulfment: the inner membrane is from the original bacterium, and the outer membrane came from the host's vesicle during engulfment.
canonical_answers: Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own circular DNA and divide by binary fission, consistent with endosymbiosis.
Their double membranes fit engulfment: the inner membrane is from the original bacterium, and the outer membrane came from the host's vesicle during engulfment.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-019

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Mitochondria contain their own circular DNA similar to bacterial chromosomes; mitochondria have 70S ribosomes like bacteria, not the 80S ribosomes of the eukaryotic cytoplasm.
accepted_variants: inner membrane resembles bacterial plasma membrane
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe two pieces of evidence from mitochondria that support the endosymbiotic theory.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Any two of: (1) mitochondria have their own circular DNA, resembling prokaryotic chromosomes; (2) mitochondria have 70S ribosomes similar to bacteria, not 80S eukaryotic ribosomes; (3) mitochondria reproduce by binary fission; (4) mitochondria have inner membranes similar in composition to bacterial plasma membranes; (5) mitochondria are similar in size to bacteria.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: The outer mitochondrial membrane came from the host cell plasma membrane when the prokaryote was engulfed; the inner membrane is the remnant of the original prokaryotic plasma membrane — two distinct origins explain the double membrane.
accepted_variants: outer membrane from host cell endocytosis
inner membrane from prokaryote plasma membrane
two membranes from two different origins
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Explain how the double membrane of the mitochondrion is consistent with the endosymbiotic theory.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: The outer membrane is derived from the host cell membrane that surrounded the engulfed prokaryote during endocytosis; the inner membrane is derived from the original prokaryotic plasma membrane. Two separate membrane origins produce the double-membrane structure.

stem: The human body maintains blood glucose concentration within a narrow range through hormonal feedback mechanisms.
stimulus: A graph shows blood glucose rising after a carbohydrate-rich meal, then returning to the set point over approximately 2 hours.
canonical_answer_1: Insulin lowers high blood glucose and glucagon raises low blood glucose through negative feedback.
canonical_answer_2: Oxytocin during childbirth is a positive feedback example: contractions trigger more oxytocin release, which intensifies contractions until delivery, making the response adaptive because it rapidly completes the process.
canonical_answers: Insulin lowers high blood glucose and glucagon raises low blood glucose through negative feedback.

Oxytocin during childbirth is a positive feedback example: contractions trigger more oxytocin release, which intensifies contractions until delivery, making the response adaptive because it rapidly completes the process.
title: APBIO-FRQ-S-020

criteria_json.minimum_fix: Rising blood glucose triggers insulin secretion from beta cells; insulin signals cells to take up glucose and convert it to glycogen; blood glucose returns to set point; reduced glucose lowers insulin release.
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Describe how a negative feedback loop returns blood glucose to the set point after a carbohydrate-rich meal.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Blood glucose rises above set point; pancreatic beta cells detect elevated glucose; insulin is secreted; insulin stimulates muscle and adipose cells to take up glucose and liver to store glucose as glycogen; blood glucose falls back to set point; falling glucose reduces insulin secretion, completing the negative feedback loop.

criteria_json.minimum_fix: During childbirth, oxytocin promotes uterine contractions; contractions stimulate more oxytocin release, amplifying contractions until delivery — positive feedback is adaptive because it drives labor to completion quickly rather than stalling.
accepted_variants: positive feedback drives process to completion
adaptive because completes a rapid necessary event
criteria_json.learner_facing_text: Identify one example of positive feedback in human physiology and explain why it is adaptive despite amplifying a deviation from a baseline.
criteria_json.evidence_requirements: Any valid example: (1) childbirth — oxytocin promotes uterine contractions; stronger contractions release more oxytocin; cycle escalates until baby is delivered, then stops (adaptive: ensures delivery is completed quickly); (2) blood clotting — platelets activate more platelets to rapidly seal a wound; (3) action potential depolarization — Na+ influx opens more Na+ channels. In each case the amplification drives a specific process to rapid completion, which is beneficial.

stem: Which property of water is most directly responsible for the needle remaining on the surface before soap was added?
stimulus: A student placed a steel needle carefully on the surface of water in a bowl. The needle floated despite being denser than water. When a drop of dish soap was added near the needle, it immediately sank. A classmate observed that water strider insects exploit the same property to walk across pond surfaces.

subtopics: 1.1 Structure of Water and Hydrogen Bonding

title: APBIO-MCQ-001

choices_json.rationale: Adhesion describes water's attraction to other materials, not water-to-water attraction.
choices_json.choice_text: Adhesion between water molecules and the needle's metal surface

choices_json.rationale: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules create cohesion, which manifests as surface tension.
choices_json.choice_text: Cohesion between water molecules generating surface tension

choices_json.rationale: Specific heat capacity describes resistance to temperature change, not surface resistance to penetration.
choices_json.choice_text: Water's high specific heat capacity, which slows the needle's movement into the surface

choices_json.rationale: Evaporation removes molecules from the surface; it does not create upward pressure.
choices_json.choice_text: The evaporation of water from the surface creating an upward pressure on the needle

stem: Which concept best explains why amylase acted on starch but not on the other substrates?
stimulus: A researcher tested the enzyme amylase by mixing it separately with: (1) a starch solution, (2) a gelatin solution, and (3) a sucrose solution. After 30 minutes at 37°C and pH 7, iodine tests revealed starch breakdown only in the first tube.
title: APBIO-MCQ-002

choices_json.rationale: Cofactors are not substrate-specific.
choices_json.choice_text: Amylase requires a metal cofactor found only in starch solutions

choices_json.rationale: Enzyme-substrate specificity is primarily shape-based, not simple electrostatic attraction.
choices_json.choice_text: Starch is negatively charged, attracting it to the positively charged active site of amylase

choices_json.rationale: Enzyme specificity arises from shape complementarity between the active site and its substrate.
choices_json.choice_text: Only starch has the complementary shape to fit amylase's active site, enabling enzyme-substrate binding

choices_json.rationale: Starch molecules are far larger than sucrose, yet amylase acts on starch. Size alone does not determine enzyme specificity.
choices_json.choice_text: Protein and sucrose molecules are too large to fit inside the enzyme's active site

stem: Which best explains why pepsin activity was lost under both conditions (2) and (3)?
stimulus: Pepsin functions optimally at pH 2. A researcher compared: (1) 37°C, pH 2 — max activity; (2) 37°C, pH 7 — near-zero activity; (3) boiled at 100°C then returned to 37°C pH 2 — near-zero activity. Western blot confirmed pepsin protein was detectable under all three conditions.
title: APBIO-MCQ-003

choices_json.rationale: Peptide bonds are covalent and are not broken by mild pH shifts or brief boiling.
choices_json.choice_text: In both conditions, pepsin's primary structure (peptide bonds) was disrupted, destroying the active site

choices_json.rationale: Protein substrates are stable at pH 7, and temperature changes do not dilute substrate.
choices_json.choice_text: At pH 7, the substrate was destroyed; at 100°C, the substrate concentration became too dilute

choices_json.rationale: Water viscosity does not change appreciably between pH 2 and pH 7.
choices_json.choice_text: At pH 7, pepsin's substrate could no longer enter the active site due to increased water viscosity; at 100°C, the substrate was digested before activity could be measured

choices_json.rationale: Protein tertiary structure is maintained by non-covalent interactions. pH changes alter ionization of R-groups; high temperature overcomes all non-covalent stabilizing interactions.
choices_json.choice_text: At pH 7, altered ionization of R-groups disrupted ionic and hydrogen bonds maintaining pepsin's tertiary structure; at 100°C, thermal energy disrupted hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds, and ionic bonds, denaturing the protein

stem: The pattern that A ≈ T and G ≈ C across all four species is best explained by which structural feature of the DNA molecule?
stimulus:
A biochemist analyzes the nucleotide composition of double-stranded DNA extracted from four different species. Results (% of total nucleotides):

Species | A | T | G | C
Human | 30.4 | 30.1 | 19.9 | 19.6
Bacteria | 24.7 | 24.9 | 25.2 | 25.2
Virus | 18.1 | 18.3 | 31.8 | 31.8
Wheat | 27.3 | 27.1 | 22.7 | 22.9

Minor deviations from exact equality are due to measurement error.
title: APBIO-MCQ-004

choices_json.rationale: Chargaff's rules are a direct consequence of complementary base pairing: A–T (two H-bonds) and G–C (three H-bonds). Every A on one strand is paired with exactly one T on the complementary strand, ensuring equal totals. The pattern holds regardless of the organism's overall GC content.
choices_json.choice_text: In the double-stranded molecule, adenine hydrogen-bonds specifically with thymine and guanine hydrogen-bonds specifically with cytosine, so each base on one strand requires exactly one complementary base on the other

choices_json.rationale: Antiparallel orientation refers to strand directionality (5'→3' opposing 3'→5'), not base composition ratios. A single strand can have any ratio of purines to pyrimidines; the A = T and G = C pattern emerges from base pairing across both strands.
choices_json.choice_text: The antiparallel orientation of the two DNA strands forces equal numbers of purines and pyrimidines on each strand

choices_json.rationale: The 1:1 ratio is a structural consequence of double-strandedness, not a product of natural selection. Single-stranded DNA and RNA do not follow Chargaff's rules, demonstrating that the ratio is a physical constraint of base pairing, not a selected trait.
choices_json.choice_text: Natural selection has conserved a 1:1 purine-to-pyrimidine ratio because unequal ratios would be lethal to all organisms

choices_json.rationale: The sugar-phosphate backbone connects to any nitrogenous base equally; there is no biochemical preference for purine vs. pyrimidine at the backbone level. The equal ratios arise from interstrand base pairing, not backbone chemistry.
choices_json.choice_text: Deoxyribose sugars in the backbone preferentially bind purines and pyrimidines in equal proportions

stem: Why do glucose, galactose, and fructose have different biological properties despite sharing the same molecular formula?
stimulus: Glucose, galactose, and fructose are all simple sugars with the identical molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆. Despite this, they taste differently, are metabolized through different pathways, and are recognized by different membrane transport proteins. Galactose cannot be directly used by cells that lack the enzyme galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase, even when glucose is abundant.
title: APBIO-MCQ-005

choices_json.rationale: All three have identical atomic counts — C₆H₁₂O₆. This distractor tests whether students understand that the same molecular formula can describe structurally distinct molecules.
choices_json.choice_text: They differ in the number of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms

choices_json.rationale: All three monosaccharides are produced by many of the same organisms, and elemental composition is identical by definition of sharing the molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆.
choices_json.choice_text: They are made by different organisms and therefore have different elemental compositions

choices_json.rationale: Glucose, galactose, and fructose are isomers — same molecular formula, different structural arrangements. These geometric differences determine how each molecule fits into enzyme active sites and transport proteins, producing distinct metabolic and sensory properties.
choices_json.choice_text: They differ in the spatial arrangement of atoms around certain carbon atoms, making them structural isomers with different molecular geometries

choices_json.rationale: Peptide bonds connect amino acids in proteins, not monosaccharides. Monosaccharides are monomers with no subunits connected by peptide bonds. This tests correct association of bond types with macromolecule classes.
choices_json.choice_text: They differ in the number of peptide bonds connecting their subunits

stem: Based on the data, which conclusion about the two inhibitors is most strongly supported?
stimulus:
A researcher measures enzyme reaction rates at increasing substrate concentrations with two inhibitors, each at the same concentration:

[S] mM | No inhibitor | + Inhibitor P | + Inhibitor Q
0.5    |     12       |      8        |      6
1.0    |     20       |     14        |     10
2.0    |     32       |     22        |     16
5.0    |     45       |     43        |     20
10.0   |     48       |     47        |     22
20.0   |     50       |     50        |     22

Reaction rates are in μmol/min.
title: APBIO-MCQ-006

choices_json.rationale: Competitive inhibitors compete with substrate for the active site; high substrate concentrations outcompete them and Vmax is restored (Inhibitor P reaches 50 μmol/min at saturation). Noncompetitive inhibitors bind allosterically and reduce Vmax regardless of substrate concentration (Inhibitor Q is capped at ~22 μmol/min at all high concentrations).
choices_json.choice_text: Inhibitor P is competitive and Inhibitor Q is noncompetitive, because Inhibitor P's effect is overcome at high substrate concentrations while Inhibitor Q permanently reduces the maximum reaction rate

choices_json.rationale: If both were competitive, both should recover to the same Vmax at saturating substrate. Inhibitor Q never reaches 50 μmol/min, indicating it does not compete for the active site. Potency differences alone cannot account for a permanently reduced Vmax.
choices_json.choice_text: Both inhibitors are competitive, but Inhibitor Q is more potent than Inhibitor P

choices_json.rationale: Inhibitor P's effect disappears at high substrate concentrations (Vmax = 50, same as no-inhibitor), which is the hallmark of competitive inhibition. A noncompetitive inhibitor would show a proportionally reduced Vmax even at substrate saturation.
choices_json.choice_text: Inhibitor P is noncompetitive because it reduces activity proportionally at all substrate concentrations

choices_json.rationale: Reduction at all tested concentrations is necessary but not sufficient to conclude noncompetitive inhibition. The definitive test is whether Vmax recovers at substrate saturation. Inhibitor P's Vmax fully recovers to 50 μmol/min, ruling out noncompetitive inhibition.
choices_json.choice_text: Both inhibitors are noncompetitive because both reduce reaction rates at all tested substrate concentrations

stem: Which property of water explains why beetles must collect water quickly before significant evaporation, and which explains why liquid water beads and rolls along the hydrophobic troughs rather than spreading flat?
stimulus: Namib Desert beetles collect water by tilting toward coastal fog at dawn. Droplets condense on hydrophilic bumps on their back surfaces and roll toward their mouths along hydrophobic troughs. Researchers noted that beetles must collect water before peak daytime heat causes significant evaporative loss from their body surface. A separate study found that transferring the same mass of water from liquid to vapor requires substantially more energy than melting the same mass of ice.

subtopics: 1.1 Structure of Water and Hydrogen Bonding

title: APBIO-MCQ-007

choices_json.rationale: Specific heat describes resistance to temperature change, not evaporation rate or surface behavior. High specific heat does not cause water to bead on hydrophobic surfaces. Conflating all water properties under one mechanism is a common error.
choices_json.choice_text: High specific heat explains both phenomena: it slows evaporation and causes water to resist spreading on surfaces

choices_json.rationale: Adhesion explains why water clings to hydrophilic bumps but does not explain beading and rolling on hydrophobic surfaces. On hydrophobic surfaces, cohesion (water-to-water) exceeds adhesion (water-to-surface), causing beading. A single property cannot explain both behaviors.
choices_json.choice_text: Adhesion explains both: water clings to hydrophilic bumps and rolls away from hydrophobic troughs due to differential adhesion

choices_json.rationale: Polarity is the underlying basis of water's hydrogen bonding but does not by itself predict evaporation urgency or beading behavior. Polarity is a proximate structural feature; cohesion and heat of vaporization are the emergent properties that explain these observations.
choices_json.choice_text: Polarity of water explains both phenomena: polar water molecules evaporate slowly and repel hydrophobic surfaces

choices_json.rationale: In hot desert conditions, thermal energy drives rapid evaporation despite the high energy cost per gram lost. Cohesion (H-bond attraction between water molecules) is stronger than water's attraction to hydrophobic surfaces, so water beads into droplets that can roll along the trough rather than spreading and evaporating from a flat film.
choices_json.choice_text: High heat of vaporization means each gram of water that evaporates in desert heat carries away substantial energy, driving rapid net evaporation; cohesion causes water molecules to remain attracted to each other and bead rather than spread on the hydrophobic troughs

stem: Which best explains the molecular basis for HbS polymerization under low-oxygen conditions?
stimulus: Sickle cell disease results from a single amino acid substitution in β-globin: glutamic acid (polar, negatively charged at pH 7.4) at position 6 is replaced by valine (nonpolar, hydrophobic). Under low-oxygen conditions, sickle hemoglobin (HbS) polymerizes into rigid fibers that deform red blood cells. Normal hemoglobin (HbA) does not polymerize under the same conditions. Structural studies show that deoxygenated HbS exposes a hydrophobic patch on its surface that complementarily fits a hydrophobic pocket on adjacent HbS molecules.
title: APBIO-MCQ-008

choices_json.rationale: Valine (MW 117 Da) is lighter than glutamic acid (MW 147 Da), and protein aggregation at cellular scales is not driven by gravity. This distractor tests whether students attribute polymerization to mass rather than intermolecular chemistry.
choices_json.choice_text: Valine at position 6 increases the molecular weight of HbS, causing aggregation driven by gravitational settling

choices_json.rationale: Deoxygenation causes a conformational change in HbS that exposes a hydrophobic pocket. Valine's nonpolar side chain fits this pocket, and the thermodynamic drive to minimize water-exposed hydrophobic surface area (the hydrophobic effect) promotes chain formation. HbA's glutamic acid at position 6 is charged and cannot insert into this hydrophobic pocket.
choices_json.choice_text: The hydrophobic valine at position 6 inserts into the complementary hydrophobic pocket exposed on adjacent deoxygenated HbS molecules, driving chain polymerization through hydrophobic interactions

choices_json.rationale: Disulfide bonds form between cysteine residues; valine does not contain a thiol group and cannot form or disrupt disulfide bonds. Hemoglobin's quaternary structure is maintained by non-covalent interactions, not disulfide bonds.
choices_json.choice_text: Valine disrupts the disulfide bonds that normally maintain hemoglobin's quaternary structure, causing uncontrolled aggregation

choices_json.rationale: HbS can bind oxygen; the problem is that deoxygenated HbS specifically polymerizes. The substitution's effect on polymerization is through the hydrophobic surface interaction, not through oxygen-binding capacity. Oxygenated HbS does not polymerize even with valine at position 6.
choices_json.choice_text: The loss of glutamic acid's negative charge at position 6 directly prevents HbS from binding oxygen, causing polymerization as an indirect consequence

stem: Which evaluation of the student's prediction is best supported by the data?
stimulus:
A researcher measures carbonic anhydrase activity (which catalyzes CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃) at various pH values:

pH  | Activity (units/min)
6.0 | 15
6.5 | 35
7.0 | 72
7.4 | 100
7.8 | 74
8.0 | 40
8.5 | 12

The researcher then adds carbonic anhydrase to a sealed buffer at pH 7.4 with excess CO₂ and measures activity over 60 minutes. A student predicts the reaction will slow over time due to product-mediated pH change.
title: APBIO-MCQ-009

choices_json.rationale: H₂CO₃ is an acid; its accumulation will lower pH in the sealed buffer. The data shows activity at pH 6.5 is only 35% of maximum — a sealed system without a sink for H⁺ will drive the reaction toward inhibitory conditions, validating the prediction through a pH-mediated mechanism.
choices_json.choice_text: The prediction is supported: H₂CO₃ produced in the sealed system will lower pH, shifting conditions away from the enzyme's optimum and progressively reducing activity

choices_json.rationale: The data show the opposite — activity drops steeply outside pH 7.4, falling to 15% at pH 6.0 and 12% at pH 8.5. Students who misread the table may conclude the enzyme is broadly tolerant when it is actually sharply pH-sensitive.
choices_json.choice_text: The prediction is unsupported: the data show enzyme activity is equally high across pH 6.0 to pH 8.5

choices_json.rationale: Product inhibition is a real regulatory mechanism. Additionally, the proposed mechanism here is indirect — not direct active-site blocking by product — further undermining this blanket claim.
choices_json.choice_text: The prediction is unsupported: enzymes are never inhibited by the products they catalyze

choices_json.rationale: The student's prediction invokes pH change, not competitive inhibition — these are mechanistically distinct. The data on pH-dependent activity directly support the prediction without requiring competitive inhibition to be the mechanism.
choices_json.choice_text: The prediction is supported only if H₂CO₃ acts as a competitive inhibitor at the active site, which the data cannot confirm

stem: Which conclusion about the evolution of these antifreeze proteins is best supported by all the evidence?
stimulus: Arctic fish (family Zoarcidae) and Antarctic fish (family Nototheniidae) both produce antifreeze proteins (AFPs) that bind nascent ice crystals and prevent their growth. Structural analysis shows both AFP types contain repetitive arrays of threonine and alanine residues forming a flat, hydrophilic ice-binding surface. However, sequence similarity between the two AFP types is only 22% (near random-chance levels), and gene-origin analysis shows Arctic AFPs evolved from a sialic acid synthase gene while Antarctic AFPs evolved from a pancreatic enzyme gene.
title: APBIO-MCQ-010

choices_json.rationale: Horizontal gene transfer is extremely rare in vertebrates and cannot explain different ancestral source genes (sialic acid synthase vs. pancreatic enzyme). The 22% sequence similarity is inconsistent with recent gene transfer.
choices_json.choice_text: Horizontal gene transfer spread AFP genes from one lineage to the other, explaining the structural similarity despite different apparent origins

choices_json.rationale: The physical constraint of blocking ice crystal growth requires a specific molecular geometry regardless of evolutionary origin. Strong directional selection for any mutation producing a flat, hydrophilic threonine-alanine surface independently drove convergence in two unrelated lineages — explaining structural similarity despite near-random sequence identity and different ancestral genes.
choices_json.choice_text: Convergent evolution driven by the same selection pressure (sub-freezing ocean temperatures) independently produced structurally similar ice-binding surfaces from different ancestral sequences

choices_json.rationale: 22% similarity is at or below random-chance levels and is inconsistent with common ancestry. Moreover, the two AFP types derive from completely different ancestral genes — they could not share a common AFP ancestor.
choices_json.choice_text: Both lineages inherited AFP genes from a common polar ancestor; the 22% sequence similarity reflects normal divergence over millions of years

choices_json.rationale: Genetic drift is a random, non-directional process that rarely produces identical functional outcomes independently. The appearance of functionally equivalent structures in two lineages exposed to the same extreme selection pressure is strong evidence of natural selection, not drift.
choices_json.choice_text: Genetic drift in isolated polar populations randomly generated identical ice-binding sequences in both lineages

stem: Which conclusion about early life is best supported by integrating all three pieces of evidence?
stimulus: Evidence supporting the RNA World hypothesis includes: (1) ribozymes that catalyze their own replication in vitro; (2) the ribosomal peptidyl transferase center — which forms peptide bonds — is composed entirely of RNA; ribosomal proteins are structural, not catalytic; (3) kinetic data for a self-replicating ribozyme: Km = 0.8 mM (similar to protein enzymes), kcat = 0.003 s⁻¹ (≈10,000× lower than typical protein enzymes), with 50-fold kcat enhancement upon adding Mg²⁺.
title: APBIO-MCQ-011

choices_json.rationale: Early pre-biotic systems did not require the metabolic throughput of modern cells. Slow catalysis is consistent with viability in a pre-cellular context. The existence of self-replicating ribozymes directly refutes the claim that RNA cannot catalyze.
choices_json.choice_text: RNA cannot have been the original catalyst because its kcat is too low to sustain any metabolism

choices_json.rationale: Ribosomal proteins are structural scaffolding, not catalytic. The RNA core performs peptide bond formation. Concluding proteins came first based on the ribosome inverts the actual evidence.
choices_json.choice_text: Proteins must have preceded RNA because the ribosome requires protein subunits to function

choices_json.rationale: Mg²⁺ is a cofactor that enhances RNA catalysis, not a replacement catalyst. The evidence positions RNA as the primary catalyst, with metal ions as assistants — not the other way around.
choices_json.choice_text: Mg²⁺ ions were the original catalysts in pre-biotic chemistry; RNA evolved later to replace metal-ion catalysis

choices_json.rationale: Evidence 1 shows RNA can self-replicate (information + catalysis combined). Evidence 2 shows RNA's catalytic role in translation was conserved even after proteins evolved — the ribosome is a molecular fossil. Evidence 3 explains why proteins superseded RNA catalytically (higher kcat) while also explaining how Mg²⁺-assisted RNA catalysis was sufficient in pre-biotic conditions.
choices_json.choice_text: RNA likely preceded proteins as both the informational and catalytic molecule, but RNA catalysis depended on metal-ion cofactors and was far slower than modern protein enzymes — explaining why proteins eventually took over most catalytic roles while RNA's catalytic role in translation was retained

stem: Which best explains why identical glucose monomers produce polysaccharides with dramatically different structures, functions, and enzyme specificities?
stimulus: Glycogen, starch, and cellulose are all polysaccharides built entirely from glucose monomers. Glycogen and starch form compact, branched or helical structures easily hydrolyzed by amylase. Cellulose forms rigid, unbranched chains that pack via hydrogen bonds into microfibrils. Amylase that efficiently digests starch cannot break down cellulose; cellulase that degrades cellulose cannot act on starch.
title: APBIO-MCQ-012

choices_json.rationale: All three polymers use identical glucose monomers (C₆H₁₂O₆). The differences arise from how those identical monomers are joined, not from compositional differences.
choices_json.choice_text: Glucose in cellulose has a different molecular formula than glucose in starch and glycogen

choices_json.rationale: Branching influences how quickly a polymer can be mobilized, but the fundamental functional difference between starch/glycogen and cellulose is the type of glycosidic bond (α vs. β), which determines 3D conformation and enzyme recognition — not branching per se.
choices_json.choice_text: The degree of branching alone determines whether a polysaccharide functions in energy storage or structural support

choices_json.rationale: α(1→4) bonds in starch and glycogen create helical, compact conformations that amylase recognizes. β(1→4) bonds in cellulose flip alternating glucose units 180°, producing straight chains that pack into rigid microfibrils. Enzymes evolved active sites complementary to one bond geometry, not the other — explaining mutual inability to cross-digest.
choices_json.choice_text: The type of glycosidic linkage (α vs. β) between glucose monomers determines the polymer's three-dimensional shape and which enzyme active sites can accommodate it

choices_json.rationale: Cellulose is composed entirely of glucose; the rigidity of microfibrils arises from inter-chain hydrogen bonding, not from covalent crosslinks or non-glucose monomers.
choices_json.choice_text: Cellulose contains additional non-glucose monomers that covalently crosslink chains, providing rigidity that starch and glycogen lack

stem: Which sequence correctly describes the endomembrane pathway tPA follows from synthesis to secretion?
stimulus: A cell biologist uses pulse-chase labeling with radioactive amino acids to track a secretory protein (tPA) in human endothelial cells. Radioactive signal appears first in a membrane-bound network studded with ribosomes, then in a compact stack of flattened membranes near the nucleus, then in small membrane vesicles, and finally outside the cell.
title: APBIO-MCQ-013

choices_json.rationale: Secretory proteins are synthesized on ribosomes bound to the rough ER, not on free ribosomes. Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and does not receive newly synthesized secretory proteins first.
choices_json.choice_text: Free ribosomes → smooth ER → Golgi apparatus → plasma membrane

choices_json.rationale: Proteins are synthesized by ribosomes on the rough ER, not in the nucleus. The nucleus contains DNA and produces mRNA; it does not produce or initially receive protein.
choices_json.choice_text: Nucleus → rough ER → Golgi apparatus → secretory vesicles

choices_json.rationale: Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and is not the initial site of secretory protein synthesis. Lysosomes are digestive compartments and are not an intermediate in the secretory pathway for tPA.
choices_json.choice_text: Smooth ER → Golgi apparatus → lysosomes → plasma membrane

choices_json.rationale: Secretory proteins are translated by ribosomes on the rough ER and enter the ER lumen. They travel in vesicles to the cis-Golgi, are modified through the Golgi cisternae, and are packaged into secretory vesicles at the trans-Golgi that fuse with the plasma membrane to release protein.
choices_json.choice_text: Rough ER → Golgi apparatus → secretory vesicles → extracellular space

stem: Which conclusion about cell classification is most directly supported by the observations?
stimulus: Two cells are compared under electron microscopy. Cell 1 is approximately 2 μm in diameter, has a single circular chromosome in the cytoplasm, 70S ribosomes, no membrane-bound organelles, and a peptidoglycan cell wall. Cell 2 is approximately 20 μm in diameter, has multiple linear chromosomes within a double-membrane nucleus, 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm, mitochondria, and an endoplasmic reticulum.
title: APBIO-MCQ-014

choices_json.rationale: All cells have ribosomes and DNA; the presence of these features does not distinguish prokaryotes from eukaryotes. The defining distinction is the presence or absence of membrane-bound compartments, particularly a membrane-enclosed nucleus.
choices_json.choice_text: Cell 1 is eukaryotic because it has ribosomes and genetic material

choices_json.rationale: Eukaryotic cells also have ribosomes and DNA. Cell 2's membrane-bound nucleus, mitochondria, and endomembrane system identify it definitively as eukaryotic.
choices_json.choice_text: Both cells are prokaryotic because both contain ribosomes and DNA

choices_json.rationale: The defining characteristic of eukaryotes is membrane-bound compartmentalization (nucleus, mitochondria, ER). Cell 1 lacks all membrane-bound organelles — a prokaryote. Cell 2 has a membrane-enclosed nucleus and organelles — a eukaryote. Ribosome size (70S vs. 80S) provides additional supporting evidence.
choices_json.choice_text: Cell 1 is prokaryotic and Cell 2 is eukaryotic, based on the presence or absence of membrane-bound organelles and a membrane-enclosed nucleus

choices_json.rationale: Multiple linear chromosomes within a membrane-bound nucleus is a hallmark of eukaryotes, not prokaryotes. This inverts the relationship between chromosome complexity and cell type.
choices_json.choice_text: Cell 2 is prokaryotic because having multiple chromosomes indicates a simpler genome organization than a single circular chromosome

stem: Based on the fluid mosaic model, what is the most likely role of cholesterol in maintaining red blood cell membrane function at 10°C?
stimulus: Researchers compared membranes of a mammalian red blood cell (containing ~40% cholesterol by mole fraction) and Mycoplasma bacteria (which lack cholesterol entirely). When both cell types are chilled from 37°C to 10°C, Mycoplasma membranes become rigid and non-functional, while mammalian red blood cell membranes remain fluid and functional. When cholesterol is extracted from red blood cell membranes using methyl-β-cyclodextrin and the cells are then chilled to 10°C, they also become rigid and lyse.
title: APBIO-MCQ-015

choices_json.rationale: At low temperatures, phospholipid fatty acid tails tend to pack tightly and solidify. Cholesterol's rigid ring structure inserts between tails at an angle, creating spacing that prevents crystallization. This explains why cholesterol-depleted red blood cells become rigid at 10°C just as Mycoplasma (which lack cholesterol) do.
choices_json.choice_text: Cholesterol inserts between phospholipid fatty acid tails, preventing them from packing into a rigid crystalline array and maintaining membrane fluidity at low temperatures

choices_json.rationale: Cholesterol is a structural membrane lipid, not an energy source. ATP hydrolysis, not cholesterol, powers active transport. This distractor conflates membrane structure with energy metabolism.
choices_json.choice_text: Cholesterol provides energy to membrane transport proteins, allowing active pumps to maintain ion gradients at low temperatures

choices_json.rationale: Cholesterol does not function as thermal insulation, and membrane thickness changes are not the mechanism by which cholesterol maintains fluidity. The mechanism is direct prevention of fatty acid tail crystallization.
choices_json.choice_text: Cholesterol increases membrane thickness, insulating the phospholipid interior from external temperature changes

choices_json.rationale: Cholesterol does not covalently or strongly crosslink phospholipid head groups. Its function is in the hydrophobic core among fatty acid tails, and it maintains fluidity at cold temperatures, not rigidity at warm ones.
choices_json.choice_text: Cholesterol crosslinks adjacent phospholipid head groups via hydrogen bonds, rigidifying the membrane only at temperatures above 37°C

stem: Which best explains why celery in distilled water becomes rigid rather than lysing, unlike animal cells in hypotonic solution?
stimulus: A student places strips of celery into three solutions for 30 minutes: (1) distilled water, (2) 0.9% NaCl solution (approximately isotonic to the cytoplasm), and (3) 20% NaCl solution. After 30 minutes, the strip in distilled water is rigid and crisp; the strip in 0.9% NaCl is slightly flexible; the strip in 20% NaCl is limp and wilted. The student notes that unlike red blood cells placed in distilled water, the celery does not burst.
title: APBIO-MCQ-016

choices_json.rationale: Plant cell membranes are permeable to water via osmosis and aquaporins — the cell does take up water, which is what causes rigidity. If the membrane were impermeable to water, no change would be observed.
choices_json.choice_text: Plant cell membranes are impermeable to water, preventing osmotic uptake in distilled water

choices_json.rationale: Plant cells typically have equal or higher solute concentrations than animal cells. The key difference is structural (cell wall), not osmotic concentration.
choices_json.choice_text: Plant cells have lower solute concentrations than animal cells, so they absorb less water in hypotonic solution

choices_json.rationale: Water enters plant cells by osmosis (cytoplasm is hyperosmotic relative to distilled water), but the cell wall exerts an equal and opposing pressure (turgor pressure) as the cell expands. Wall pressure prevents lysis even as internal pressure rises, making the cell rigid. Animal cells lack walls and lyse when water influx exceeds membrane tolerance.
choices_json.choice_text: The rigid cell wall resists expansion as water enters via osmosis, generating turgor pressure that makes the cell and tissue rigid without allowing the cell to burst

choices_json.rationale: Plant cells do not have water-pumping mechanisms. Turgor regulation in the short term is passive (governed by wall pressure), not driven by active water export. Active water pumping is not a mechanism available to plant cells.
choices_json.choice_text: Plant cells actively pump water out of the cell to counteract osmotic influx, maintaining constant volume

stem: Which best explains why the Na⁺/K⁺ pump must consume ATP rather than operating spontaneously like ion leak channels?
stimulus: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump in neurons transports 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ into the cell per ATP hydrolyzed. In a resting neuron, Na⁺ concentration is approximately 145 mM outside and 12 mM inside; K⁺ is approximately 4 mM outside and 140 mM inside. When neurons are treated with ouabain (a pump inhibitor) and deprived of ATP, these concentration gradients dissipate over 30 minutes as both ions diffuse down their gradients via leak channels.
title: APBIO-MCQ-017

choices_json.rationale: The pump moves Na⁺ and K⁺ in opposite directions (Na⁺ out, K⁺ in), not the same direction. Even if they moved together, simple co-direction would not require ATP — the thermodynamic requirement is about moving ions against their individual electrochemical gradients.
choices_json.choice_text: The pump moves Na⁺ and K⁺ in the same direction, requiring energy to overcome electrostatic repulsion between co-transported ions

choices_json.rationale: The resting concentrations of both ions are highly unequal across the membrane. The pump works to maintain — not equalize — these gradients. This distractor inverts the direction of work.
choices_json.choice_text: The pump moves both ions at equal concentrations on both sides of the membrane, and ATP provides the energy to maintain equal distribution

choices_json.rationale: Ion channel proteins facilitate dehydration and passage without consuming ATP. The energy requirement of the pump is thermodynamic (moving ions against their gradients), not mechanical (overcoming hydration shells).
choices_json.choice_text: The pump requires ATP because Na⁺ and K⁺ ions are too hydrated to pass through membrane proteins without chemical assistance to strip their water shells

choices_json.rationale: Na⁺ is already highly concentrated outside (145 vs. 12 mM) and would spontaneously diffuse inward; pumping it out is work. K⁺ is concentrated inside (140 vs. 4 mM) and would diffuse outward; pumping it in is work. ATP hydrolysis couples to these unfavorable movements, driving them forward.
choices_json.choice_text: The pump moves Na⁺ out against its inward electrochemical gradient and K⁺ in against its outward concentration gradient — both movements are thermodynamically unfavorable and require free energy input from ATP hydrolysis

stem: Which prediction about individuals with familial hypercholesterolemia is best supported by the described mechanism?
stimulus: Liver cells take up LDL cholesterol via receptor-mediated endocytosis. LDL receptors cluster in clathrin-coated pits on the plasma membrane, bind LDL particles, and internalize them as endocytic vesicles. In the acidic endosome, LDL releases from its receptor; cholesterol is liberated in the cytoplasm and the receptor recycles to the plasma membrane. In familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), mutations eliminate functional LDL receptors from the cell surface.
title: APBIO-MCQ-018

choices_json.rationale: Non-specific phagocytosis does not selectively compensate for missing LDL receptors, and liver cells do not typically engage in phagocytosis of lipoproteins. There is no evidence that alternative bulk uptake is sufficient to maintain normal LDL clearance.
choices_json.choice_text: Their liver cells will upregulate non-specific phagocytosis to compensate for the lack of receptor-mediated endocytosis

choices_json.rationale: Without surface LDL receptors, clathrin-coated pits cannot concentrate LDL for internalization. LDL cannot be cleared from the blood by liver cells, causing plasma LDL cholesterol to rise dramatically — the defining clinical feature of FH and a major cardiovascular risk factor.
choices_json.choice_text: LDL particles will accumulate in the bloodstream because liver cells cannot specifically recognize and internalize them without functional receptors

choices_json.rationale: While cholesterol delivery is impaired, the question asks about LDL particle accumulation in blood. Increased intracellular synthesis is a downstream consequence but is not the primary predicted outcome asked about in this question.
choices_json.choice_text: Cholesterol synthesis inside liver cells will increase because LDL-derived cholesterol never reaches the cytoplasm to inhibit synthesis

choices_json.rationale: Without functional receptors, LDL never enters the cell at all — so lysosomes cannot accumulate LDL. Lysosomal accumulation would require internalization, which is precisely what is absent in FH.
choices_json.choice_text: Lysosomes in FH liver cells will accumulate undigested LDL because the recycling pathway for receptors is blocked

stem: Which pair of molecular properties best predicts the rate at which a molecule crosses a pure phospholipid bilayer without protein assistance?
stimulus:
A researcher measures the rate at which different molecules cross a pure phospholipid bilayer (no membrane proteins present):

Molecule  | Size   | Charge/Polarity | Crossing rate
O₂        | Small  | Nonpolar        | Very fast
Ethanol   | Small  | Slightly polar  | Fast
H₂O       | Small  | Polar           | Slow
Glucose   | Large  | Polar           | Not detectable
Na⁺       | Small  | Charged ion     | Not detectable
Cl⁻       | Small  | Charged ion     | Not detectable
title: APBIO-MCQ-019

choices_json.rationale: The data show O₂ (small + nonpolar) crosses very fast; ethanol (small + slightly polar) crosses fast; H₂O (small + polar) crosses slowly despite small size; glucose (large + polar) and ions (charged) do not cross detectably. Both lipid solubility and size matter — size alone cannot explain why small Na⁺ cannot cross while small O₂ can.
choices_json.choice_text: Lipid solubility (nonpolarity) and small molecular size together predict fast crossing; large size or charge/polarity reduces or eliminates crossing

choices_json.rationale: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are small but do not cross detectably; O₂ and Na⁺ are similar in size yet have dramatically different crossing rates. Size alone cannot account for the observed pattern — polarity and charge are critical variables.
choices_json.choice_text: Molecular size alone: smaller molecules always cross faster regardless of polarity

choices_json.rationale: H₂O is neutral but crosses only slowly; glucose is neutral but does not detectably cross. Charge is important (ions are excluded), but neutrality alone is not sufficient — polarity and size also determine crossing rates.
choices_json.choice_text: Electrical charge alone: neutral molecules always cross; charged molecules never cross

choices_json.rationale: This predicts the opposite of what is observed. Ions and glucose are highly water-soluble yet cannot cross. Nonpolar O₂ has very low water solubility and crosses fastest. Higher water solubility correlates with lower, not higher, membrane permeability.
choices_json.choice_text: Water solubility: the more water-soluble a molecule is, the faster it crosses the membrane

stem: Which set of solution osmolarities is most consistent with the observed outcomes for Solutions X, Y, and Z respectively?
stimulus: Red blood cells (which lack a cell wall) were placed in three unlabeled solutions for 5 minutes and photographed. In Solution X, cells appeared as normal biconcave discs. In Solution Y, cells swelled to a spherical shape and approximately 30% lysed. In Solution Z, cells developed irregular spiked protrusions (crenation) and shrank. Normal red blood cell cytoplasm has an osmolarity of approximately 300 mOsm/L.
title: APBIO-MCQ-020

choices_json.rationale: This assigns the hypertonic solution (500 mOsm/L) to the normal-appearing cells and isotonic (300 mOsm/L) to the swelling cells — both backwards. Cells in 500 mOsm/L would crenate, not appear normal.
choices_json.choice_text: X = 500 mOsm/L; Y = 300 mOsm/L; Z = 100 mOsm/L

choices_json.rationale: X (300 mOsm/L) = isotonic → no net water movement → normal biconcave shape. Y (100 mOsm/L) = hypotonic → net water influx → swelling and lysis when membrane tension is exceeded. Z (500 mOsm/L) = hypertonic → net water efflux → cell shrinkage and crenation.
choices_json.choice_text: X = 300 mOsm/L; Y = 100 mOsm/L; Z = 500 mOsm/L

choices_json.rationale: This reverses Y and Z. A 500 mOsm/L solution causes crenation (water leaves the cell), not swelling and lysis. A 100 mOsm/L solution causes swelling, not crenation.
choices_json.choice_text: X = 300 mOsm/L; Y = 500 mOsm/L; Z = 100 mOsm/L

choices_json.rationale: Cells in 100 mOsm/L (hypotonic) would swell and lyse, not appear as normal biconcave discs. This assigns the hypotonic solution to the normal-appearance group, which is inconsistent with osmotic principles.
choices_json.choice_text: X = 100 mOsm/L; Y = 300 mOsm/L; Z = 500 mOsm/L

stem: Which outcome for the mutant secretory enzyme is most likely?
stimulus: Secretory proteins destined for export are targeted to the rough ER during translation by a hydrophobic N-terminal signal peptide. As the ribosome synthesizes the signal peptide, a signal recognition particle (SRP) binds it and docks the ribosome-mRNA complex to the rough ER membrane. Translation resumes and the protein is threaded into the ER lumen. A researcher creates a mutant form of a secretory enzyme in which the signal peptide sequence has been deleted.
title: APBIO-MCQ-021

choices_json.rationale: Without a signal peptide, the ribosome is never directed to the rough ER membrane. Translation occurs on free ribosomes in the cytoplasm — the enzyme never enters the ER and so cannot accumulate in the lumen.
choices_json.choice_text: The enzyme is synthesized normally by membrane-bound ribosomes, but accumulates inside the ER lumen instead of being secreted

choices_json.rationale: The Golgi receives cargo from the ER via vesicles; it does not directly receive proteins from free ribosomes. No direct ribosome-to-Golgi pathway exists in eukaryotic cells.
choices_json.choice_text: The enzyme enters the Golgi directly from free ribosomes, bypassing the ER

choices_json.rationale: The signal peptide is required for SRP recognition and ER targeting. Without it, ribosomes continue translation in the cytoplasm and release the completed protein there. The protein cannot enter the secretory pathway, lacks glycosylation or other ER-dependent modifications, and is not secreted.
choices_json.choice_text: The enzyme is translated on free cytoplasmic ribosomes, remains in the cytoplasm, and is never secreted

choices_json.rationale: The proteasome degrades ubiquitin-tagged proteins, typically those that are misfolded or damaged — not all proteins lacking signal peptides. Many cytoplasmic proteins function normally without signal peptides. Immediate proteasomal degradation is not a predicted outcome for a properly folded protein that simply lacks a targeting sequence.
choices_json.choice_text: The enzyme is immediately degraded by the proteasome because proteins lacking signal peptides are recognized as misfolded

stem: Which single piece of evidence most specifically supports the mechanism of endosymbiosis — that a bacterium was engulfed by a proto-eukaryote — rather than simply demonstrating bacterial ancestry?
stimulus: Evidence supporting the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria includes: (1) mitochondria have a double membrane — the inner membrane resembles a bacterial plasma membrane while the outer membrane resembles eukaryotic endomembrane; (2) mitochondria contain 70S ribosomes sensitive to bacterial antibiotics (e.g., streptomycin) that do not inhibit cytoplasmic 80S ribosomes; (3) mitochondria have their own circular DNA lacking histones; (4) mitochondria replicate by binary fission independently of nuclear division.
title: APBIO-MCQ-022

choices_json.rationale: Evidence (1) is specific to the engulfment mechanism: the inner membrane = original bacterial plasma membrane; the outer membrane = phagosomal membrane derived from the host cell. This directly describes the physical consequence of endocytosis. Evidence (2), (3), and (4) demonstrate bacterial ancestry but do not specifically describe the mechanism of acquisition.
choices_json.choice_text: The double membrane structure, with the outer membrane resembling host endomembrane and the inner membrane resembling a bacterial plasma membrane, is consistent with a bacterium being surrounded by a phagocytic membrane that became the outer mitochondrial membrane

choices_json.rationale: Circular, histone-free DNA demonstrates bacterial ancestry but does not prove independent viability — modern mitochondria have transferred most of their original genome to the nuclear genome and are obligately dependent on the host cell.
choices_json.choice_text: Circular DNA lacking histones proves mitochondria are currently capable of independent survival outside the cell

choices_json.rationale: Binary fission is consistent with bacterial ancestry but does not specifically address the mechanism by which bacteria came to reside inside eukaryotic cells. It distinguishes mitochondria from eukaryotic organelles that arise de novo but does not describe the engulfment event.
choices_json.choice_text: Replication by binary fission proves that mitochondria were once free-living bacteria

choices_json.rationale: Antibiotic sensitivity demonstrates bacterial ribosome type but does not prove mitochondria are independent bacteria — modern mitochondria are obligate endosymbionts, not free-living bacteria. This evidence supports bacterial ancestry, not the current status as autonomous bacteria.
choices_json.choice_text: Sensitivity to antibiotics targeting 70S ribosomes proves that mitochondria are currently bacteria living inside eukaryotic cells

stem: Which characterization of this protein is best supported by all three experimental results?
stimulus: Researchers characterize membrane proteins in red blood cells using three techniques: (1) Detergent (Triton X-100) solubilizes the lipid bilayer and releases integral proteins into detergent micelles; (2) High-salt washes (1M NaCl) disrupt ionic interactions and release proteins from membrane surfaces without dissolving the bilayer; (3) Impermeant biotin-NHS (a labeling reagent too large to cross the membrane) is applied to intact cells, labeling only extracellular-facing protein domains. A newly discovered red blood cell protein is released by high-salt wash, is not labeled by impermeant biotin, and is not found in Triton X-100 micelles.
title: APBIO-MCQ-023

choices_json.rationale: Integral transmembrane proteins require detergent for removal (Triton X-100) — high-salt wash cannot release them. Also, not being labeled by impermeant biotin does not distinguish extracellular vs. cytoplasmic facing for a transmembrane protein.
choices_json.choice_text: An integral transmembrane protein with its primary domain on the extracellular face

choices_json.rationale: Lipid-anchored proteins on the extracellular face would be labeled by impermeant biotin-NHS, since their protein domain is exposed extracellularly. The protein of interest is not biotin-labeled, ruling out an extracellular-facing surface location.
choices_json.choice_text: A lipid-anchored protein on the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane

choices_json.rationale: Secreted extracellular matrix proteins would be exposed to the impermeant biotin label. Not being labeled means this protein faces the cytoplasm, not the extracellular space.
choices_json.choice_text: A secreted extracellular matrix protein that is loosely associated with the outer membrane surface

choices_json.rationale: High-salt release (not detergent required) = peripheral protein, not integral. Not labeled by impermeant biotin = cytoplasmic face, not extracellular. Absence from Triton micelles confirms it is not embedded in the lipid bilayer. All three results are consistent with a peripheral protein on the cytoplasmic leaflet held by ionic interactions.
choices_json.choice_text: A peripheral protein associated with the cytoplasmic face of the membrane via electrostatic interactions

stem: Which conclusion integrating membrane biochemistry and evolutionary ecology is best supported by the data?
stimulus:
Researchers compared plasma membrane phospholipid composition in desert lizards (body temperature 42°C) and deep-sea Antarctic fish (body temperature −1°C):

Species           | % Saturated FA | % Monounsaturated FA | % Polyunsaturated FA
Desert lizard     |      61        |         30           |         9
Antarctic fish    |      17        |         43           |         40

Both species maintain functional (fluid) membranes at their respective environmental temperatures. Desert lizard membranes solidify when cooled to −1°C; Antarctic fish membranes become excessively fluid when warmed to 42°C.
title: APBIO-MCQ-024

choices_json.rationale: Membrane phospholipid composition is a structural feature, not an energy reserve. Energy storage uses triacylglycerols, not membrane phospholipids. This distractor conflates membrane lipid composition with metabolic energy storage.
choices_json.choice_text: Desert lizards evolved high saturated fat content as an energy reserve because hot environments provide insufficient caloric food sources

choices_json.rationale: Unsaturated fatty acid tails contain double bonds that create kinks, preventing close packing even at low temperatures — maintaining fluidity in Antarctic fish at −1°C. Saturated tails pack tightly, requiring higher temperatures to become fluid — appropriate for desert lizards at 42°C. The inverse relationship between environmental temperature and membrane unsaturation across independent lineages reflects homeoviscous adaptation by natural selection.
choices_json.choice_text: Natural selection has independently favored membrane compositions that maintain optimal fluidity at each species' functional temperature: unsaturated fatty acids (which have kinked tails that resist tight packing) are enriched in cold-adapted species to prevent membrane crystallization, while saturated fatty acids predominate in heat-adapted species to prevent excessive membrane fluidity

choices_json.rationale: While dietary fatty acids can influence membrane composition, the highly precise temperature-correlated regulation of membrane unsaturation across unrelated organisms reflects active enzymatic desaturation driven by selective pressure — not passive dietary incorporation. This explanation also fails to account for why the selection pressure specifically matches thermal environment.
choices_json.choice_text: Antarctic fish have more polyunsaturated fatty acids because their diet of krill is rich in omega-3 fatty acids, which are directly incorporated unchanged into membranes

choices_json.rationale: Saturated and unsaturated fatty acid synthesis have similar energetic costs; the difference is the presence or absence of desaturase enzyme activity. Thermodynamic economy of synthesis is not a documented driver of the observed membrane composition differences — thermal adaptation of fluidity is.
choices_json.choice_text: Desert lizards produce saturated fatty acids because saturated fats are metabolically less expensive to synthesize, providing a fitness advantage in resource-limited hot environments

stem: Which chain of reasoning correctly connects the cellular membrane change to the whole-organism survival outcome in dehydrated wild-type mice?
stimulus: Aquaporin-2 (AQP2) is a water channel protein in kidney collecting duct cells regulated by antidiuretic hormone (ADH). In dehydrated animals, ADH is secreted from the posterior pituitary and causes AQP2-containing vesicles inside collecting duct cells to fuse with the apical (urine-facing) plasma membrane, inserting AQP2 channels within 15 minutes. AQP2 density on the apical membrane increases 5-fold. In mice with AQP2 mutations preventing hormone-regulated membrane insertion, urine output is 10× greater than in wild-type mice; these mice die within 48 hours without unlimited water access.
title: APBIO-MCQ-025

choices_json.rationale: The kidney medulla is hyperosmotic relative to tubular urine. AQP2 insertion into the apical membrane allows water to flow down its osmotic gradient from tubular lumen into the medulla and ultimately into blood. Without AQP2 insertion, water cannot move across the apical membrane efficiently, so it remains in the tubule and is excreted as dilute urine — as seen in the mutant mice.
choices_json.choice_text: ADH → AQP2 inserts into apical membrane → increased water permeability of collecting duct → osmotic movement of water from the hypoosmotic tubular lumen into the hyperosmotic kidney medulla → urine becomes concentrated → body water is conserved → survival during dehydration

choices_json.rationale: This inverts the mechanism. ADH causes AQP2 insertion, not degradation. Fewer channels would produce the mutant phenotype (excess dilute urine), not water conservation. The chain of causation is reversed.
choices_json.choice_text: ADH → AQP2 is degraded from the apical membrane → fewer water channels → less water reabsorption → more dilute urine → blood becomes hyperosmotic → kidney retains water by osmosis

choices_json.rationale: AQP2 inserts into the apical (urine-facing) membrane, not the basolateral membrane. Water must first cross the apical membrane from the tubular lumen into the cell before exiting via constitutively expressed aquaporins on the basolateral side. Moving water from blood into the tubule would worsen dehydration, not correct it.
choices_json.choice_text: ADH → AQP2 inserts into the basolateral (blood-facing) membrane → water moves from blood into the kidney tubule → urine becomes dilute → blood volume increases → dehydration is reversed

choices_json.rationale: AQP2 is a water channel; it does not block sodium channels. Na⁺ retention in the tubule would retain water in the lumen and produce concentrated urine through an osmotic effect, but this is not the AQP2 mechanism.
