Na⁺ transport in the collecting duct is regulated by aldosterone acting on epithelial sodium channels (ENaC), a separate hormonal pathway.
choices_json.choice_text: ADH → AQP2 blocks sodium channels on the apical membrane → Na⁺ accumulates in the tubule → high tubular osmolarity retains water in the lumen → concentrated urine is produced

stem: Which correctly classifies the three types of chemical signaling described?
stimulus: A hormone (insulin) is secreted from pancreatic β-cells and travels through the bloodstream to target cells in the liver, muscle, and adipose tissue many centimeters away. Prostaglandins released from damaged skin cells act on capillary endothelial cells less than 1 mm away. Acetylcholine released from a motor neuron diffuses across a 20 nm synaptic cleft to bind receptors on the adjacent muscle cell.
title: APBIO-MCQ-026

choices_json.rationale: Insulin travels long distances through the circulatory system — the defining feature of endocrine signaling, not paracrine. Prostaglandins act on nearby cells — paracrine, not endocrine. Acetylcholine crosses a synapse to act on an adjacent cell — synaptic, not autocrine. All three classifications are reversed or misassigned.
choices_json.choice_text: Insulin = paracrine; prostaglandin = endocrine; acetylcholine = autocrine

choices_json.rationale: Endocrine signaling uses the bloodstream to reach distant target cells (insulin). Paracrine signaling involves local diffusion to nearby cells (prostaglandins, <1 mm). Synaptic signaling is a specialized form in which a neurotransmitter crosses a narrow cleft to act on an immediately adjacent target cell (acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction).
choices_json.choice_text: Insulin = endocrine; prostaglandin = paracrine; acetylcholine = synaptic

choices_json.rationale: Autocrine signaling requires a cell to respond to its own secreted signal — pancreatic β-cells do not respond to insulin they secrete. Synaptic signaling requires a structured synapse, not the diffuse spread of prostaglandins through tissue. Acetylcholine acts locally across a cleft, not through the circulatory system.
choices_json.choice_text: Insulin = autocrine; prostaglandin = synaptic; acetylcholine = endocrine

choices_json.rationale: Release into extracellular space is shared by all forms of chemical signaling, not a defining criterion of endocrine signaling. The defining feature of endocrine signaling is systemic transport via the circulatory system to act on distant targets — prostaglandins and acetylcholine act locally and never enter the bloodstream as signaling agents.
choices_json.choice_text: All three are examples of endocrine signaling because all involve chemical messengers released into the extracellular space

stem: Which best explains why epinephrine and cortisol produce responses at such different timescales despite acting on the same cell type?
stimulus: Epinephrine (a water-soluble catecholamine) and cortisol (a lipid-soluble glucocorticoid) both regulate the stress response in liver cells. Epinephrine triggers glycogen breakdown within seconds; cortisol alters gene expression patterns over 4–6 hours. Cellular fractionation shows epinephrine binds to membrane fractions while cortisol is detected in nuclear fractions. Blocking protein synthesis with cycloheximide eliminates cortisol's metabolic effects but leaves epinephrine's effects intact.
title: APBIO-MCQ-027

choices_json.rationale: Epinephrine produces the faster response (seconds), not the slower one. Additionally, molecular size does not govern response speed in this context — receptor location and signaling mechanism do. This choice inverts the relationship between the two hormones.
choices_json.choice_text: Epinephrine is a larger molecule and requires more time to find and bind its receptor, explaining the delayed response

choices_json.rationale: Cortisol is lipid-soluble and crosses the membrane to bind intracellular receptors — not membrane receptors. This choice inverts the receptor locations of the two hormones.
choices_json.choice_text: Cortisol binds membrane receptors that activate a longer second-messenger cascade than epinephrine's intracellular receptor pathway

choices_json.rationale: Water-soluble epinephrine cannot cross the membrane and acts through surface receptors coupled to rapid second-messenger cascades (no new protein needed). Lipid-soluble cortisol crosses the membrane and its receptor complex acts as a transcription factor, requiring hours for new mRNA to be transcribed and new proteins to be translated and active — which cycloheximide blocks.
choices_json.choice_text: Epinephrine binds membrane receptors and activates pre-existing cytoplasmic signaling proteins via second messengers; cortisol diffuses across the membrane, binds intracellular receptors, and the hormone-receptor complex directly regulates gene transcription — requiring new mRNA and protein synthesis before effects appear

choices_json.rationale: The mechanisms are fundamentally different (membrane receptor/second messenger vs. intracellular receptor/gene regulation). Concentration differences do not account for a seconds-vs-hours timescale discrepancy, and cortisol is not necessarily present at higher concentration.
choices_json.choice_text: Both hormones act through identical intracellular mechanisms; the timescale difference reflects the higher concentration of cortisol in the bloodstream

stem: Which effect of forskolin on cardiac cells is most directly predicted by the described pathway?
stimulus: Beta-adrenergic receptors on cardiac muscle cells are GPCRs. When epinephrine binds, the receptor activates the Gs protein, which activates adenylyl cyclase, converting ATP to cAMP. cAMP activates protein kinase A (PKA), which phosphorylates ion channels and contractile proteins, increasing heart rate and force. A researcher applies forskolin — a plant-derived compound that directly activates adenylyl cyclase — to cardiac cells in the absence of epinephrine or any other ligand.
title: APBIO-MCQ-028

choices_json.rationale: Forskolin acts directly on adenylyl cyclase, the enzyme that produces cAMP. Because all pathway components downstream of adenylyl cyclase (cAMP → PKA → phosphorylation of targets) are intact, the cellular response — increased heart rate and contractility — is identical to that triggered by epinephrine, even though the receptor and Gs were never activated.
choices_json.choice_text: Forskolin will raise intracellular cAMP and activate PKA, producing the same downstream effects as epinephrine despite bypassing the receptor and Gs protein

choices_json.rationale: Forskolin acts directly on adenylyl cyclase, bypassing both the receptor and the Gs protein entirely. It does not interact with Gs. This choice misidentifies the site of forskolin's action.
choices_json.choice_text: Forskolin will activate the Gs protein, which then activates adenylyl cyclase through the same mechanism as epinephrine

choices_json.rationale: Phosphodiesterase inhibitors (such as theophylline or IBMX) block cAMP degradation. Forskolin activates cAMP synthesis by directly stimulating adenylyl cyclase — a mechanistically distinct action.
choices_json.choice_text: Forskolin will block cAMP degradation by phosphodiesterase, amplifying the basal cAMP level already present in resting cells

choices_json.rationale: The entire significance of forskolin as a research tool is that it activates adenylyl cyclase independently of Gs. This makes it useful for bypassing upstream receptor/G-protein steps to directly test downstream cAMP-dependent signaling.
choices_json.choice_text: Forskolin will have no effect because adenylyl cyclase requires an activated Gs protein in order to respond to any stimulus

stem: Why does a single epinephrine molecule produce a cellular response orders of magnitude larger than directly introducing a single PKA molecule into the same cell?
stimulus: One epinephrine molecule binds one receptor, which activates many Gs proteins. Each Gs activates one adenylyl cyclase, and each adenylyl cyclase catalyzes production of many cAMP molecules per unit time. Each cAMP activates one PKA, and each PKA phosphorylates hundreds of target proteins per unit time. In a control experiment, a single active PKA molecule is microinjected directly into a cell — bypassing all upstream steps — and target phosphorylation is measured.
title: APBIO-MCQ-029

choices_json.rationale: Binding affinity describes how tightly a molecule associates with its target, not how many downstream reactions it triggers. The amplification advantage of epinephrine comes from the multiplicative cascade, not from affinity differences.
choices_json.choice_text: Epinephrine has higher binding affinity for its receptor than PKA has for its substrates, making receptor-mediated signaling intrinsically more efficient per molecule

choices_json.rationale: Cascade amplification is multiplicative: at each step, one activated molecule produces multiple activated molecules at the next level. The total response from one epinephrine molecule equals (Gs per receptor) × (cAMP per adenylyl cyclase) × (phosphorylations per PKA) — far exceeding the activity of a single PKA. This is the fundamental purpose of signal transduction cascades.
choices_json.choice_text: Epinephrine triggers multiple sequential amplification steps — one receptor activates many Gs proteins, each producing many cAMP molecules, each activating one PKA — so the response reflects the product of amplification at each step, while a single injected PKA molecule produces only that one enzyme's activity

choices_json.rationale: cAMP is a second messenger that allosterically activates PKA by binding its regulatory subunits — it does not itself phosphorylate target proteins. Phosphorylation is exclusively carried out by the kinase (PKA), not by cAMP.
choices_json.choice_text: The cAMP molecules generated by epinephrine directly phosphorylate target proteins in addition to activating PKA, providing a parallel amplification pathway absent from direct PKA injection

choices_json.rationale: The described pathway involves only the GPCR → Gs → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA cascade. The amplification advantage comes from the multiplicative steps within this one pathway, not from activating a second independent cascade.
choices_json.choice_text: Epinephrine simultaneously activates the adenylyl cyclase pathway and a separate parallel kinase cascade, doubling the number of phosphorylated targets compared to PKA alone

stem: Which best explains why apoptosis — rather than necrosis — is essential for sculpting the spaces between developing digits?
stimulus: During human hand development, interdigital cells undergo programmed cell death (apoptosis). Caspase enzymes are activated by cytochrome c release from mitochondria (intrinsic pathway) and by death-ligand binding to surface receptors (extrinsic pathway). Active caspases systematically dismantle the cell: cleaving cytoskeletal proteins, fragmenting DNA, and producing membrane-bound apoptotic bodies that are phagocytosed by neighboring cells without rupturing. In necrosis, cellular contents spill into surrounding tissue, triggering inflammation. Mice lacking the pro-apoptotic genes Bax and Bak retain webbing between their digits.
title: APBIO-MCQ-030

choices_json.rationale: Apoptosis consumes energy (ATP-dependent) rather than releasing usable ATP to neighbors. Apoptotic bodies are phagocytosed for recycling of macromolecules, not as an energy donation. Digit growth is not fueled by energy from dying cells.
choices_json.choice_text: Apoptosis provides energy to neighboring digit cells by releasing ATP from dying interdigital cells, fueling the growth of digits

choices_json.rationale: Apoptotic cells package themselves into membrane-bound bodies that are cleanly phagocytosed, releasing no inflammatory signals. This allows selective elimination of specific cells — the interdigital mesenchyme — without damaging the neighboring digit progenitor cells. Necrosis would trigger inflammation that could disrupt digit development. The Bax/Bak knockout phenotype directly confirms that pro-apoptotic signaling is required for interdigital clearance.
choices_json.choice_text: Apoptosis eliminates interdigital cells in an orderly, contained manner that prevents inflammation and preserves the integrity of adjacent digit tissue, allowing precise sculpting of the hand

choices_json.rationale: Necrosis is typically faster than apoptosis (minutes vs. hours). The developmental advantage of apoptosis is its controlled, inflammation-free nature — not its speed.
choices_json.choice_text: Apoptosis is faster than necrosis, ensuring interdigital cells are eliminated within the narrow developmental window before digit formation is complete

choices_json.rationale: Apoptosis results in cell death and removal, not reprogramming or differentiation. Apoptotic cells do not become osteoblasts; they are eliminated and their molecular components recycled by phagocytes.
choices_json.choice_text: Apoptosis reprograms interdigital cells into digit bone-forming osteoblasts, increasing the number of cells available for skeletal development

stem: A drug specifically blocks receptor dimerization without affecting G proteins. Which receptor type is affected and what signaling consequence is predicted?
stimulus: Two receptor classes are compared. Receptor class X (GPCR): a single 7-transmembrane polypeptide that, upon ligand binding, undergoes conformational change and activates a trimeric G protein by promoting GDP-to-GTP exchange on the α subunit. Receptor class Y (RTK): two separate receptor monomers that, upon ligand binding, come together (dimerize) and each phosphorylates tyrosine residues on the other (transphosphorylation), creating docking sites for intracellular signaling proteins bearing SH2 domains.
title: APBIO-MCQ-031

choices_json.rationale: GPCRs are single polypeptides and do not require dimerization for activation. The drug has no effect on GPCRs. G protein dissociation is initiated by the receptor's conformational change after ligand binding, not by receptor dimerization.
choices_json.choice_text: GPCR; the drug would prevent G protein dissociation into α and βγ subunits, blocking downstream signaling

choices_json.rationale: RTK activation absolutely requires dimerization: only when two monomers come together can each phosphorylate the other's tyrosines in trans. Without dimerization, no transphosphorylation occurs, no SH2-domain proteins are recruited, and the entire downstream cascade (including RAS and MAPK activation) is blocked — despite the ligand binding normally.
choices_json.choice_text: RTK; the receptor monomers would remain present at the cell surface but could not transphosphorylate each other, eliminating the phosphotyrosine docking sites required for SH2-domain signaling protein recruitment

choices_json.rationale: GPCRs are monomeric and achieve their activating conformational change as a single polypeptide upon ligand binding. Dimerization is a mechanistic requirement only for RTKs, not GPCRs.
choices_json.choice_text: Both receptor types; both GPCRs and RTKs require dimerization to undergo the conformational change that activates their respective downstream signaling partners

choices_json.rationale: RTK activation requires transphosphorylation in trans between two monomers. While some kinase activity in cis is possible at very high expression levels, physiological RTK activation depends on dimerization-dependent transphosphorylation. A drug blocking dimerization would substantially eliminate signaling.
choices_json.choice_text: RTK; but signaling would be unaffected because each RTK monomer can phosphorylate its own tyrosines (autophosphorylation in cis) without needing a partner

stem: What does the db-cAMP rescue experiment most directly demonstrate about the role of Gs in this pathway?
stimulus: A GPCR signal transduction pathway operates as: Ligand → Receptor → Gs protein → Adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA → Transcription factor phosphorylation → Gene X expression. Drug 1 blocks Gs protein activation. When cells are treated with Drug 1 alone, Gene X expression falls to zero. When cells are then treated with Drug 1 plus membrane-permeable dibutyryl-cAMP (db-cAMP, a cAMP analog that enters cells directly), Gene X expression is fully restored.
title: APBIO-MCQ-032

choices_json.rationale: This reasoning is backwards. If Gs were truly not involved, blocking it would not suppress Gene X expression in the first place. The rescue demonstrates that Gs is upstream of cAMP — exactly the pathway shown. Drug 1 acting on Gs is consistent with the rescue working.
choices_json.choice_text: Drug 1 must be acting on the receptor rather than Gs, because if Gs were blocked, bypassing it with cAMP would not restore signaling

choices_json.rationale: The rescue logic is: Drug 1 stops Gs → no cAMP → no Gene X. Supplying db-cAMP externally skips the Gs step entirely and re-enters the pathway at cAMP, restoring PKA activation and downstream signaling. This confirms that Gs's only required function in this pathway is generating cAMP, and that all components downstream of cAMP are unaffected by Drug 1.
choices_json.choice_text: Gs protein activity is upstream of cAMP production; the pathway downstream of cAMP (PKA → transcription factor → Gene X) is intact, so providing cAMP directly bypasses the Gs block and restores full signaling

choices_json.rationale: db-cAMP is added exogenously and bypasses adenylyl cyclase entirely — the experiment says nothing about whether adenylyl cyclase is constitutively active. The restoration comes from the external cAMP analog, not from endogenous adenylyl cyclase activity.
choices_json.choice_text: Adenylyl cyclase must be constitutively active because db-cAMP restores signaling without requiring adenylyl cyclase activation

choices_json.rationale: A single-target drug blocking Gs would be expected to be fully rescued by db-cAMP — precisely because Gs's only function in this pathway is generating cAMP. Full rescue with db-cAMP is consistent with Drug 1 having a single target (Gs), not multiple targets.
choices_json.choice_text: Drug 1 must be acting at multiple steps in the pathway, because a single-target drug would not require cAMP addition for rescue

stem: If the IP₃ receptor on the ER is blocked pharmacologically, what effect on PKC activity is most directly predicted?
stimulus: Activation of a phospholipase C (PLC)-coupled receptor cleaves PIP₂ into two second messengers: IP₃ and DAG. IP₃ diffuses to the ER membrane and opens ligand-gated Ca²⁺ channels, releasing stored Ca²⁺ into the cytoplasm. DAG remains anchored in the plasma membrane. Protein kinase C (PKC) is activated by the simultaneous presence of both DAG at the membrane and elevated cytoplasmic Ca²⁺. When both co-activators are present, PKC activity is maximal; DAG or Ca²⁺ alone provides only weak partial activation.
title: APBIO-MCQ-033

choices_json.rationale: IP₃ activates Ca²⁺ release from the ER; it does not directly activate PKC. PKC is activated by DAG (still present) and Ca²⁺ (now absent). Confusing the IP₃ function (Ca²⁺ release) with direct PKC activation is a common error.
choices_json.choice_text: PKC activity is completely eliminated because IP₃ is the direct activator of PKC

choices_json.rationale: PLC still cleaves PIP₂, producing both IP₃ and DAG normally. DAG inserts into the membrane as usual. But without Ca²⁺ (its IP₃ receptor is blocked), PKC lacks its second co-activator. The stimulus states that DAG alone provides only weak partial activation — so PKC activity drops dramatically but is not completely zero.
choices_json.choice_text: PKC activity is substantially reduced: blocking the IP₃ receptor prevents ER Ca²⁺ release, removing Ca²⁺ as a required co-activator, but DAG (still generated from PIP₂ cleavage) provides residual weak partial activation

choices_json.rationale: The stimulus explicitly states that DAG alone provides only weak partial activation and that maximal PKC activity requires both DAG and Ca²⁺. This choice contradicts the given information.
choices_json.choice_text: PKC activity is completely unaffected because DAG alone is sufficient for full PKC activation without Ca²⁺

choices_json.rationale: IP₃ does not activate PKC through any pathway — its only function in this context is opening ER Ca²⁺ channels. IP₃ accumulation would have no stimulatory effect on PKC because there is no IP₃ binding site on PKC.
choices_json.choice_text: PKC activity increases because blocking IP₃ receptors causes IP₃ to accumulate and directly activate PKC through an alternative mechanism

stem: Which conclusion about cAMP signaling is best supported by all three experimental results taken together?
stimulus:
Researchers measure a cAMP-dependent cellular response under three conditions:

Condition | Treatment | Response (units)
1         | Ligand alone | 100
2         | Ligand + phosphodiesterase inhibitor | 400
3         | Phosphodiesterase inhibitor alone (no ligand) | 5

Phosphodiesterase (PDE) is the enzyme that degrades cAMP to AMP. The ligand acts through a Gs-coupled receptor.
title: APBIO-MCQ-034

choices_json.rationale: Condition 3 shows that PDE inhibitor alone produces only 5 units — nearly no response — demonstrating that the PDE inhibitor cannot drive the response on its own. The ligand is essential for generating cAMP that is then preserved by PDE inhibition.
choices_json.choice_text: The PDE inhibitor is the primary driver of the response; the ligand merely sensitizes cells to its effect

choices_json.rationale: Condition 1 (ligand alone = 100) sets the baseline. Condition 2 (ligand + PDE inhibitor = 400) shows 4-fold amplification when cAMP is not degraded — confirming PDE normally terminates the signal quickly. Condition 3 (PDE inhibitor alone = 5) confirms basal cAMP is negligible without ligand-driven synthesis, demonstrating that PDE inhibition amplifies ligand-generated signal rather than creating its own.
choices_json.choice_text: cAMP degradation by PDE normally limits the magnitude of the ligand-induced response: the ligand generates cAMP, and extending cAMP half-life by blocking PDE amplifies the response by reducing cAMP turnover

choices_json.rationale: 100 + 5 = 105, far less than 400. The synergistic result (400) indicates the two treatments interact multiplicatively — the PDE inhibitor extends the half-life of the cAMP produced by the ligand, not an independent additive pathway.
choices_json.choice_text: The ligand and PDE inhibitor act through independent additive pathways: their combined response (400) equals the sum of their individual responses (100 + 5 = 105)

choices_json.rationale: Five units of response in condition 3 most likely reflects the small amount of cAMP produced by basal (ligand-independent) adenylyl cyclase activity, not a constitutively active receptor. A constitutively active receptor would be expected to produce much more than 5% of the ligand-stimulated response.
choices_json.choice_text: Condition 3 reveals a constitutively active receptor that generates basal cAMP independently of ligand, because 5 units of response are observed without ligand

stem: Which combination of interventions would most likely restore normal insulin secretion in β-cells where somatostatin signaling is chronically elevated?
stimulus: In pancreatic β-cells, glucose uptake raises the ATP:ADP ratio, closing ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels (K_ATP). Membrane depolarization opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels, and Ca²⁺ influx triggers insulin vesicle exocytosis. A parallel pathway: elevated cAMP (via glucagon or GLP-1 acting on Gs-coupled receptors) enhances insulin secretion by sensitizing Ca²⁺ channels and priming vesicles. Somatostatin, released from neighboring δ-cells, binds a Gi-coupled receptor on β-cells: Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase (lowering cAMP) and opens K⁺ channels (hyperpolarizing the membrane). In a disease model, somatostatin is chronically elevated.
title: APBIO-MCQ-035

choices_json.rationale: Blocking glucose uptake would reduce ATP, keep K_ATP channels open, prevent depolarization, and eliminate Ca²⁺ entry — further suppressing insulin secretion. This intervention worsens the defect rather than correcting it.
choices_json.choice_text: Block glucose uptake to reduce the ATP:ADP ratio; this would counteract somatostatin's membrane effects

choices_json.rationale: Chronically elevated somatostatin suppresses insulin via two mechanisms: (1) lowering cAMP (via Gi inhibition of adenylyl cyclase) and (2) hyperpolarizing the membrane (via Gi-activated K⁺ channels). Blocking the somatostatin receptor stops both effects at the source. Adding exogenous cAMP restores the cAMP-dependent enhancement of Ca²⁺ channel sensitivity and vesicle priming. Together these interventions reverse both arms of somatostatin's inhibition.
choices_json.choice_text: Apply a membrane-permeable cAMP analog to restore cAMP signaling AND block the somatostatin receptor to prevent ongoing Gi activation

choices_json.rationale: Somatostatin reduces insulin secretion — Ca²⁺ influx is already suppressed, not excessive. Blocking Ca²⁺ channels would further reduce insulin secretion, not restore it.
choices_json.choice_text: Block voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels to prevent excessive Ca²⁺ influx that may be desensitizing the secretory machinery

choices_json.rationale: K_ATP channels are already being opened by somatostatin (via Gi), which is part of the problem. Activating K_ATP channels further would deepen hyperpolarization, making Ca²⁺ channel opening even less likely and further reducing insulin secretion.
choices_json.choice_text: Activate K_ATP channels pharmacologically to hyperpolarize the membrane and reset the β-cell to a more responsive resting state

stem: Based on the observations, which cell cycle phase accounts for the largest fraction of cells in this population, and what is the evidence?
stimulus: Flow cytometry of a rapidly proliferating cell population reveals: 65% of cells have 2N DNA content; 20% have DNA content between 2N and 4N; 15% have 4N DNA content. Chromosome condensation is visible in fewer than 2% of cells. BrdU (a thymidine analog incorporated only during active DNA synthesis) labels exactly 20% of cells.
title: APBIO-MCQ-036

choices_json.rationale: BrdU labeling confirms S phase cells constitute 20% of the population — not the largest fraction. S phase duration varies by cell type and is not universally the longest phase. G1 accounts for 65% here.
choices_json.choice_text: S phase, because BrdU labels 20% of cells and S phase is always the longest phase of the cell cycle

choices_json.rationale: Cells in G1 have completed the previous division (2N content) but have not yet entered S phase (no BrdU incorporation) or mitosis (no chromosome condensation). The 65% with 2N content minus the <2% in M phase accounts for the large G1 population, reflecting the time cells spend in G1 before committing to division at the G1/S checkpoint.
choices_json.choice_text: G1 phase, because 65% of cells have 2N DNA content without BrdU labeling or chromosome condensation, indicating they have not yet begun DNA replication and are not in mitosis

choices_json.rationale: The 4N fraction (15%) represents G2 + M phase cells. G2 cells have fully replicated DNA but no condensed chromosomes. However, 15% is smaller than the 65% in G1. G2 is not the largest fraction in this population.
choices_json.choice_text: G2 phase, because cells with 4N DNA content are preparing to divide and would be expected to accumulate before the slower M phase

choices_json.rationale: Chromosome condensation is visible in fewer than 2% of cells — the smallest fraction. M phase is typically one of the shortest cell cycle phases in rapidly dividing cells. This choice contradicts both the flow cytometry data and the chromosome condensation observation.
choices_json.choice_text: M phase, because chromosome condensation is required for accurate segregation and cells spend the most time ensuring proper spindle attachment

stem: Which correctly matches each microscopy observation to its stage of mitosis?
stimulus: A student images four cells from a dividing onion root tip. Cell 1: chromosomes are maximally condensed and aligned precisely at the cell's equatorial plane; spindle fibers attach to each chromosome at the kinetochore. Cell 2: sister chromatids have separated and two identical sets of chromosomes are moving toward opposite poles. Cell 3: chromosomes are condensing and the nuclear envelope is breaking down, but chromosomes are not yet aligned. Cell 4: two new nuclear envelopes are forming around chromosome sets at opposite poles; chromosomes are decondensing; a cell plate is forming at the midline.
title: APBIO-MCQ-037

choices_json.rationale: Cell 1 shows chromosomes aligned at the equatorial plane with kinetochore attachments — this is Metaphase, not Prophase. Cell 2 shows chromatid separation and poleward movement — Anaphase, not Metaphase. All four assignments are incorrect.
choices_json.choice_text: Cell 1 = Prophase; Cell 2 = Metaphase; Cell 3 = Anaphase; Cell 4 = Telophase

choices_json.rationale: Metaphase: chromosomes aligned at the metaphase plate with spindle attachment (Cell 1). Anaphase: sister chromatids separating toward poles (Cell 2). Prophase: chromosomes condensing, nuclear envelope breaking down, no alignment yet (Cell 3). Telophase: nuclear envelopes reforming, chromosomes decondensing, cytokinesis beginning — cell plate in plant cells (Cell 4).
choices_json.choice_text: Cell 1 = Metaphase; Cell 2 = Anaphase; Cell 3 = Prophase; Cell 4 = Telophase

choices_json.rationale: In Anaphase, chromatids are moving apart — not aligned at the equator. In Telophase, chromosomes are at poles with nuclear envelopes forming — not segregating. All assignments are incorrect.
choices_json.choice_text: Cell 1 = Anaphase; Cell 2 = Telophase; Cell 3 = Metaphase; Cell 4 = Prophase

choices_json.rationale: Cell 2 shows active chromosome movement toward poles — this is Anaphase, not Telophase. Cell 3 shows condensation with nuclear envelope breakdown but no alignment — this is Prophase, not Anaphase. Two of the four assignments are swapped.
choices_json.choice_text: Cell 1 = Metaphase; Cell 2 = Telophase; Cell 3 = Anaphase; Cell 4 = Prophase

stem: Which set of cell cycle arrest points is most consistent with checkpoint regulation for each treatment?
stimulus: Researchers treat dividing cells with three agents and use flow cytometry to determine where cells arrest. Hydroxyurea depletes the deoxyribonucleotide pool, stalling DNA replication forks. Nocodazole depolymerizes spindle microtubules, preventing kinetochore attachment. UV radiation creates thymine dimers, causing DNA lesions that block replication and transcription.
title: APBIO-MCQ-038

choices_json.rationale: Hydroxyurea stalls replication within S phase — cells arrest with intermediate DNA content, not at G2/M. The G1 and intra-S DNA damage checkpoints exist specifically for damage detected before G2. Nocodazole acts on the spindle, which is a G2/M (spindle assembly) checkpoint — but UV can arrest at multiple points. Not all agents activate the same checkpoint.
choices_json.choice_text: All three agents arrest cells at G2/M because all interfere with DNA and DNA damage activates only the G2/M checkpoint

choices_json.rationale: Hydroxyurea blocks nucleotide synthesis, stalling forks mid-replication — cells accumulate in S phase with intermediate DNA content. Nocodazole destroys the spindle, triggering the spindle assembly checkpoint that prevents anaphase until kinetochores are attached — 4N arrest. UV lesions activate ATR/ATM kinases; if in G1, cells arrest before replication (2N); if in G2, cells arrest before division (4N). Multiple checkpoints respond to UV.
choices_json.choice_text: Hydroxyurea: arrest within S phase (intermediate DNA content); Nocodazole: arrest at G2/M with 4N DNA content (spindle assembly checkpoint); UV radiation: arrest at G1 or G2/M (DNA damage checkpoints depending on when damage is detected)

choices_json.rationale: Hydroxyurea arrests cells within S phase (where replication is occurring), not in G1. Nocodazole acts on the mitotic spindle, which is assembled in M phase, so arrest occurs at the G2/M boundary or within M phase — not G1. UV damage can arrest in G1, but not exclusively in S phase.
choices_json.choice_text: Hydroxyurea: arrest in G1; Nocodazole: arrest in G1; UV radiation: arrest in S phase

choices_json.rationale: Cell cycle checkpoints exist precisely to prevent cells with incomplete replication or damaged DNA from dividing. Unless checkpoint genes are mutated (as in many cancer cells), these checkpoints actively halt progression. This choice describes checkpoint failure, not normal checkpoint function.
choices_json.choice_text: All three treatments are overcome by normal checkpoint signaling, allowing cells to complete division with damaged DNA or incomplete replication

stem: Which conclusion about CDK1 regulation is best supported by the oscillating Cyclin B data and the non-degradable mutant experiment?
stimulus: Cyclin B protein levels oscillate during the cell cycle: low in G1, rising through S and G2, peaking just before mitosis, then dropping sharply as cells enter anaphase. CDK1 protein is present at constant levels throughout the cell cycle. CDK1 is inactive without a cyclin partner. Cyclin B degradation at mitotic exit is triggered by the APC/C (Anaphase-Promoting Complex/Cyclosome), which ubiquitinates Cyclin B for proteasomal destruction. Cells injected with a non-degradable form of Cyclin B (with the APC/C recognition sequence deleted) enter mitosis normally but cannot exit: they arrest in a permanent mitotic state.
title: APBIO-MCQ-039

choices_json.rationale: CDK1 protein is present at constant levels throughout the cycle — it is not rate-limiting. Cyclin B oscillation is the regulatory variable. This choice inverts the relationship between CDK1 and its cyclin partner.
choices_json.choice_text: CDK1 protein abundance is the primary regulator of cell cycle progression; Cyclin B oscillation is a byproduct of CDK1 activity

choices_json.rationale: CDK1 is constitutively present but inactive without its cyclin. Cyclin B accumulation allows CDK1/B complex formation and kinase activation — driving mitotic entry. The non-degradable Cyclin B experiment proves the point: without Cyclin B degradation, CDK1 remains active and the cell cannot exit mitosis. Cyclin B oscillation is therefore the molecular switch controlling CDK1 activity timing.
choices_json.choice_text: CDK1 kinase activity is gated by Cyclin B abundance: when Cyclin B rises, CDK1/B complexes accumulate and drive mitotic entry; when APC/C degrades Cyclin B at anaphase, CDK1 becomes inactive and mitotic exit proceeds

choices_json.rationale: APC/C is a ubiquitin ligase that targets substrates (including Cyclin B and securin) for degradation — it does not phosphorylate CDK1 or activate it. CDK1 activation requires cyclin binding, not APC/C activity.
choices_json.choice_text: APC/C directly phosphorylates and activates CDK1 at the onset of anaphase; Cyclin B degradation is a consequence, not a cause, of CDK1 activation

choices_json.rationale: While there is a positive feedback relationship between active CDK1/B and APC/C inhibition, the primary explanation from the data is simpler: sustained Cyclin B = sustained CDK1 activity = cell cannot exit mitosis. The question asks what the data most directly support, and persistent CDK1/B activity is the direct conclusion.
choices_json.choice_text: Non-degradable Cyclin B arrests cells in mitosis by blocking APC/C from ubiquitinating other targets including securin, creating a feed-forward loop that prevents anaphase

stem: Which best explains why a permanently GTP-bound RAS mutation leads to uncontrolled cell proliferation?
stimulus: RAS is a GTPase signaling protein. Normal RAS cycles between an active GTP-bound state (activated by growth factor receptors) and an inactive GDP-bound state (restored by RAS's intrinsic GTPase activity, accelerated by GTPase-activating proteins/GAPs). Active RAS-GTP activates the RAF-MEK-ERK kinase cascade (MAPK pathway), which enters the nucleus and promotes transcription of Cyclin D1, driving cells through the G1/S checkpoint. A point mutation in RAS eliminates its GTPase activity, leaving RAS permanently bound to GTP.
title: APBIO-MCQ-040

choices_json.rationale: This inverts the mechanism. RAS-GDP is the inactive state. RAS-GTP is the active, pro-proliferative state. The mutation locks RAS in the GTP-bound (active) form, not the GDP-bound form.
choices_json.choice_text: Permanently GDP-bound RAS drives proliferation; the mutation prevents GTP hydrolysis, trapping RAS in the inactive state that stimulates cell division

choices_json.rationale: Growth factor signaling normally activates RAS transiently; GTPase activity ensures RAS returns to the inactive GDP-bound state within seconds. A GTPase-dead RAS stays active indefinitely, continuously feeding ERK signals to the nucleus and maintaining Cyclin D1 levels that keep CDK4/6 active and Rb phosphorylated — bypassing the requirement for external growth factors to pass G1/S.
choices_json.choice_text: Permanently GTP-bound RAS constitutively activates the RAF-MEK-ERK cascade, continuously inducing Cyclin D1 transcription and driving cells through the G1/S checkpoint without requiring growth factor signals

choices_json.rationale: RAS does not directly degrade p53. RAS signals through the MAPK pathway to promote proliferation. p53 degradation occurs through MDM2-mediated ubiquitination, which is a separate regulatory system. The connection between oncogenic RAS and p53 is indirect.
choices_json.choice_text: Permanent RAS-GTP directly degrades the p53 tumor suppressor, eliminating the DNA damage checkpoint and allowing unchecked replication of damaged DNA

choices_json.rationale: Caspases mediate apoptosis, not proliferation. Constitutively active RAS in normal cells actually can trigger oncogene-induced senescence (a growth arrest program), not apoptotic cycling. The proliferative effect of oncogenic RAS comes through the MAPK/Cyclin D1 axis, not caspases.
choices_json.choice_text: Constitutively active RAS activates caspases, triggering a paradoxical cycle in which cells proliferate more rapidly to compensate for apoptotic losses

stem: Which accurately characterizes both genetic changes and correctly identifies each gene category?
stimulus: Two genes are studied in cancer biopsies. Gene A encodes a growth factor receptor. In tumor sample 1, Gene A is present at 80 copies per cell instead of the normal 2, producing approximately 40× the normal receptor protein. Gene B encodes the Rb protein, which normally binds and inactivates E2F transcription factors, preventing S-phase entry. In tumor sample 2, DNA sequencing reveals one Gene B allele carries a nonsense mutation and the other allele is deleted entirely.
title: APBIO-MCQ-041

choices_json.rationale: Tumor suppressors lose function in cancer; amplification of a growth factor receptor gene is a gain-of-function change characteristic of a proto-oncogene converted to an oncogene. Gene B (Rb) is a classic tumor suppressor, not a proto-oncogene. Both classifications are reversed.
choices_json.choice_text: Gene A is a tumor suppressor amplified to a gain-of-function oncogene; Gene B is a proto-oncogene with loss-of-function mutations in both alleles

choices_json.rationale: Proto-oncogenes encode growth-promoting proteins; amplification overproduces a functional growth factor receptor, driving constitutive proliferative signaling — a dominant gain-of-function change where even one overactive allele suffices. Rb is a tumor suppressor (brake); the first allele is disabled by nonsense mutation (first hit) and the second is deleted (second hit) — both must be lost to release E2F and allow uncontrolled S-phase entry, consistent with Knudson's two-hit model.
choices_json.choice_text: Gene A is a proto-oncogene converted to an oncogene by amplification (gain-of-function; a single overactive allele drives proliferation); Gene B is a tumor suppressor inactivated by biallelic loss-of-function (consistent with the two-hit hypothesis requiring both alleles to be lost)

choices_json.rationale: Gene A amplification produces excess growth factor receptor — a gain-of-function change in a proto-oncogene. It does not dilute tumor suppressors. Gene A is not a tumor suppressor. This choice misclassifies Gene A.
choices_json.choice_text: Both are tumor suppressor genes; Gene A amplification indirectly reduces tumor suppressor activity by diluting suppressor protein, while Gene B mutations directly eliminate suppressor function

choices_json.rationale: Rb is the prototypical example of a tumor suppressor following the two-hit hypothesis. One wild-type Rb allele is sufficient to suppress tumor development; both alleles must be inactivated. Haploinsufficiency is a property of some tumor suppressors but not Rb.
choices_json.choice_text: Gene B requires only one allele to be mutated to cause cancer because Rb is haploinsufficient — one normal copy cannot maintain sufficient growth suppression

stem: Which conclusion about the drug's mechanism of action is best supported by the flow cytometry data?
stimulus:
Flow cytometry of a cancer cell line before and after drug treatment (24 hours):

Fraction     | Control | After Drug
2N content   |   60%   |     8%
2N–4N (S)    |   20%   |    80%
4N content   |   20%   |    12%

The drug is known to affect a specific enzymatic process required for DNA replication.
title: APBIO-MCQ-042

choices_json.rationale: G1/S checkpoint activation would dramatically increase the 2N fraction. The 2N fraction actually dropped from 60% to 8%, the opposite of what G1 arrest predicts. Cells are entering S phase normally but stalling there.
choices_json.choice_text: The drug activates the G1/S checkpoint, preventing cells from entering S phase and causing accumulation with 2N content

choices_json.rationale: The dramatic shift from 20% to 80% in the S-phase fraction, combined with depletion of the 2N fraction (cells continue entering S phase but cannot exit it), is the signature of an intra-S phase block. Cells complete the previous cycle normally (enter S phase), but replication stalls midway due to the drug's inhibition of a replication enzyme. This is consistent with hydroxyurea-like or topoisomerase inhibitor mechanisms.
choices_json.choice_text: The drug blocks DNA replication within S phase, causing cells to accumulate with intermediate DNA content between 2N and 4N

choices_json.rationale: Spindle inhibition (e.g., nocodazole) would dramatically increase the 4N fraction, not the S-phase fraction. The 4N fraction dropped slightly from 20% to 12%. This pattern is inconsistent with a mitotic spindle block.
choices_json.choice_text: The drug inhibits spindle formation, arresting cells in mitosis with fully replicated 4N DNA

choices_json.rationale: The S-phase fraction increased from 20% to 80% — the opposite of depletion. Accelerating S phase would decrease the S-phase fraction (cells pass through S phase more quickly). The data indicate S phase is prolonged, not shortened.
choices_json.choice_text: The drug accelerates S phase progression, reducing the time cells spend replicating and causing depletion of the S-phase fraction

stem: Which comparison of the two division types is most accurate based on the observations?
stimulus: A species with a diploid number of 8 (2n = 8) is studied. Cell type P divides in 2 hours and produces two daughter cells, each with 8 chromosomes. Cell type Q undergoes two sequential nuclear divisions over 18 hours and produces four daughter cells, each with 4 chromosomes. During the first division of type Q, homologous chromosome pairs align together at the equatorial plate and then separate. During the second division of type Q, sister chromatids separate.
title: APBIO-MCQ-043

choices_json.rationale: Producing diploid daughter cells is the outcome of mitosis, not meiosis. Meiosis halves chromosome number. Maintaining the same chromosome number as the parent (8 chromosomes in a 2n = 8 organism) is the definition of a mitotic outcome.
choices_json.choice_text: Cell type P undergoes meiosis because its daughter cells have the same chromosome number as the parent cell, maintaining ploidy

choices_json.rationale: Mitosis: one division, daughter cells genetically identical to parent, diploid chromosome number maintained (2n = 8 → 8 chromosomes per daughter). Meiosis: two divisions, homologs separate in meiosis I, sister chromatids separate in meiosis II, producing haploid cells (n = 4). The behavioral description — homologs aligning together then separating — is the defining hallmark of meiosis I, distinguishing it from mitosis where homologs do not pair.
choices_json.choice_text: Cell type P undergoes mitosis (produces diploid daughter cells for growth and repair); cell type Q undergoes meiosis (two sequential divisions produce haploid cells; first division separates homologs, second separates sister chromatids)

choices_json.rationale: Meiosis involves one round of DNA replication followed by two divisions; it does not replicate DNA twice. Additionally, cell type Q produces haploid cells (4 chromosomes in a 2n = 8 species), which is impossible for mitosis. Cell type Q is meiosis.
choices_json.choice_text: Both cell types undergo mitosis; cell type Q is a slower variant because it performs two rounds of DNA replication

choices_json.rationale: Mitosis always maintains chromosome number — it cannot reduce it. The reduction in chromosome number in cell type Q is the result of meiotic mechanisms: homolog pairing and separation in meiosis I, without DNA replication between the two divisions.
choices_json.choice_text: Cell type Q undergoes a modified form of mitosis that randomly distributes chromosomes into four cells, explaining the reduced chromosome count

stem: A mutation makes securin resistant to APC/C-mediated ubiquitination. Which cell cycle consequence is most directly predicted?
stimulus: Sister chromatid cohesion is maintained by cohesin protein complexes that encircle both chromatids. At the metaphase-to-anaphase transition, the protease separase cleaves cohesin's Scc1 subunit, releasing sister chromatids to move toward opposite poles. Separase is kept inactive throughout most of mitosis by binding to its inhibitor, securin. The APC/C ubiquitin ligase is activated at the metaphase-to-anaphase transition: it ubiquitinates securin (and Cyclin B), targeting both for proteasomal degradation. Securin destruction liberates active separase.
title: APBIO-MCQ-044

choices_json.rationale: Non-degradable securin keeps securin protein present, which means securin continues to bind and inhibit separase. Securin is an inhibitor of separase, not an activator. Persistent securin means persistent separase inhibition — the opposite of premature cleavage.
choices_json.choice_text: Cohesin will be cleaved prematurely in prophase because non-degradable securin stabilizes separase in its active form throughout mitosis

choices_json.rationale: The pathway requires: APC/C degrades securin → separase is released and activated → separase cleaves cohesin Scc1 → sister chromatids separate. Non-degradable securin blocks the first step: APC/C cannot destroy it. Securin remains present, bound to separase, keeping it inactive. Without separase activity, cohesin is intact and sister chromatids remain joined — cells arrest at metaphase with a full complement of chromosomes unable to segregate.
choices_json.choice_text: Sister chromatids will fail to separate at the metaphase-to-anaphase transition because securin cannot be degraded, separase remains bound and inactive, and cohesin is never cleaved

choices_json.rationale: Cyclin B accumulation (driven by synthesis) drives mitotic entry regardless of securin stability. APC/C degrades both securin and Cyclin B, but these are independent substrates. Blocking securin degradation does not prevent Cyclin B from accumulating. Cells would enter mitosis normally but fail to exit it.
choices_json.choice_text: Cells will enter mitosis prematurely because non-degradable securin prevents APC/C from degrading Cyclin B, causing Cyclin B to accumulate and activate CDK1 earlier than normal

choices_json.rationale: Securin's only described function is inhibiting separase. It has no known direct role in replication origin licensing or CDK2 regulation. This choice invents a securin function not described in or implied by the stimulus.
choices_json.choice_text: Cells will undergo multiple rounds of DNA replication without division because non-degradable securin prevents CDK2 from licensing replication origins

stem: Why do PARP inhibitors selectively kill BRCA1-null cancer cells while sparing normal cells with one functional BRCA1 allele?
stimulus: BRCA1 is a tumor suppressor essential for homologous recombination (HR) repair of double-strand DNA breaks (DSBs). Cells with two functional BRCA1 alleles efficiently repair DSBs via HR. Cells with one mutant allele (heterozygous) retain normal HR. Cancer cells that lose the second BRCA1 allele (loss of heterozygosity) become BRCA1-null and cannot perform HR; they rely on alternative repair — primarily base-excision repair (BER) initiated by PARP-1 enzyme. PARP inhibitors block BER. In BRCA1-competent cells, PARP inhibition is well tolerated because HR compensates for any DSBs.
title: APBIO-MCQ-045

choices_json.rationale: PARP inhibitors are not selectively transported into cancer cells — they distribute to all cells. The selectivity is not pharmacokinetic (where the drug goes) but rather pharmacodynamic (which cells are vulnerable because of their genotype). This choice misidentifies the mechanism of selectivity.
choices_json.choice_text: PARP inhibitors are selectively imported into cancer cells by tumor-specific transporters, ensuring they only accumulate where BRCA1 is absent

choices_json.rationale: This is synthetic lethality: combining two individually survivable deficiencies (BRCA1 loss alone is tolerated; PARP inhibition alone is tolerated in normal cells) creates a lethal combination specifically in cells carrying both. BRCA1-null cancer cells have no fallback when BER is blocked — unrepaired DSBs accumulate, chromosomes break, and cells die. Heterozygous normal cells maintain HR as an intact backup and survive PARP inhibition. This tumor-genotype-dependent vulnerability is the basis of clinical PARP inhibitor therapy in BRCA-mutant cancers.
choices_json.choice_text: BRCA1-null cancer cells have lost HR repair and depend entirely on PARP-mediated BER to survive replication-associated DNA damage; blocking PARP eliminates their only functional DSB repair pathway, causing lethal DNA damage accumulation — while heterozygous normal cells retain HR and can tolerate PARP inhibition

choices_json.rationale: PARP inhibitors block PARP enzymatic activity; they do not activate BRCA1 expression. The protection of heterozygous cells comes from their pre-existing single wild-type BRCA1 allele being sufficient for HR, not from drug-induced BRCA1 upregulation.
choices_json.choice_text: PARP inhibitors activate BRCA1 expression in heterozygous normal cells, upregulating HR repair and specifically protecting them from drug toxicity

choices_json.rationale: This explanation would predict that all rapidly dividing cancer cells are sensitive to PARP inhibitors, which is not observed clinically. PARP inhibitors show specific efficacy in BRCA-mutant tumors — the selectivity is genotype-specific (BRCA1/2 status), not proliferation-rate-dependent.
choices_json.choice_text: Cancer cells divide more rapidly than normal cells and therefore accumulate more PARP-dependent DNA damage per unit time, making them generally more sensitive to PARP inhibition regardless of BRCA1 status

stem: Which best explains why this patient's thyroid hormone levels remain elevated despite already-high circulating T3?
stimulus: Thyroid hormone (T3) homeostasis depends on a negative feedback loop: low T3 → hypothalamus releases TRH → pituitary releases TSH → thyroid gland produces T3 → elevated T3 feeds back to suppress both TRH and TSH release. A patient is found to have a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma (benign tumor) that produces TSH constitutively, independent of T3 levels. The patient's serum T3 is 4× the normal upper limit.
title: APBIO-MCQ-046

choices_json.rationale: In normal physiology, elevated T3 would suppress TSH release, closing the feedback loop and reducing T3 to baseline. The adenoma bypasses this regulation by producing TSH regardless of T3 concentration. Without TSH suppression, the thyroid continues receiving stimulatory signals and maintains excess T3 production — a classic example of feedback loop disruption by autonomous hormone secretion.
choices_json.choice_text: The pituitary adenoma has lost sensitivity to T3 negative feedback and secretes TSH constitutively; continuous TSH stimulation drives the thyroid to overproduce T3 despite already-elevated levels

choices_json.rationale: T3 suppresses TRH release through transcriptional and signaling mechanisms, not by destroying neurons. Additionally, the problem is in the pituitary adenoma secreting TSH autonomously — even if hypothalamic TRH were eliminated, the tumor would continue producing TSH. Neurotoxicity is not the mechanism.
choices_json.choice_text: High T3 destroys TRH-secreting neurons in the hypothalamus through excitotoxicity, removing the upstream signal that would reduce TSH

choices_json.rationale: A TSH-secreting adenoma producing 4× normal T3 is not an incidental finding — it is causal. The thyroid is responding to excessive TSH stimulation; the primary defect is in the pituitary, not the thyroid. The thyroid remains TSH-dependent.
choices_json.choice_text: The thyroid gland has become autonomous and produces T3 independently of TSH; the pituitary adenoma is an incidental finding unrelated to elevated T3

choices_json.rationale: T3 normally suppresses TSH release at the pituitary — this is negative feedback, not positive. A T3-driven increase in TSH secretion would be an inversion of the known feedback relationship. The adenoma secretes TSH constitutively (not in response to T3), and T3 does not stimulate TSH in normal physiology.
choices_json.choice_text: Elevated T3 activates a positive feedback loop at the pituitary, causing the adenoma to secrete even more TSH in response to high hormone levels

stem: Which correctly explains why testosterone's effects on Sertoli cells take hours while FSH effects begin within 30 seconds, even though both hormones ultimately act on the same cells?
stimulus: Testosterone (a lipid-soluble steroid) and FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone, a water-soluble glycoprotein) both regulate Sertoli cell function in the testis. FSH binds receptors on the Sertoli cell plasma membrane and activates adenylyl cyclase via Gs protein, raising cAMP within 30 seconds. Testosterone diffuses across the plasma membrane and binds intracellular androgen receptors (AR); the testosterone-AR complex translocates to the nucleus and acts as a transcription factor, binding androgen-response elements in promoters. Adding the transcription inhibitor actinomycin D eliminates testosterone's effects but not FSH's effects.
title: APBIO-MCQ-047

choices_json.rationale: Testosterone is actually a small lipid molecule (MW ~288 Da) that crosses membranes and diffuses rapidly. FSH is a large glycoprotein (~30 kDa). The delay in testosterone's effects is not due to slow diffusion but to the requirement for new gene transcription and translation after receptor activation.
choices_json.choice_text: Testosterone is a larger molecule that diffuses more slowly through the cytoplasm to reach nuclear receptors, explaining the hours-long delay

choices_json.rationale: FSH signal transduction is immediate because it activates proteins already present in the cell — no new synthesis needed. Testosterone must: (1) bind AR, (2) translocate to nucleus, (3) activate transcription, (4) produce mRNA, (5) export mRNA, (6) translate protein, (7) fold and activate protein. Each step takes time, and the cumulative delay is hours. Actinomycin D (transcription inhibitor) blocks testosterone's effects but not FSH's — directly confirming that testosterone requires new mRNA synthesis.
choices_json.choice_text: FSH acts through pre-existing cytoplasmic proteins (Gs, adenylyl cyclase, PKA) that are instantly activated by second messengers; testosterone's effects require the hormone-receptor complex to activate gene transcription, followed by new mRNA export, translation, and protein folding before functional changes appear

choices_json.rationale: FSH binds its plasma membrane receptor directly without intracellular conversion. This choice invents a processing step for FSH that does not exist. Hormones are generally biologically active as secreted.
choices_json.choice_text: FSH must first be converted to an active form inside the cell before binding its receptor; this conversion step adds a 30-second delay that is much shorter than testosterone's conversion time

choices_json.rationale: Testosterone and FSH act through entirely separate receptors — androgen receptor (intracellular, testosterone) and FSH receptor (plasma membrane GPCR, FSH). They do not share a receptor. This competition model has no mechanistic basis in the described pathway.
choices_json.choice_text: Testosterone competes with FSH for the same intracellular receptor, and the hours-long delay reflects the time required for FSH to be displaced from shared binding sites by testosterone

stem: After drug treatment is washed out, which prediction about cell behavior would best distinguish the mechanisms of Drug A and Drug B?
stimulus:
Two cancer drugs are tested on a dividing cell line. Flow cytometry after 24 hours of treatment:

Fraction   | Control | Drug A | Drug B
2N (G1)    |   60%   |  88%   |   5%
2N–4N (S)  |   20%   |   5%   |   8%
4N (G2/M)  |   20%   |   7%   |  87%

Drug A's known target is required for G1 cyclin-CDK complex formation. Drug B's known target is a structural component of the mitotic spindle.
title: APBIO-MCQ-048

choices_json.rationale: Drug A arrests cells in G1 (2N). Upon release, these cells still need to traverse S phase and G2 before reaching mitosis. Drug B-arrested cells at G2/M (4N, fully replicated). Upon release, spindle reassembly allows cells to complete mitosis immediately — they do not need to re-enter G1 first.
choices_json.choice_text: Drug A-released cells would immediately enter S phase and complete mitosis; Drug B-released cells would need to re-enter G1 before they could divide

choices_json.rationale: Drug A arrests cells in G1 — they have unreplicated (2N) DNA. Release from G1 arrest means cells must complete S phase (DNA replication), G2, and then M phase before dividing — a multi-hour journey. Drug B arrests cells in mitosis with fully replicated chromosomes. Washing out the spindle inhibitor allows spindle reassembly and immediate progression through anaphase, telophase, and cytokinesis — daughter cells appear within 1–2 hours of washout.
choices_json.choice_text: Drug A-released cells would first traverse S phase then G2/M before producing daughter cells; Drug B-released cells would complete mitosis directly from their 4N arrested state, producing daughter cells rapidly

choices_json.rationale: Drug B-arrested cells are mid-mitosis with fully replicated DNA — they are close to division, not at the beginning of the cycle. Only Drug A-arrested cells (in G1) need to traverse most of the cycle to reach division.
choices_json.choice_text: Drug A-released and Drug B-released cells would both require 24 hours to complete division because re-entering the cell cycle requires traversal of all phases

choices_json.rationale: 4N DNA content means DNA replication is complete. Drug B arrests in mitosis (at the spindle assembly checkpoint with fully replicated, condensed chromosomes). These cells do not need to re-enter S phase — they are waiting to complete chromatid segregation, not waiting to replicate.
choices_json.choice_text: Drug B-released cells would need to complete S phase before dividing because their 4N DNA content indicates they have not yet finished replication

stem: A mutation renders MEK constitutively active, independent of upstream RAS signaling. Which cellular consequence is most directly predicted?
stimulus: EGF (epidermal growth factor) binds EGFR, an RTK, triggering receptor dimerization and transphosphorylation. Phosphotyrosines recruit GRB2/SOS, which activates RAS-GTP. RAS-GTP activates RAF, which phosphorylates and activates MEK, which phosphorylates and activates ERK. ERK enters the nucleus and phosphorylates transcription factors that induce Cyclin D1 transcription. Cyclin D1/CDK4 complexes phosphorylate Rb, releasing E2F transcription factors that activate S-phase entry genes. Normally, removal of EGF causes RAS to return to the inactive GDP state within seconds, terminating the cascade.
title: APBIO-MCQ-049

choices_json.rationale: Constitutively active MEK drives ERK into the nucleus, inducing continuous Cyclin D1 transcription — it would increase Cyclin D1 levels, not exhaust them. MEK does not directly phosphorylate Cyclin D1. This choice inverts the pathway outcome.
choices_json.choice_text: Cells would arrest in G1 because constitutively active MEK exhausts the supply of Cyclin D1 through hyperphosphorylation, preventing CDK4 from forming active complexes

choices_json.rationale: MEK is the bottleneck that normally requires RAS-GTP (which requires EGF) to be active. Making MEK constitutively active uncouples the proliferative signal from growth factor availability: ERK is always active, Cyclin D1 is always induced, CDK4/Cyclin D1 is always active, Rb is always hyperphosphorylated, E2F is always free, and S-phase genes are always expressed. This is equivalent to a permanently activated oncogene at the MEK level.
choices_json.choice_text: Cells would proliferate uncontrollably: constitutively active MEK permanently activates ERK, which continuously induces Cyclin D1, maintaining CDK4 activity and Rb hyperphosphorylation, releasing E2F and driving S-phase entry independently of EGF

choices_json.rationale: MEK specifically activates ERK1/2, not JNK or p38 (those are activated by different upstream kinases in the MAPK superfamily). While very high ERK activity can induce senescence in some contexts, the described constitutively active MEK primarily drives proliferation through the Cyclin D1/Rb/E2F axis described in the pathway.
choices_json.choice_text: Cells would undergo apoptosis because constitutively active MEK activates JNK/p38 stress kinases that phosphorylate pro-apoptotic proteins

choices_json.rationale: MEK is downstream of RAS. Active MEK does not feedback to inactivate RAS — ERK can phosphorylate SOS (creating a negative feedback on RAS activation in normal cells), but constitutively active MEK bypasses RAS entirely; it does not trap RAS in the inactive state.
choices_json.choice_text: Cells would become resistant to EGF signaling because constitutively active MEK sequesters RAS in the inactive GDP-bound form through a negative feedback mechanism

stem: Which combination of phenotypic consequences is most directly predicted for cells expressing dominant-negative p53?
stimulus: p53 is a tetrameric transcription factor activated by DNA damage, oncogene overactivation, and hypoxia. Active p53 induces: (1) p21, a CDK inhibitor that blocks CDK2/Cyclin E complexes, arresting cells in G1; (2) pro-apoptotic genes PUMA and BAX, triggering mitochondrial apoptosis when damage is irreparable; (3) TIGAR, an enzyme that reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) and limits oxidative DNA damage. A dominant-negative p53 mutant protein (p53-DN) cannot bind DNA but can still form tetramers with wild-type p53 protein, preventing the entire tetramer from binding DNA.
title: APBIO-MCQ-050

choices_json.rationale: Enhanced G1 arrest would require functional p53 to induce p21. p53-DN inactivates wild-type p53 by forming non-functional tetramers — G1 arrest would be impaired, not enhanced. Only resistance to apoptosis (loss of PUMA/BAX induction) is correctly predicted here; the others are wrong.
choices_json.choice_text: Enhanced G1 arrest after DNA damage; increased resistance to apoptosis; reduced oxidative stress

choices_json.rationale: p53-DN inactivates all three wild-type p53 transcriptional functions by preventing DNA binding of mixed tetramers: (1) p21 is not induced → CDK2/Cyclin E remains active → no G1 arrest; (2) PUMA and BAX are not induced → mitochondrial apoptosis pathway is not activated even with irreparable damage; (3) TIGAR is not induced → ROS cannot be quenched → oxidative DNA damage accumulates. This triple loss of function is why dominant-negative p53 mutations are so potent in cancer — one mutant allele disables the function of the remaining wild-type allele.
choices_json.choice_text: Failure to arrest in G1 after DNA damage; failure to activate apoptosis after irreparable damage; increased accumulation of reactive oxygen species

choices_json.rationale: All three listed p53 functions (p21, PUMA/BAX, TIGAR induction) are transcriptional — all require p53 to bind DNA as a transcription factor. If p53-DN prevents DNA binding, all three transcriptional outputs are simultaneously lost. Apoptosis induction and ROS control are not mediated by separate non-transcriptional p53 pathways in this context.
choices_json.choice_text: Loss of G1 checkpoint function only; apoptosis and ROS control remain intact because p53 uses separate non-transcriptional pathways for those functions

choices_json.rationale: p53-DN inhibits p53 transcriptional function — it does not directly inhibit CDK2. CDK2 inhibition occurs through p21 (which is a p53 transcriptional target). Without functional p53, p21 is not induced and CDK2 activity is not suppressed — cells would proliferate more rapidly, not less. This choice inverts the outcome of p53 loss.
choices_json.choice_text: Reduced cell proliferation because dominant-negative p53 directly inhibits CDK2, preventing S-phase entry

stem: Which conclusion about allele dominance is best supported by the F1 and F2 cross results?
stimulus: In garden peas, a true-breeding purple-flowered plant is crossed with a true-breeding white-flowered plant. All F1 offspring have purple flowers. When F1 plants are self-fertilized, the F2 generation produces 705 purple-flowered plants and 224 white-flowered plants (ratio ≈ 3.1:1). The flower-color trait is controlled by a single gene with two alleles.
title: APBIO-MCQ-051

choices_json.rationale: White flowers are the minority in F2 (approximately 1/4), while purple flowers are the majority (approximately 3/4). The dominant allele is expressed in both homozygous dominant and heterozygous individuals — purple appears in 3/4 of F2 offspring, consistent with purple being dominant.
choices_json.choice_text: White is dominant over purple because white-flowered plants are produced in greater proportion in the F2 generation

choices_json.rationale: Key evidence: (1) F1 uniformly purple — the purple allele masks white in heterozygotes; (2) white reappears in F2, proving the white allele was present but hidden in F1 plants; (3) 3:1 ratio matches the expected Mendelian segregation of a Pp × Pp cross, producing 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp, where PP and Pp are both purple and pp is white.
choices_json.choice_text: Purple is dominant over white: all F1 offspring show the purple phenotype (masking white), and the 3:1 F2 ratio indicates F1 plants are heterozygous (Pp), with white reappearing only in the 1/4 of F2 offspring that are homozygous recessive (pp)

choices_json.rationale: Codominance would produce a blended or intermediate phenotype in heterozygotes (e.g., purple-and-white streaked flowers) or require three distinct phenotypes in F2. Instead, F1 plants are uniformly purple (not intermediate), and F2 shows only two phenotypes in a 3:1 ratio — the hallmark of simple dominance.
choices_json.choice_text: The two alleles are codominant because F2 plants express both purple and white phenotypes

choices_json.rationale: Blending inheritance would predict F1 plants to be intermediate (e.g., light purple) and F2 to show a continuous range of colors — not the discrete 3:1 ratio observed. The reappearance of pure white phenotype in F2 (identical to the white grandparents) specifically rules out blending and confirms particulate inheritance with dominance.
choices_json.choice_text: No dominance relationship can be determined from these data alone because the F1 phenotype could reflect blending of the two parental traits

stem: If seed color and seed shape assort independently, what fraction of offspring from this cross is predicted to have wrinkled yellow seeds?
stimulus: In peas, round seed shape (R) is dominant over wrinkled (r), and yellow seed color (Y) is dominant over green (y). A plant heterozygous for both traits (RrYy) is crossed with a plant that is homozygous recessive for seed shape and heterozygous for seed color (rrYy). The two genes are located on different chromosomes.
title: APBIO-MCQ-052

choices_json.rationale: Wrinkled yellow (rrY_) requires r from each parent for seed shape AND Y_ for color. Shape: Rr × rr → 1/2 Rr (round) : 1/2 rr (wrinkled). Color: Yy × Yy → 1/4 YY : 2/4 Yy : 1/4 yy → 3/4 yellow (Y_) : 1/4 green (yy). Wrinkled yellow = 1/2 × 3/4 = 3/8, not 1/4.

Applying the product rule for independent genes: seed shape cross Rr × rr yields 1/2 round (Rr) and 1/2 wrinkled (rr). Seed color cross Yy × Yy yields 3/4 yellow (Y_) and 1/4 green (yy). Wrinkled yellow = P(rr) × P(Y_) = 1/2 × 3/4 = 3/8. This is the expected fraction when two independent loci are considered separately and multiplied.

1/8 would result if both parental genotypes were heterozygous for both traits (RrYy × RrYy), where wrinkled yellow = 1/4 × 3/4 is not 1/8. The actual calculation for this cross (Rr × rr for shape, Yy × Yy for color) gives 1/2 × 3/4 = 3/8.

3/16 would result from a different cross combination. Here the shape cross is Rr × rr (not Rr × Rr), giving 1/2 wrinkled rather than 1/4 wrinkled. 1/4 × 3/4 = 3/16 only applies if both parents were Rr for the shape locus.

stem: What does the test cross result reveal about the genotype of the unknown plant?
stimulus: A plant with purple flowers is crossed with a white-flowered plant known to be homozygous recessive (pp). Purple flowers are dominant (P) over white flowers (p). The cross produces 46 purple-flowered offspring and 51 white-flowered offspring. A second unknown purple-flowered plant is crossed with the same pp tester: this cross produces 94 purple-flowered offspring and 0 white-flowered offspring (out of 94 total).
title: APBIO-MCQ-053

choices_json.rationale: Any purple-flowered plant must carry at least one P allele — this logic alone cannot distinguish PP from Pp. A Pp × pp cross would be expected to produce approximately 50% purple (Pp) and 50% white (pp) offspring. Producing 94 purple and 0 white offspring is inconsistent with Pp genotype.
choices_json.choice_text: The second plant is heterozygous (Pp) because it produced purple offspring, which requires at least one P allele

choices_json.rationale: The test cross logic: PP × pp → all Pp (purple); Pp × pp → 1/2 Pp (purple) : 1/2 pp (white). The second plant yielded 94/94 purple and 0 white. The probability of getting 0 white offspring from 94 trials if the plant were Pp is (1/2)^94, effectively impossible. All-purple offspring strongly indicate PP. The first plant (≈1:1 ratio) is Pp by contrast.
choices_json.choice_text: The second plant is homozygous dominant (PP): a PP × pp cross produces only Pp offspring (all purple), and producing zero white offspring out of 94 is consistent with PP — while a Pp parent would be expected to yield ~47 white offspring

choices_json.rationale: While absolute certainty is never possible in genetics, the probability of a Pp parent producing zero white offspring in 94 trials is (0.5)^94, which is vanishingly small. This is sufficient statistical evidence to conclude the plant is PP. Test crosses are specifically designed to resolve such genotype questions.
choices_json.choice_text: No conclusion can be drawn because 94 offspring is not a large enough sample to determine genotype with certainty

choices_json.rationale: Invoking an unobserved mutation is not a parsimonious interpretation when a simpler explanation (PP genotype) fully explains the data. The test cross is designed precisely to distinguish PP from Pp using offspring phenotype ratios; lethality would require additional evidence beyond phenotype ratios alone.
choices_json.choice_text: The second plant's genotype is unknown because it might carry a new dominant mutation that prevents white offspring from surviving

stem: Which inheritance pattern is demonstrated by the flower color data, and what is the genotype of the pink F1 plants?
stimulus: Two true-breeding snapdragon strains are crossed: one with red flowers and one with white flowers. All F1 offspring have pink flowers. When F1 pink plants are self-fertilized, the F2 generation produces 1/4 red, 1/2 pink, and 1/4 white flowered plants. Biochemical analysis shows red plants produce a full amount of red pigment protein, pink plants produce half the amount, and white plants produce no pigment protein.
title: APBIO-MCQ-054

choices_json.rationale: Codominance produces distinct simultaneous expression of both alleles in separate regions (e.g., red AND white patches on the same petal). The F1 plants are uniformly pink — an intermediate phenotype resulting from reduced total pigment, not a mosaic of red and white. The biochemical data (half the pigment protein) confirm blending of expression levels, not separate domains.
choices_json.choice_text: Codominance; the F1 genotype is C^R C^W, and both alleles are simultaneously and equally expressed as distinct red and white patches

choices_json.rationale: Incomplete dominance: neither allele fully masks the other in heterozygotes, producing an intermediate phenotype. Key evidence: (1) F1 are uniformly pink (not red or white) — intermediate; (2) F2 ratio is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white — the heterozygous class is phenotypically distinct from both homozygotes; (3) biochemical data confirm a dose-response relationship (2 alleles = full red, 1 allele = half pigment = pink, 0 alleles = white).
choices_json.choice_text: Incomplete dominance; the F1 genotype is C^R C^W (or using standard notation, heterozygous for the pigment gene), and the single functional pigment allele in F1 produces half the pigment, yielding an intermediate pink phenotype

choices_json.rationale: Variable expressivity would not produce the precise 1:2:1 F2 ratio or the perfectly predictable pigment dosage relationship. The F2 data show a discrete three-phenotype ratio that tracks genotype exactly — inconsistent with environmental variation. The biochemical dose-response directly links genotype to phenotype.
choices_json.choice_text: Simple dominance with variable expressivity; the F1 and F2 pink plants are genetically identical to red plants but environmentally influenced to appear pink

choices_json.rationale: Blending inheritance would predict that F2 plants are all uniformly pink (blended alleles cannot re-separate). Instead, F2 shows 1/4 red and 1/4 white — both original parental phenotypes reappear intact. This "unblending" in F2 is the classic evidence that alleles remain as discrete particles (as Mendel showed) rather than permanently blending.
choices_json.choice_text: Blending inheritance; the parental alleles fuse in F1 and cannot be separated in subsequent generations

stem: Which statement about the inheritance of color blindness in this family is best supported by the pedigree?
stimulus:
A pedigree shows: Generation I — unaffected father (I-1) and unaffected mother (I-2). Generation II — three sons: II-1 color blind, II-2 unaffected, II-3 color blind; one daughter: II-4 unaffected. Generation III — II-4 married an unaffected man (III-1); their children are III-2 (son, color blind) and III-3 (daughter, unaffected).

Color blindness is caused by a recessive allele. The trait appears only in males in this pedigree.
title: APBIO-MCQ-055

choices_json.rationale: If autosomal recessive, unaffected female II-4 would need genotype Cc. Her unaffected husband III-1 must also be Cc to produce affected son III-2. While this is possible, the consistent male-only expression across two generations (4 affected males, 0 affected females) strongly favors X-linkage. Autosomal would require two carriers marrying in both generations without any affected females.
choices_json.choice_text: The gene is autosomal recessive; the pattern of only males being affected is coincidental in this small pedigree

choices_json.rationale: X-linked recessive explains all observations: (1) Males are affected (X^c Y hemizygous, no second X to provide dominant allele); (2) Females are unaffected carriers (X^C X^c — dominant allele on second X masks the recessive); (3) I-2 must be carrier (X^C X^c) because she has affected sons who received X^c from her; (4) II-4 inherited X^c from mother I-2, making her X^C X^c carrier, explaining her affected son III-2.
choices_json.choice_text: The gene is X-linked recessive: males are hemizygous (X^c Y) and express the recessive allele without a dominant allele to mask it; carrier females (X^C X^c) are unaffected; unaffected mother I-2 is a carrier who passed X^c to her affected sons

choices_json.rationale: Y-linked traits appear in ALL sons of an affected father — but I-1 (the father) is unaffected while two of his sons (II-1, II-3) are affected. Y-linked inheritance requires an affected father. Since I-1 is unaffected, Y-linkage cannot explain the pattern.
choices_json.choice_text: The gene is Y-linked; it passes directly from father to all sons

choices_json.rationale: X-linked dominant traits would affect females in each generation because a carrier mother (having one dominant allele) would be affected herself, not just a carrier. Additionally, X-linked dominant traits affect daughters of affected fathers 100% of the time. Neither feature matches this pedigree where all affected individuals are male and no females are affected.
choices_json.choice_text: The gene is X-linked dominant; affected males inherited the dominant allele from their carrier mother

stem: Which explanation best accounts for the modified 9:7 ratio rather than the expected 9:3:3:1 ratio?
stimulus: In a flower color experiment, two true-breeding white-flowered plants from different strains are crossed. All F1 offspring have purple flowers. When F1 plants are self-fertilized, the F2 generation shows 9/16 purple and 7/16 white — not the classic 9:3:3:1 ratio. Biochemical analysis reveals: a colorless precursor is converted to a purple pigment by two sequential enzymes, each encoded by a separate gene (gene C and gene P). Both enzymes are required to produce any purple pigment.
title: APBIO-MCQ-056

choices_json.rationale: Linkage reduces recombinant classes but does not produce a 9:7 ratio — it would skew the proportions of the four phenotypic classes while still producing four distinct classes. The 9:7 ratio specifically reflects two phenotypic classes (purple vs. white), which is the hallmark of complementary epistasis, not linkage.
