choices_json.choice_text: The two genes are linked on the same chromosome, which reduces recombination and collapses the expected four phenotypic classes

choices_json.rationale: In a CcPp × CcPp cross, the 16 possible genotypic combinations yield: 9 C_P_ (purple, both enzymes present), 3 C_pp (white, no enzyme P), 3 ccP_ (white, no enzyme C), and 1 ccpp (white, no enzyme). The three white genotypic classes collapse into one white phenotypic class because all three lack at least one enzyme. 9 purple : 7 white is the signature of complementary gene interaction.
choices_json.choice_text: Complementary epistasis: purple pigment requires functional alleles at BOTH loci (C and P); any genotype lacking a dominant allele at either locus (cc__ or __pp) produces white, so the 7/16 white fraction combines the three white genotypic classes (C_pp + ccP_ + ccpp = 3+3+1 = 7) from a standard dihybrid cross

choices_json.rationale: De novo mutation producing purple in all F1 offspring is statistically implausible. The cross of two different white strains producing purple F1 is explained by complementation: one parent provides gene C, the other provides gene P, and F1 heterozygotes (CcPp) have both functional alleles for the first time.
choices_json.choice_text: The two white parental strains are genetically identical, and mutation in F1 created a new purple allele not present in either parent

choices_json.rationale: Multiple alleles at one locus would modify proportions within phenotypic classes but would not explain why two independent genes produce only two phenotypic classes. The 9:7 ratio specifically requires two independently assorting genes whose products are both needed for the purple phenotype.
choices_json.choice_text: One gene has three alleles rather than two, and the additional allele accounts for the extra white class beyond the standard 9:3:3:1

stem: What does the recombination frequency between genes A and B indicate, and how does it affect expected offspring ratios?
stimulus: Genes A and B are on the same chromosome. A double heterozygote with parental chromosomes AB and ab (written in cis configuration) is test-crossed against an aabb individual. Instead of the expected 1:1:1:1 ratio from independent assortment, the offspring are: 430 AB, 420 ab, 48 Ab, 42 aB (total = 940). The AB and ab classes are called parental types; Ab and aB are recombinant types.
title: APBIO-MCQ-057

choices_json.rationale: Recombination frequency = (recombinant offspring / total) × 100 = (48 + 42) / 940 × 100 = 90/940 × 100 ≈ 9.6%. A frequency of 50% would mean the genes behave as if unlinked — the observed 9.6% is well below 50%, confirming strong linkage.
choices_json.choice_text: The recombination frequency is approximately 50%, indicating the genes are unlinked and assort independently

choices_json.rationale: Recombination frequency = (48 + 42) / 940 = 90 / 940 ≈ 0.096 = 9.6%. In map units (centimorgans), this is 9.6 cM — a short genetic distance. Close linkage means most offspring inherit the parental chromosome combinations intact (AB or ab), and only ~9.6% result from crossover events that produce recombinant chromosomes (Ab or aB).
choices_json.choice_text: The recombination frequency is approximately 9.6 map units (cM), indicating the genes are closely linked; crossovers between them are rare, so parental combinations (AB and ab) are inherited together in ~90% of offspring

choices_json.rationale: The test cross is the standard method for detecting linkage and calculating recombination frequency. Because the tester is homozygous recessive (aabb), all gametes from the tester carry ab, so offspring phenotypes directly reveal the gamete genotypes from the heterozygous parent — making recombinant classes easy to count.
choices_json.choice_text: The recombination frequency cannot be calculated from a test cross; only F2 self-fertilization data can reveal gene linkage

choices_json.rationale: Recombination (crossing over) is a normal meiotic process that generates novel chromosome combinations — it does not destroy chromosomes. Recombinant offspring are simply less frequent than parental offspring when genes are linked because crossing over between any two specific loci is a probabilistic event that occurs in only a fraction of meioses.
choices_json.choice_text: The excess of parental types over recombinant types indicates that recombination is a mutagenic process that selectively destroys recombinant chromosomes before they can be transmitted

stem: What is the probability that a child of this couple will have blood type O?
stimulus: The ABO blood group system has three alleles at one locus: I^A (codes for A antigen, codominant with I^B), I^B (codes for B antigen, codominant with I^A), and i (recessive, no antigen). A woman with blood type A has a father with blood type O. Her husband has blood type B and his mother has blood type O. Blood type O individuals are genotype ii.
title: APBIO-MCQ-058

choices_json.rationale: Both parents carry an i allele. The woman's father is O (ii), so she received i from him; she is I^A i. The husband's mother is O (ii), so he received i from her; he is I^B i. Each parent can transmit i, so ii offspring (blood type O) are possible.
choices_json.choice_text: 0 (impossible)

choices_json.rationale: Determining parental genotypes from family history: Woman is type A with an O father (ii) → she received i from father and must be I^A i (not I^A I^A, since her father only has i to give). Husband is type B with an O mother (ii) → he received i from mother and must be I^B i. Cross: I^A i × I^B i → 1/4 I^A I^B (AB), 1/4 I^A i (A), 1/4 I^B i (B), 1/4 ii (O). Probability of blood type O = 1/4.

1/2 would only be correct if one parent were ii (type O) and the other were I^A i or I^B i. Neither parent in this problem is type O — both are heterozygous carriers. The cross of two single-allele carriers (I^A i × I^B i) produces four genotypic classes in equal 1/4 proportions.

1/3 is not a Mendelian probability that arises from this cross. It might result from conditional probability calculations (e.g., given the child is not AB, what is the probability of O?), but the question asks for the unconditional probability of type O among all offspring, which is 1/4.

stem: Which best explains why human height does not follow the simple Mendelian ratios observed for seed color or flower color in peas?
stimulus: Human height is influenced by at least 400 different genetic loci identified in genome-wide association studies, each contributing a small additive effect. Environmental factors (nutrition, health during development) also influence final adult height. In a large population, adult height values form a continuous, approximately normal distribution rather than discrete categories. Identical twin studies show a heritability of approximately 80% for height, meaning roughly 80% of the variation in height within a population is attributable to genetic differences.
title: APBIO-MCQ-059

choices_json.rationale: While multiple alleles at one locus exist in populations, height is determined by hundreds of different loci (polygenic), not hundreds of alleles at one locus. The normal distribution arises from the additive effects of many independent loci — a key distinction from multiple allelism at a single locus.
choices_json.choice_text: Height is determined by a single gene with hundreds of alleles, each specifying a slightly different height; the large allele number produces a continuous distribution

choices_json.rationale: Mendelian ratios apply when one or a few loci each have large, discrete effects. For polygenic traits, each locus contributes a tiny increment to the phenotype. With 400+ loci each having 2+ alleles, the number of possible genotypic combinations is astronomically large, producing a near-continuous range of phenotypes. Environmental effects further blur any remaining discontinuities, producing the bell-curve distribution seen in human height.
choices_json.choice_text: Height is a polygenic trait: many loci each contribute a small additive effect, and when combined with environmental influences, the cumulative result is a continuous normal distribution rather than discrete phenotypic classes — unlike single-gene traits where a small number of allele combinations produce a few distinct phenotypes

choices_json.rationale: Heritability is specifically defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance attributable to genetic variance — it accounts for shared environments in twin studies by comparing identical vs. fraternal twin correlations. An 80% heritability indicates a strong genetic component. Attributing heritability entirely to shared environment contradicts the methodology of twin studies.
choices_json.choice_text: Height is entirely determined by environment; the 80% heritability figure reflects correlation between family environments rather than shared genes

choices_json.rationale: While epigenetic factors contribute to gene expression variation, the primary explanation for height's continuous distribution is polygenic inheritance — many loci each with small additive DNA sequence effects. The 80% heritability from twin studies reflects heritable differences in DNA sequence, not exclusively epigenetic effects, which have lower intergenerational heritability.
choices_json.choice_text: Height does not follow Mendelian ratios because it is controlled by epigenetic modifications rather than DNA sequence variation, making it unpredictable from parental genotypes

stem: Which conclusion about the bicoid gene and its product is most directly supported by the experiment?
stimulus: The bicoid gene in Drosophila encodes a transcription factor that is maternally expressed: the mother's nurse cells deposit bicoid mRNA into the anterior end of the egg before fertilization. After fertilization, Bicoid protein forms a gradient (high at anterior, low at posterior) that determines head and thorax development. Experiment: eggs from bicoid mutant mothers (which deposit no bicoid mRNA) develop into embryos with no head or thorax — instead, a mirror-image abdomen develops at both ends. When pure bicoid mRNA is injected into the posterior end of a bicoid-null egg, a second head forms at the injection site.
title: APBIO-MCQ-060

choices_json.rationale: While Bicoid does repress some posterior determinants (notably it represses caudal mRNA translation), the primary mechanism is that Bicoid is a transcriptional activator of anterior identity genes (like orthodenticle and hunchback). The rescue experiment — injecting mRNA at the posterior produces a head there — most directly demonstrates that Bicoid is sufficient to specify anterior identity, not merely that it represses posterior fate.
choices_json.choice_text: Bicoid protein determines anterior cell fate by repressing posterior-specific genes; without Bicoid, posterior fate is the default state, producing a double-abdomen phenotype

choices_json.rationale: The injection experiment is the key evidence: bicoid mRNA injected at a new location creates Bicoid protein locally, and cells exposed to sufficient Bicoid protein above the threshold adopt anterior identity regardless of their physical position in the embryo. This demonstrates that the spatial distribution of bicoid mRNA (set up by the mother before fertilization) is sufficient to specify the anterior-posterior body axis — a maternal effect on offspring phenotype independent of the offspring's own genotype.
choices_json.choice_text: Bicoid mRNA is a positional determinant: its local concentration after fertilization determines cell fate; wherever Bicoid protein is present above a threshold, cells adopt anterior (head/thorax) identity, as demonstrated by the ectopic head at the injection site

choices_json.rationale: Bicoid mRNA is deposited by the mother, but its translation and function occur in the embryo after fertilization. The rescue by injecting bicoid mRNA directly demonstrates that Bicoid protein itself acts in embryonic cells to specify fate — it is not a proxy for a separate embryonic gene.
choices_json.choice_text: The bicoid gene product acts only during the mother's oogenesis and has no direct role in the developing embryo; the mRNA injection rescue works by activating a distinct gene expressed by the embryo

choices_json.rationale: Maternal effect genes are the opposite of Mendelian recessive traits in one key respect: offspring phenotype is determined by the mother's genotype, not the offspring's own genotype. Bicoid mutant mothers produce abnormal offspring even if the offspring inherit a wild-type bicoid allele from the father — because the embryo cannot produce Bicoid protein from its own paternal allele early enough to rescue anterior identity.
choices_json.choice_text: The phenotype of bicoid mutant offspring depends on the offspring's own bicoid genotype, not the mother's genotype, making this a standard Mendelian recessive trait

stem: Which correctly describes the directionality and template strand usage in transcription and translation?
stimulus: The central dogma describes information flow: DNA → RNA → Protein. During transcription, RNA polymerase moves along the DNA template strand and synthesizes a complementary RNA strand. During translation, the ribosome reads mRNA codons and assembles a polypeptide chain. Both processes follow strict directionality rules based on the chemistry of nucleotide and amino acid addition.
title: APBIO-MCQ-061

choices_json.rationale: Transcription direction is correct (RNA polymerase reads template 3'→5', synthesizes RNA 5'→3'), but translation direction is wrong. Ribosomes read mRNA 5'→3' (from the 5' end toward the 3' end) and add amino acids to the C-terminus of the growing polypeptide chain — the first amino acid at the N-terminus.
choices_json.choice_text: Transcription proceeds 3'→5' along the template strand, synthesizing RNA 5'→3'; translation reads mRNA 3'→5', adding amino acids to the N-terminus

choices_json.rationale: RNA polymerase reads the DNA template strand in the 3'→5' direction (antiparallel to the RNA it synthesizes), producing RNA in the 5'→3' direction — the universal direction of nucleic acid synthesis (new nucleotides added to the 3'-OH end). The ribosome reads codons from the 5' end of mRNA toward the 3' end, and each new aminoacyl-tRNA is added to the free carboxyl (C) terminus of the growing chain.
choices_json.choice_text: Transcription reads the template strand 3'→5' and synthesizes RNA 5'→3'; translation reads mRNA codons 5'→3' and adds each new amino acid to the C-terminus of the growing polypeptide

choices_json.rationale: RNA polymerase reads the TEMPLATE (antisense) strand, not the coding (sense) strand. The coding strand has the same sequence as the RNA (with T instead of U) and is not used as the template. This choice confuses the two DNA strands.
choices_json.choice_text: Transcription reads the coding (non-template) strand 5'→3' to synthesize RNA; translation reads mRNA 5'→3' adding amino acids to the N-terminus

choices_json.rationale: New monomers (nucleotides during transcription, amino acids during translation) are added to the 3' end (for RNA) or C-terminus (for polypeptides), not the 5' end. The growing chain is extended at its 3'/C-terminal end, not at the 5'/N-terminal end.
choices_json.choice_text: Both transcription and translation proceed 5'→3' along their respective templates, and new monomers are always added to the 5' end of the growing chain

stem: In which condition will the lac operon structural genes (lacZ, lacY, lacA) be most highly transcribed?
stimulus: The E. coli lac operon encodes genes for lactose metabolism. The lac repressor protein binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase when active. Allolactose (a metabolite of lactose) acts as an inducer by binding the repressor and causing it to release the operator. Additionally, catabolite activator protein (CAP) binds a site upstream of the promoter when bound to cAMP; CAP-cAMP complex enhances RNA polymerase binding. Intracellular cAMP is high when glucose is absent and low when glucose is present (glucose inhibits adenylyl cyclase).
title: APBIO-MCQ-062

choices_json.rationale: With glucose present, cAMP is low, CAP is inactive, and there is no positive stimulation of the promoter. With lactose absent, there is no allolactose to inactivate the repressor, so the repressor blocks the operator. Both regulatory mechanisms suppress transcription: no CAP activation AND repressor blocking.
choices_json.choice_text: Glucose present, lactose absent

choices_json.rationale: Maximal lac operon transcription requires two conditions simultaneously: (1) Negative control off — allolactose from lactose metabolism binds and inactivates the repressor, freeing the operator; (2) Positive control on — absence of glucose raises cAMP, CAP-cAMP binds upstream and strongly enhances RNA polymerase recruitment. Both conditions are met only when glucose is absent and lactose is present, producing the highest transcription rate.
choices_json.choice_text: Glucose absent, lactose present

choices_json.rationale: With glucose present, cAMP is low and CAP is inactive — the positive control is off. Even though lactose inactivates the repressor (removing the negative control block), without CAP activation transcription occurs only at basal levels — much lower than when both controls are optimal.
choices_json.choice_text: Glucose present, lactose present

choices_json.rationale: Without lactose, allolactose is not produced, the repressor remains active and blocks the operator. Even though glucose absence raises cAMP and activates CAP (positive control on), the repressor prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing. Both controls must be favorable: repressor off AND CAP on.
choices_json.choice_text: Glucose absent, lactose absent

stem: Which best explains why treating cells with a drug that blocks 5' capping would disrupt gene expression even though capping occurs after transcription begins?
stimulus: Eukaryotic pre-mRNA undergoes three processing steps in the nucleus before export to the cytoplasm: (1) 5' capping — a modified guanosine nucleotide (7-methylguanosine) is added to the 5' end shortly after transcription begins; (2) 3' polyadenylation — a poly-A tail of ~200 adenine nucleotides is added after cleavage at a specific signal sequence; (3) splicing — introns are removed by the spliceosome and exons are joined. The mature mRNA is then exported through nuclear pores and translated by ribosomes.
title: APBIO-MCQ-063

choices_json.rationale: While RNA processing steps are coordinated through the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain (CTD), the 5' cap and poly-A tail are added by distinct enzymes. Blocking capping primarily affects cap-dependent processes, not polyadenylation directly. Poly-A tail addition depends on recognition of the polyadenylation signal sequence (AAUAAA), independent of the cap.
choices_json.choice_text: Blocking 5' capping prevents the poly-A tail from being added, because capping and polyadenylation are coupled in a single enzymatic complex

choices_json.rationale: The 5' cap serves multiple essential functions: (1) protection — the cap's inverted methylguanosine resists 5'→3' exonucleases that would otherwise rapidly degrade the mRNA from its 5' end; (2) nuclear export — cap-binding complex CBC recognizes the cap and facilitates export through nuclear pores; (3) translation initiation — eIF4E binds the cap and recruits the 43S ribosomal pre-initiation complex. Blocking capping thus disrupts mRNA stability, localization, and translation simultaneously.
choices_json.choice_text: The 5' cap protects mRNA from 5'→3' exonuclease degradation, enables nuclear export through cap-binding proteins, and is recognized by the eIF4E translation initiation factor; without a cap, uncapped transcripts are rapidly degraded and cannot be translated

choices_json.rationale: While the cap does influence splicing of the first intron through interactions between CBC and the spliceosome, this is not the primary consequence of blocking capping. The dominant effects are mRNA degradation and failure of translation initiation — both of which are more directly and universally disruptive than incomplete splicing of one intron.
choices_json.choice_text: The 5' cap is required for splicing of the first intron; without capping, introns adjacent to the 5' end cannot be removed and the mRNA cannot be translated in frame

choices_json.rationale: RNA polymerase II can continue elongation without the 5' cap — capping is added co-transcriptionally but is not required for polymerase to continue. Uncapped transcripts are produced but are unstable and non-functional. The drug disrupts downstream mRNA fate, not polymerase activity.
choices_json.choice_text: Blocking 5' capping arrests RNA polymerase II immediately after initiation, so no full-length transcript is ever produced

stem: Which feature of eukaryotic gene expression represents the most fundamental structural difference from prokaryotic gene expression?
stimulus: Bacteria and eukaryotes both use DNA as their hereditary material and both transcribe DNA to mRNA that is then translated. However, key structural and mechanistic differences exist between the two systems. In bacteria: transcription occurs in the cytoplasm, ribosomes begin translating mRNA while it is still being transcribed (coupled transcription-translation), and mRNAs are often polycistronic (encoding multiple proteins). In eukaryotes: transcription occurs in the nucleus, translation occurs in the cytoplasm, and mRNAs are typically monocistronic.
title: APBIO-MCQ-064

choices_json.rationale: Both bacteria and eukaryotes use RNA polymerase for transcription. DNA polymerase replicates DNA in both organisms. This choice confuses DNA replication with transcription.
choices_json.choice_text: Eukaryotes use RNA polymerase while prokaryotes use DNA polymerase for transcription

choices_json.rationale: The nuclear envelope is the defining structural difference. Its consequence for gene expression is profound: eukaryotic pre-mRNA must be processed (capped, spliced, polyadenylated) and exported through nuclear pores before ribosomes can access it — adding multiple regulatory checkpoints and time delays. Bacteria have no such barrier, enabling ribosomes to begin translating the 5' end of mRNA while RNA polymerase is still elongating from the 3' end, making bacterial gene expression faster but less regulated.
choices_json.choice_text: The nuclear membrane in eukaryotes physically separates transcription (nucleus) from translation (cytoplasm), requiring mRNA processing and export before translation; prokaryotes lack this compartmentalization and can couple transcription and translation simultaneously

choices_json.rationale: The genetic code (64 codons specifying 20 amino acids plus stop codons) is nearly universal across all life — bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes use the same codon assignments with very minor exceptions. This is one of the strongest pieces of evidence for common ancestry.
choices_json.choice_text: Eukaryotes use the genetic code while prokaryotes use a different codon system

choices_json.rationale: Prokaryotes have abundant transcription regulatory proteins (repressors, activators, sigma factors) that control gene expression — the lac repressor and CAP activator are classic examples. Prokaryotic gene regulation differs from eukaryotic regulation in mechanism and complexity but is not absent.
choices_json.choice_text: Prokaryotes cannot regulate gene expression because they lack transcription factors

stem: Which best explains why treatment with histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors increases transcription of many genes in cancer cells?
stimulus: Eukaryotic DNA is packaged around histone proteins to form nucleosomes. The accessibility of DNA to transcription machinery is regulated by histone modifications. Histone acetyltransferases (HATs) add acetyl groups to lysine residues on histone tails, reducing the positive charge on histones and weakening their interaction with negatively charged DNA. Histone deacetylases (HDACs) remove acetyl groups, restoring the positive charge and tightening histone-DNA interactions. Many cancer cells show abnormally high HDAC activity at tumor suppressor gene promoters.
title: APBIO-MCQ-065

choices_json.rationale: HDAC inhibitors block HDAC enzyme activity — they do not add acetyl groups themselves. The acetyl groups that accumulate are those added by HATs and no longer removed by the inhibited HDACs. HDAC inhibitors are enzyme blockers, not HAT mimics.
choices_json.choice_text: HDAC inhibitors add acetyl groups to histones directly, replacing HDAC enzyme function and activating transcription through a novel mechanism

choices_json.rationale: In cancer cells, abnormally active HDACs deacetylate histones at tumor suppressor promoters, creating tightly packed, inaccessible chromatin (heterochromatin) that silences transcription. Inhibiting HDACs allows acetyl groups added by HATs to persist, maintaining or restoring the open chromatin (euchromatin) state. Reduced histone-DNA interaction exposes promoter sequences, enabling transcription factor binding and RNA polymerase recruitment to previously silenced genes including tumor suppressors.
choices_json.choice_text: HDAC inhibitors prevent removal of acetyl groups from histone tails; acetylation neutralizes histone's positive charge, loosening nucleosome packaging and making promoter DNA more accessible to transcription factors and RNA polymerase

choices_json.rationale: HDAC inhibitors specifically target HDAC enzymes — they do not intercalate into DNA. DNA intercalation is the mechanism of certain anticancer drugs (e.g., doxorubicin) but is mechanistically distinct from histone modification. HDAC inhibitors work by preserving histone acetylation, not by directly displacing nucleosomes.
choices_json.choice_text: HDAC inhibitors intercalate between DNA base pairs at promoters, physically displacing nucleosomes and exposing the DNA template directly

choices_json.rationale: RNA polymerase II CTD phosphorylation is carried out by cyclin-dependent kinases (particularly CDK7 and CDK9), not by HDAC inhibitors. HDAC inhibitors act upstream of polymerase recruitment — they change chromatin structure to allow transcription factor and polymerase access, not by directly modifying polymerase.
choices_json.choice_text: HDAC inhibitors activate RNA polymerase II directly by phosphorylating its C-terminal domain, bypassing the need for chromatin remodeling

stem: A mutation inactivates the trp repressor protein so that it can no longer bind tryptophan. What is the predicted effect on trp operon transcription in cells grown with excess tryptophan?
stimulus: The trp (tryptophan) operon encodes enzymes for tryptophan biosynthesis. Unlike the inducible lac operon, the trp operon is repressible: transcription is on by default and turned off when the end product (tryptophan) accumulates. The inactive trp aporepressor becomes an active repressor only when tryptophan (the corepressor) binds it; the active tryptophan-repressor complex then binds the operator and blocks transcription. When tryptophan is scarce, the aporepressor remains inactive and transcription proceeds.
title: APBIO-MCQ-066

choices_json.rationale: Tryptophan is a small amino acid that does not bind DNA directly. Its regulatory role is as a corepressor that allosterically activates the repressor protein — tryptophan alone cannot repress the operon without a functional repressor. The operator sequence is recognized by protein, not by tryptophan.
choices_json.choice_text: Transcription is repressed, because tryptophan accumulates and directly binds the operator to block RNA polymerase

choices_json.rationale: Wild-type regulation: high tryptophan → tryptophan binds aporepressor → active repressor-tryptophan complex blocks operator → transcription off. Mutant repressor: cannot bind tryptophan → always stays in inactive aporepressor form → never blocks operator → transcription is constitutively on even with excess tryptophan. This is the opposite of the normal repressible logic and demonstrates that the corepressor-repressor interaction is essential for feedback control.
choices_json.choice_text: Transcription occurs constitutively even in the presence of excess tryptophan: the mutant repressor cannot bind tryptophan, so it never becomes active; the operator remains unbound and RNA polymerase transcribes the trp genes continuously regardless of tryptophan levels

choices_json.rationale: The question specifies the repressor cannot bind tryptophan — not that it is degraded. Even if some reduction in repressor activity occurred due to instability, the primary predicted effect is constitutive transcription (always on) because the tryptophan-sensing mechanism is broken, not that transcription is merely reduced.
choices_json.choice_text: Transcription is reduced because the mutant repressor is unstable and is degraded, leaving fewer repressor molecules to block transcription under all conditions

choices_json.rationale: Attenuation is a secondary regulatory mechanism for the trp operon (involving ribosome stalling at a leader sequence), but the repressor is a primary and independent control mechanism. Inactivating the repressor disrupts repressor-mediated control regardless of attenuation. The question asks about the repressor mutation's effect, which is constitutive transcription.
choices_json.choice_text: Transcription is unaffected because the trp operon is regulated by attenuation, not by the repressor

stem: Which conclusion about the liver-specific enhancer is best supported by the experimental results?
stimulus:
A gene (Gene X) is expressed at high levels in liver cells but not in muscle cells. The same DNA sequence (same gene) is present in both cell types. Researchers identify a 300 bp enhancer element located 50 kb upstream of Gene X's promoter. Experiments:

1. Deleting the enhancer in liver cells: Gene X expression drops to near zero.
2. Inserting the 300 bp enhancer upstream of a reporter gene (luciferase) in liver cells: luciferase is strongly expressed.
3. Inserting the same enhancer-luciferase construct into muscle cells: luciferase is not expressed.
4. Adding liver-specific transcription factors to muscle cells (via transfection) with the enhancer-luciferase construct: luciferase is expressed.
title: APBIO-MCQ-067

choices_json.rationale: Experiment 2 shows the enhancer must be paired with a promoter (the luciferase reporter's promoter) to drive expression — the enhancer alone is not sufficient and does not contain an independent promoter. Enhancers work by looping to contact and activate proximal promoters, not by independently initiating transcription.
choices_json.choice_text: The enhancer contains its own promoter that independently drives Gene X transcription; the Gene X promoter is dispensable

choices_json.rationale: Each experiment supports a distinct conclusion: (1) deletion → enhancer is necessary; (2) transfer to reporter gene drives expression → sufficient for transcriptional activation; (3) inactive in muscle → tissue-specific; (4) liver transcription factors restore activity in muscle → the enhancer requires binding by cell-type-specific factors that are present in liver but absent from muscle. Together these results establish the mechanistic basis of tissue-specific gene expression through enhancer-transcription factor specificity.
choices_json.choice_text: The enhancer is necessary for Gene X transcription in liver cells, is sufficient to confer liver-specific expression on a heterologous gene, and its activity requires liver-specific transcription factors that are present in liver but not muscle cells

choices_json.rationale: Experiment 1 (deletion in adult liver cells drops expression to near zero) directly contradicts this hypothesis. If Gene X maintained itself independently after initial activation, deleting the enhancer in already-expressing liver cells would have no effect. The enhancer is continuously required for maintained expression.
choices_json.choice_text: The enhancer is required only for the initial activation of Gene X during liver development; once activated, Gene X maintains its own expression through a positive feedback loop independent of the enhancer

choices_json.rationale: Experiment 3 shows the enhancer-reporter construct is inactive in muscle cells — but this is most simply explained by the absence of liver-specific activating transcription factors (as confirmed by experiment 4). There is no evidence from these experiments that the enhancer recruits muscle-specific repressors; absence of activators in muscle is sufficient to explain the muscle-specific silence.
choices_json.choice_text: The enhancer acts as a silencer in muscle cells by actively recruiting repressor proteins that block Gene X transcription in non-hepatic tissues

stem: Which best explains why overexpressing a specific miRNA in cancer cells reduces the protein level of its target gene without changing the target gene's transcription rate?
stimulus: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small (~22 nucleotide) non-coding RNA molecules encoded in the genome. Primary miRNA transcripts are processed in the nucleus by Drosha into pre-miRNAs, then exported and processed by Dicer into mature miRNA duplexes. One strand of the duplex associates with the RISC (RNA-induced silencing complex) protein complex. The miRNA guide strand within RISC base-pairs with complementary sequences typically in the 3' UTR of target mRNAs. Perfect complementarity leads to mRNA cleavage; imperfect complementarity leads to translational repression and/or accelerated mRNA decay.
title: APBIO-MCQ-068

choices_json.rationale: Mature miRNAs function in the cytoplasm as part of the RISC complex — they regulate post-transcriptional gene expression. They do not enter the nucleus to block promoters. The question specifies that transcription rate is unchanged, which is consistent with cytoplasmic post-transcriptional regulation, not nuclear transcriptional repression.
choices_json.choice_text: The miRNA enters the nucleus and blocks the target gene's promoter by forming a DNA-RNA hybrid, preventing RNA polymerase from initiating transcription

choices_json.rationale: Post-transcriptional regulation: miRNA-RISC binds the target mRNA's 3' UTR. With imperfect complementarity (typical in animals), RISC blocks translation by interfering with ribosome function and promotes mRNA deadenylation and decapping, leading to mRNA decay. Both effects reduce protein production from mRNAs that are still being produced at the same transcriptional rate — explaining unchanged transcription but reduced protein.
choices_json.choice_text: The miRNA, incorporated into RISC, base-pairs with complementary sequences in the 3' UTR of the target mRNA; this triggers translational repression (reduced ribosome association) and/or accelerated mRNA decay, decreasing protein output without affecting transcription

choices_json.rationale: Some small RNA pathways do influence chromatin, but mature miRNAs primarily function through RISC-mediated post-transcriptional mechanisms in the cytoplasm. More importantly, the question states that transcription rate is unchanged — any mechanism that reduces transcription contradicts the given observation.
choices_json.choice_text: The miRNA recruits histone deacetylases to the target gene locus, causing chromatin compaction that silences transcription despite appearing unchanged by standard assays

choices_json.rationale: miRNAs are RNA molecules that interact with other RNAs through base-pairing — they do not directly bind proteins. Protein degradation through the proteasome is mediated by ubiquitin tagging, not by RNA molecules. miRNA regulation occurs at the mRNA level (translational repression or mRNA decay), not at the protein level.
choices_json.choice_text: The miRNA directly binds the target protein and tags it for proteasomal degradation, reducing protein levels without affecting mRNA

stem: How does alternative splicing of the DSCAM gene in Drosophila illustrate the relationship between genome size and proteome complexity?
stimulus:
The Drosophila DSCAM gene encodes a neuronal cell-surface adhesion protein. The gene contains 115 exons organized into 4 clusters of alternatively spliced exons:
- Cluster 1: 12 alternative exons (one included)
- Cluster 2: 48 alternative exons (one included)
- Cluster 3: 33 alternative exons (one included)
- Cluster 4: 2 alternative exons (one included)

Each neuron is believed to express a unique combination of DSCAM isoforms that provides a molecular identity code for axon self-avoidance.
title: APBIO-MCQ-069

choices_json.rationale: This is precisely what DSCAM disproves. Alternative splicing allows one gene to encode many distinct protein isoforms. The DSCAM example is a famous demonstration that proteome complexity can vastly exceed gene count — one gene, thousands of proteins.
choices_json.choice_text: DSCAM illustrates that proteome complexity is strictly limited by genome size; since Drosophila has only ~14,000 genes, each gene can encode at most one protein

choices_json.rationale: Combinatorial alternative splicing: because one exon from each cluster is independently selected, the total number of combinations is the product of the choices in each cluster: 12 × 48 × 33 × 2 = 38,016. Drosophila has ~14,000 total genes yet one gene alone can encode ~38,000 protein isoforms. This illustrates why proteome complexity in complex organisms cannot be estimated from gene count alone — the transcriptome and splicing patterns are equally important.
choices_json.choice_text: Alternative splicing allows one gene to generate combinatorially enormous protein diversity: DSCAM can produce 12 × 48 × 33 × 2 = 38,016 distinct isoforms from a single gene locus, demonstrating that proteome complexity can far exceed the number of genes in the genome

choices_json.rationale: DSCAM is a single gene locus. The 38,016 isoforms are generated from the same genomic DNA sequence through differential inclusion of alternative exon clusters during pre-mRNA splicing — not from 38,016 separate genes on different chromosomes.
choices_json.choice_text: DSCAM encodes 38,016 separate proteins because it has 38,016 separate coding sequences on different chromosomes that are individually regulated

choices_json.rationale: The statement that one exon from each cluster is included is correct — but this IS alternative splicing, not constitutive splicing. The "alternative" aspect is which exon from each cluster is selected (e.g., which of the 48 exons in cluster 2 is included). Constitutive splicing would include all exons from all clusters in every mRNA, which would produce only one possible protein, not 38,016.
choices_json.choice_text: The 4 exon clusters are used simultaneously in each mRNA, producing a protein containing one exon from each cluster; this is constitutive, not alternative, splicing

stem: Which best explains why Igf2 is expressed from the paternal chromosome only, and what happens to Igf2 expression in offspring with two maternal chromosomes 7 (uniparental disomy)?
stimulus: Insulin-like growth factor 2 (Igf2) is a growth-promoting gene located on mouse chromosome 7. In normal offspring (one maternal, one paternal chromosome 7): only the paternal Igf2 allele is expressed; the maternal allele is silenced. The silencing is caused by a differentially methylated region (DMR) that is methylated on the maternal chromosome only. Methylation of the DMR on the maternal chromosome blocks binding of an insulator protein (CTCF), which normally prevents an enhancer from activating Igf2. On the paternal chromosome, the DMR is unmethylated, CTCF does not bind, and the enhancer freely activates Igf2.
title: APBIO-MCQ-070

choices_json.rationale: This is not a mutation-based difference — it is an epigenetic difference (methylation pattern) established during gametogenesis. The DNA sequences of maternal and paternal Igf2 alleles are identical; only the methylation pattern of the DMR differs. Both alleles are capable of expression if the insulator is not blocking the enhancer.
choices_json.choice_text: Igf2 is expressed only from the paternal chromosome because the paternal Igf2 allele carries a gain-of-function mutation absent from the maternal allele; uniparental disomy of maternal chromosomes would produce no Igf2 expression

choices_json.rationale: Mechanism on normal paternal chromosome: unmethylated DMR → no CTCF binding → enhancer contacts and activates Igf2. Mechanism on normal maternal chromosome: methylated DMR → CTCF binds → insulator between enhancer and Igf2 → enhancer cannot reach Igf2 → silenced. With two maternal chromosomes: both DMRs are methylated (both inherited from eggs) → CTCF binds both → both Igf2 alleles silenced → no growth factor production → undergrowth phenotype, as confirmed in mouse knockout studies.
choices_json.choice_text: Paternal Igf2 is expressed because on the paternal chromosome the DMR is unmethylated, CTCF insulator cannot bind, and the enhancer activates Igf2. Uniparental maternal disomy (two maternal chromosomes 7) produces offspring with both DMRs methylated — CTCF binds both chromosomes, blocking the enhancer at both loci, resulting in zero Igf2 expression and growth retardation

choices_json.rationale: Igf2 is located on chromosome 7 (an autosome), not the Y chromosome. Genomic imprinting is an autosomal phenomenon where parent-of-origin epigenetic marks determine which allele is expressed, entirely independent of sex chromosomes.
choices_json.choice_text: Igf2 is a Y-linked gene expressed only when a paternal Y chromosome is inherited; uniparental maternal disomy produces XX females who cannot express Igf2

choices_json.rationale: This inverts the imprinting logic. The MATERNAL allele is the SILENCED copy (methylated DMR → CTCF bound → enhancer blocked). Two maternal chromosomes means two silenced Igf2 alleles, not two active ones. It is the PATERNAL allele that is active. Two maternal chromosomes = zero active Igf2 = undergrowth, not overgrowth.
choices_json.choice_text: Uniparental maternal disomy doubles Igf2 expression because two maternal alleles are present, and maternal alleles are the active copies; this would cause overgrowth

stem: What does the chi-square analysis reveal about whether these two genes assort independently?
stimulus:
A student crosses two true-breeding pea strains (AABB × aabb) and self-fertilizes the F1 (AaBb). The expected 9:3:3:1 ratio for 400 F2 offspring predicts: 225 A_B_, 75 A_bb, 75 aaB_, 25 aabb.

Observed: 220 A_B_, 68 A_bb, 72 aaB_, 40 aabb.

Chi-square calculation:
χ² = (220-225)²/225 + (68-75)²/75 + (72-75)²/75 + (40-25)²/25
= 0.11 + 0.65 + 0.12 + 9.00
= 9.88

Critical value at p=0.05, df=3: χ²_crit = 7.815
title: APBIO-MCQ-071

choices_json.rationale: Statistical decisions require comparing the total chi-square value to the critical value — not evaluating individual class deviations separately. The total χ² = 9.88 exceeds the critical value of 7.815, meaning the overall deviation from the expected 9:3:3:1 ratio is statistically significant. The aabb class (O=40, E=25) contributes a very large deviation (9.00) that drives the rejection.
choices_json.choice_text: The null hypothesis (independent assortment) is supported because most phenotypic classes are close to their expected values

choices_json.rationale: Chi-square logic: if χ² calculated > χ² critical, reject the null hypothesis. Here 9.88 > 7.815, so we reject the null that these genes assort independently. The largest contributor is the aabb class (observed 40, expected 25) — an excess of double-recessive individuals consistent with linkage in repulsion (Ab and aB in coupling), where parental combinations are more common than expected under independent assortment. Additional experiments (test cross, recombination frequency) would be needed to confirm linkage.
choices_json.choice_text: The null hypothesis (independent assortment) is rejected: χ² = 9.88 exceeds the critical value of 7.815 at p=0.05 with 3 degrees of freedom, indicating the deviation from 9:3:3:1 is unlikely to be due to chance alone — suggesting the genes may be linked

choices_json.rationale: This inverts the decision rule. A chi-square value GREATER than the critical value leads to rejection of the null hypothesis. A value less than the critical value would support the null hypothesis (independent assortment). Additionally, statistical rejection does not "prove" linkage — it indicates the data are inconsistent with independent assortment and warrants further investigation.
choices_json.choice_text: The null hypothesis is rejected because the chi-square value is less than the critical value, proving the genes must be on the same chromosome

choices_json.rationale: Chi-square analysis has no minimum sample size requirement of 1000. The commonly cited guideline is that expected values in each class should be ≥5 (to ensure the chi-square approximation is valid). All four expected values here (225, 75, 75, 25) exceed 5, so the test is appropriate for this sample of 400.
choices_json.choice_text: No conclusion can be drawn because chi-square analysis requires at least 1000 offspring to be valid

stem: A female calico cat is heterozygous for coat color (X^O X^o, where O = orange and o = black). Which correctly explains her patchy orange-and-black pattern and predicts the coat pattern of her male calico offspring?
stimulus: In mammals, one of the two X chromosomes in each somatic cell of females is randomly and permanently inactivated early in embryonic development (Lyon hypothesis). The inactivated X condenses into a Barr body. X-inactivation is random in each cell but mitotically heritable: all daughter cells derived from a cell in which the maternal X was inactivated will also have the maternal X inactivated. X-inactivation is incomplete — pseudoautosomal regions and some other genes on the inactive X escape inactivation.
title: APBIO-MCQ-072

choices_json.rationale: The coat color gene in cats is X-linked. The orange/black patches directly result from random X-inactivation in heterozygous females — cells expressing X^O produce orange pigment, cells expressing X^o produce black. Males are XY and cannot be heterozygous for this X-linked locus in the usual sense, making male calicos essentially impossible without sex chromosome abnormalities.
choices_json.choice_text: The patches result from differential gene expression controlled by the coat pattern gene independently of the X chromosomes; male calico offspring are equally likely as females

choices_json.rationale: The clonal expansion of cells after random X-inactivation creates visible patches because each patch is derived from one embryonic cell. A cell that inactivates X^o expresses only X^O → orange patch; a cell that inactivates X^O expresses only X^o → black patch. Males have only one X chromosome (X^O or X^o from the mother) — they are hemizygous and express only one color. True male calicos require chromosomal abnormalities (e.g., XXY — Klinefelter syndrome in cats) and are extremely rare (~1 in 3,000 calico males).
choices_json.choice_text: Patches arise because X-inactivation early in development is random per cell; each cell independently silences one X permanently, and all mitotic descendants maintain the same inactive X — creating clonal patches where X^O is active (orange) or X^o is active (black). Male calico offspring are essentially impossible because males are XY (hemizygous for one coat color allele) and cannot form orange-and-black patches

choices_json.rationale: Somatic mutations do not cause calico patterns. The patches are inherited clonally from X-inactivation decisions, not from new mutations. Every cell in a calico female contains the same two X-linked alleles; only the choice of which to inactivate differs between cells.
choices_json.choice_text: The patchy pattern is caused by somatic mutations in the coat color gene that occur randomly during development; male calico offspring carrying these mutations would also be patchy

choices_json.rationale: X-inactivation in eutherian mammals is random (not imprinted) in somatic cells — either the maternal or paternal X can be inactivated in any given cell with roughly equal probability. (In marsupials, X-inactivation is imprinted and preferentially silences the paternal X — but this is not the case in cats or humans.)
choices_json.choice_text: X-inactivation is not random — the maternal X is always inactivated in females; a female calico's orange patches all express the paternal X while black patches express the maternal X

stem: What do the complementation test results reveal about the number of genes responsible for the white-eye mutant strains?
stimulus:
Four independently isolated white-eye Drosophila mutant strains (1, 2, 3, 4) are crossed in all pairwise combinations. Offspring eye color is recorded (W = wild-type red eyes; white = mutant white eyes):

Cross         | Offspring
Strain 1 × 2  | white
Strain 1 × 3  | red (W)
Strain 1 × 4  | red (W)
Strain 2 × 3  | red (W)
Strain 2 × 4  | red (W)
Strain 3 × 4  | white

Note: all strains are recessive mutations; cross results show F1 phenotype.
title: APBIO-MCQ-073

choices_json.rationale: If all four strains were mutant in the same gene, all pairwise crosses would produce white-eyed offspring (fail to complement). Instead, four crosses produce red-eyed offspring (complementation occurs), indicating the mutations are in different genes in those crosses. Same-gene prediction is falsified by the complementing crosses.
choices_json.choice_text: All four strains carry mutations in the same gene because all produce white eyes

choices_json.rationale: Complementation logic: if two strains fail to complement (cross gives white offspring), they carry mutations in the SAME gene — neither parent can supply a functional copy of that gene. If they complement (cross gives red offspring), they carry mutations in DIFFERENT genes — each parent supplies a functional allele at the other's mutant locus. Cross 1×2 = white (same gene: Group A). Cross 3×4 = white (same gene: Group B). All other crosses (1×3, 1×4, 2×3, 2×4) = red (different genes complement). Conclusion: 2 genes, 2 complementation groups.
choices_json.choice_text: The mutations define two complementation groups (genes): Strains 1 and 2 fail to complement each other (same gene, Group A); Strains 3 and 4 fail to complement each other (same gene, Group B); all cross-group combinations complement (red offspring)

choices_json.rationale: Independent isolation does not mean different genes — multiple independent mutations can occur in the same gene. Complementation tests directly reveal whether mutations affect the same or different genes, regardless of how many strains were isolated. The cross results, not the isolation history, determine complementation group assignment.
choices_json.choice_text: The mutations define four complementation groups because each strain was independently isolated and must carry a unique mutation

choices_json.rationale: Complementation tests can be applied to X-linked genes with appropriate cross designs (e.g., using females heterozygous for both mutations). Moreover, the question does not specify X-linkage for all strains, and complementation tests are a general tool applicable to autosomal and X-linked recessive mutations.
choices_json.choice_text: No conclusion about gene number can be drawn because white eyes in Drosophila are always X-linked and X-linked genes cannot be analyzed by complementation tests

stem: Which correctly explains why changing only the guide RNA sequence (and not the Cas9 protein) is sufficient to redirect CRISPR-Cas9 to a completely different genomic target?
stimulus: CRISPR-Cas9 is a genome editing system derived from bacterial adaptive immunity. It consists of two components: (1) the Cas9 endonuclease protein, which makes double-strand DNA cuts; and (2) a single guide RNA (sgRNA) that contains a ~20-nucleotide spacer sequence complementary to the DNA target, plus a scaffold structure that binds Cas9. The sgRNA directs Cas9 to the target by base-pairing with one strand of the genomic DNA at the protospacer sequence, provided the sequence is adjacent to a PAM (protospacer adjacent motif, 5'-NGG in most systems). Cas9 then cuts both DNA strands.
title: APBIO-MCQ-074

choices_json.rationale: Cas9's DNA recognition is mediated by the guide RNA, not by an intrinsic sequence-specific DNA-binding domain in the protein. Cas9 itself recognizes only the PAM sequence (NGG) through a PAM-interacting domain — it has no sequence-specific recognition beyond the PAM. Target specificity is entirely determined by Watson-Crick base-pairing between the sgRNA spacer and the DNA.
choices_json.choice_text: Cas9 contains a DNA-binding domain that recognizes specific sequences; changing the guide RNA modifies Cas9's DNA-binding domain through allosteric conformational changes

choices_json.rationale: Target specificity is encoded entirely in the sgRNA spacer through Watson-Crick complementarity — this is the key design principle of CRISPR. Cas9 is a programmable nuclease: its protein structure is constant and invariant, but its genomic address is determined by whichever sgRNA is associated with it. Swapping the 20-nt spacer sequence is sufficient to move Cas9 to a completely different genomic locus, provided a PAM is present there. This modularity — constant protein, variable RNA — is what makes CRISPR so powerful for genome engineering.
choices_json.choice_text: The 20-nucleotide spacer in the guide RNA base-pairs with the complementary genomic DNA strand at the target site; Cas9 follows the guide RNA to wherever it hybridizes; changing the spacer sequence redirects Cas9 to any new genomic sequence containing that spacer complement adjacent to a PAM

choices_json.rationale: CRISPR-Cas9 does not involve reverse transcription or DNA integration of the guide RNA. The sgRNA remains as RNA and functions through direct RNA-DNA base-pairing at the target. Reverse transcription is the mechanism of retroviruses and retrotransposons — not CRISPR.
choices_json.choice_text: The guide RNA undergoes reverse transcription to create a DNA copy that integrates near the target site and recruits Cas9 through protein-DNA interactions

choices_json.rationale: The PAM recognition domain of Cas9 is fixed in the protein structure and always recognizes NGG (for SpCas9). It is not changed by the guide RNA sequence. Target selection is determined by the 20-nt spacer matching the protospacer, with the PAM requirement remaining constant regardless of which guide RNA is used.
choices_json.choice_text: Changing the guide RNA sequence modifies the PAM recognition domain of Cas9, allowing it to bind different PAM sequences at the new target

stem: Which set of predictions is most consistent with all the molecular data for this patient's tumor?
stimulus:
A patient's tumor biopsy reveals the following molecular profile:
1. The BRCA2 gene has a frameshift mutation in exon 11 (both alleles).
2. The KRAS gene has a missense mutation (G12V) in one allele; the other allele is wild-type.
3. Hypermethylation of CpG islands at the promoter of the MLH1 mismatch repair gene.
4. No mutations in the coding sequences of the p53 gene, but p53 protein levels are undetectable.
5. The tumor cells show microsatellite instability (MSI) throughout the genome.
title: APBIO-MCQ-075

choices_json.rationale: Epigenetic promoter methylation silences gene transcription and directly reduces protein production — it is a major mechanism of tumor suppressor inactivation in cancer. p53 undetectable protein with normal coding sequence most likely reflects increased degradation (e.g., via MDM2), not constitutive activation. MSI is directly explained by MLH1 silencing. All findings are mechanistically connected.
choices_json.choice_text: Finding 3 (MLH1 methylation) is irrelevant because epigenetic changes do not affect protein production; Finding 4 indicates p53 is constitutively active; Finding 5 is unrelated to any of the other findings

choices_json.rationale: Integrating all findings: (1) BRCA2 biallelic frameshift = loss of HR repair tumor suppressor (two-hit); (2) KRAS G12V = dominant gain-of-function oncogene (locks RAS in GTP-bound state, one mutant allele sufficient); (3) MLH1 CpG methylation = epigenetic silencing of mismatch repair → microsatellite instability (MSI) throughout genome as unfixed replication errors accumulate; (4) p53 undetectable without coding mutation = post-translational mechanism (most likely MDM2 amplification or viral E6 protein tagging p53 for degradation); (5) MSI explained by MLH1 silencing. This tumor has accumulated genetic and epigenetic disruptions across multiple cancer-relevant pathways.
choices_json.choice_text: BRCA2 loss impairs homologous recombination DNA repair; KRAS G12V is a dominant oncogenic mutation constitutively activating RAS signaling; MLH1 methylation silences mismatch repair, explaining MSI; absent p53 protein despite intact coding sequence suggests post-translational degradation (e.g., MDM2 overexpression); together these findings represent multiple hallmarks of cancer through both genetic and epigenetic mechanisms

choices_json.rationale: Mismatch repair (MMR) corrects single base mismatches and small insertion/deletion loops from replication errors — it does not correct established frameshift mutations in the DNA sequence after they have been stably incorporated. A frameshift in both BRCA2 alleles produces truncated, non-functional protein. Furthermore, MMR itself is impaired in this tumor (MLH1 silenced), making this argument doubly incorrect.
choices_json.choice_text: The frameshift in BRCA2 exon 11 does not affect protein function because frameshift mutations are always corrected by mismatch repair before translation occurs

choices_json.rationale: KRAS is a proto-oncogene, not a tumor suppressor. A single activating mutation (like G12V, which locks RAS in the GTP-bound state) is sufficient to drive constitutive proliferative signaling — this is a dominant gain-of-function change. The two-hit hypothesis applies to tumor suppressor genes (like BRCA2 and Rb), not to oncogenes. KRAS mutations are among the most common single-allele oncogenic drivers in human cancers.
choices_json.choice_text: KRAS G12V must be a loss-of-function mutation because it affects only one allele; tumor suppressors require both alleles to be mutated to drive cancer

stem: Which set of conditions must ALL be true for a population to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
stimulus: The Hardy-Weinberg principle states that allele and genotype frequencies in a population remain constant from generation to generation in the absence of disturbing influences. For a diploid population with two alleles (A and a) at frequencies p and q (where p + q = 1), the expected genotype frequencies are: AA = p², Aa = 2pq, aa = q². Deviations from expected Hardy-Weinberg frequencies indicate that one or more evolutionary forces are acting on the population.
title: APBIO-MCQ-076

choices_json.rationale: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium requires five conditions to hold simultaneously: (1) No natural selection — all genotypes must have equal survival and reproductive success (fitness); (2) No mutation — allele frequencies cannot change through mutation; (3) No gene flow — no migration of individuals (and their alleles) into or out of the population; (4) Random mating — individuals must mate without regard to genotype; (5) Large (effectively infinite) population size — to prevent genetic drift (random sampling error). When all five conditions hold, allele frequencies remain constant across generations and genotype frequencies follow the p², 2pq, q² distribution.
choices_json.choice_text: Large population size, no mutation, no migration, random mating, and no natural selection

choices_json.rationale: These are precisely the conditions that VIOLATE Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, not maintain it. Small population → genetic drift; high mutation rate → allele frequency change; assortative mating → non-random mating; directional selection → differential survival. Each of these is an evolutionary force that causes allele frequencies to change and genotype frequencies to deviate from Hardy-Weinberg expectations.
choices_json.choice_text: Small population size, high mutation rate, isolation from other populations, assortative mating, and strong directional selection

choices_json.rationale: Even equal forward and reverse mutation rates would not maintain Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium unless the rates are zero. While bidirectional mutation at equal rates produces a mutation-selection equilibrium, it still alters allele frequencies relative to their current values. Hardy-Weinberg requires NO mutation (or mutation rates so low as to be negligible), not merely balanced mutation.
choices_json.choice_text: Large population size, no selection, random mating, but high mutation rates are acceptable as long as they are equal in both directions

choices_json.rationale: Population size is critical — small populations experience genetic drift (random sampling variation in allele transmission), which changes allele frequencies even without selection. Mutation also changes allele frequencies. Both violate equilibrium. All five H-W conditions are necessary.
choices_json.choice_text: No natural selection and random mating are sufficient; population size and mutation rate are irrelevant to equilibrium

stem: Which correctly describes how antibiotic resistance evolves in a bacterial population exposed to an antibiotic?
stimulus: A hospital introduces a new antibiotic to treat a bacterial infection. Before antibiotic use, the bacterial population consists mostly of antibiotic-sensitive strains with a small fraction carrying a pre-existing random mutation that confers antibiotic resistance. After one week of antibiotic treatment, nearly all surviving bacteria are resistant to the antibiotic. The resistant bacteria did not arise in response to the antibiotic — genetic analysis confirms the resistance mutations pre-existed antibiotic exposure.
title: APBIO-MCQ-077

choices_json.rationale: This Lamarckian view is incorrect. Mutations are random — they are not directed by environmental conditions. The antibiotic does not induce resistance mutations; it selects among variants that already exist. The stimulus confirms that resistance mutations pre-existed antibiotic exposure, which is the key evidence that mutations are random and pre-adaptive, not environment-directed.
choices_json.choice_text: The antibiotic caused mutations in sensitive bacteria, allowing them to become resistant — the environment directed the creation of new resistance mutations

choices_json.rationale: This is directional selection in action: (1) Pre-existing variation — resistance mutations arose randomly before the antibiotic was introduced; (2) Selection pressure — the antibiotic is a selective agent that differentially kills sensitive bacteria; (3) Differential reproduction — resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing resistance alleles to offspring; (4) Heritable — resistance is genetically encoded and inherited; (5) Result — allele frequency shifts: resistance allele goes from rare to common. No new mutations are needed; selection acts on standing genetic variation.
choices_json.choice_text: Pre-existing random mutations conferring resistance were present in the population before antibiotic use; the antibiotic acted as a selective agent, killing sensitive bacteria while allowing resistant bacteria to survive and reproduce — increasing the frequency of the resistance allele through differential reproduction

choices_json.rationale: This confuses physiological acclimation with genetic evolution. Bacteria cannot modify their DNA in response to an environmental stressor and then pass those changes to offspring (that would require Lamarckian inheritance). Resistance is due to inherited allelic differences, not lifetime physiological adaptation.
choices_json.choice_text: Bacteria evolved resistance by collectively adapting their physiology during their lifetimes to tolerate the antibiotic; this acquired resistance was then passed to offspring

choices_json.rationale: Resistance is specific — bacteria resistant to one antibiotic are not necessarily resistant to others. Fitness is context-dependent: the resistance mutation confers a fitness advantage only in the presence of the specific antibiotic. In the absence of the antibiotic, resistance mutations may even be costly (reduced growth rate), meaning "fit" depends entirely on the environment.
choices_json.choice_text: Antibiotic resistance evolved because bacteria that survived by chance were inherently more fit across all environments; resistance is unrelated to the specific antibiotic used

stem: Which prediction about phenotypic variation in birth weight is consistent with stabilizing selection?
stimulus: Studies of human birth weight show that babies born at intermediate weights (approximately 3–4 kg) have the highest survival rates. Babies born too small (premature or underweight) face respiratory distress and infection risk. Babies born too large face delivery complications and birth injuries. These patterns have been stable across many decades of data from multiple countries.
title: APBIO-MCQ-078

choices_json.rationale: This describes directional selection (consistent shift toward one extreme). Stabilizing selection does the opposite — it acts against both extremes and maintains the intermediate phenotype. Large birth weight is specifically selected against due to delivery complications, so the population does not drift toward larger babies.
choices_json.choice_text: Over time, the population will evolve toward exclusively producing very large babies, as larger body mass correlates with greater survival of adults

choices_json.rationale: Stabilizing selection acts when intermediate phenotypes have higher fitness than either extreme. Both tails of the birth weight distribution face elevated mortality (small → respiratory/infection risk; large → delivery trauma). The result over generations: variance narrows around the optimal intermediate value. This is the classic textbook example of stabilizing selection. It does not shift the mean (that would be directional selection); it reduces the spread around the existing mean.
choices_json.choice_text: Stabilizing selection reduces phenotypic variance over time, maintaining intermediate birth weight as the most common phenotype while reducing the frequency of very small and very large birth weights

choices_json.rationale: This describes disruptive selection, which favors both extremes and eliminates the intermediate. Stabilizing selection is the opposite: it favors intermediates and eliminates extremes. For disruptive selection to produce two groups, both extremes would need to have higher fitness than the intermediate — the opposite of what the birth weight data show.
choices_json.choice_text: The population will split into two distinct groups — one adapted to produce small babies and one adapted to produce large babies — with intermediate birth weights disappearing

choices_json.rationale: Birth weight has significant heritability (genetic components exist, even though environment also matters). Stabilizing selection can act on any heritable trait. If birth weight were entirely non-heritable, selection would not produce evolutionary change — but the question's premise (long-term stable pattern) is consistent with heritable variation and ongoing selection.
choices_json.choice_text: No evolutionary change will occur because birth weight is determined entirely by maternal environment and nutrition, not by heritable genetic factors

stem: Which scenario best explains the beak polymorphism observed in this bird population?
stimulus: A population of seed-eating finches on an island feeds on two types of seeds: very small soft seeds and very large hard seeds. Birds with small thin beaks can efficiently crack small seeds but cannot crack large seeds. Birds with large thick beaks can efficiently crack large seeds but are inefficient at handling small seeds. Birds with intermediate beaks are poor at cracking both seed types. Data collected over 20 years show a bimodal distribution of beak size with few birds in the intermediate range.
title: APBIO-MCQ-079

choices_json.rationale: Stabilizing selection would maintain intermediate beak sizes and reduce the frequency of both extremes — the opposite of what is observed. The data show a bimodal distribution (two peaks, few intermediates), which is the signature of disruptive selection or character displacement, not stabilizing selection.
choices_json.choice_text: Stabilizing selection is acting to maintain intermediate beak sizes because intermediate beaks represent a compromise between the two seed types

choices_json.rationale: Disruptive (diversifying) selection acts when both extremes have higher fitness than the intermediate phenotype. Here: small beaks → fit for small seeds; large beaks → fit for large seeds; intermediate beaks → poor at both seed types = lowest fitness. Differential survival/reproduction favors both extremes, generating a bimodal distribution over time. This can be a precursor to sympatric speciation if reproductive isolation evolves between the two morphs.
choices_json.choice_text: Disruptive selection is favoring birds with extreme beak sizes (small thin or large thick) because each extreme specializes efficiently on one seed type, while intermediate beaks are inefficient at both resources — reducing fitness of intermediates relative to both extremes

choices_json.rationale: Directional selection would shift the mean in one direction, producing a unimodal distribution that moves over time. The bimodal distribution (two phenotypic peaks) is not consistent with directional selection, which would eliminate small beaks, not maintain them alongside large beaks.
choices_json.choice_text: Directional selection is shifting the entire population toward large beak size because large seeds provide more calories per seed

choices_json.rationale: There is no information given about mate choice or sexual selection. The explanation provided in the stimulus (beak efficiency on different seed types) is ecological — it invokes natural selection based on foraging efficiency and food availability, not sexual selection based on mate preferences.
choices_json.choice_text: Sexual selection is the primary driver, with females preferring extreme beak sizes because intermediates are visually less attractive

stem: Which best explains why honest signaling theory predicts that costly ornaments are reliable indicators of male quality?
stimulus: In many bird species, males display elaborate ornamental traits (bright plumage, large tail feathers, complex songs) that are used by females during mate choice. Evolutionary paradox: if these traits reduce survival (making males more visible to predators, energetically costly to produce and maintain), why do they persist and why do females prefer them? The handicap hypothesis proposes that costly ornaments can only be maintained by high-quality males who can afford the fitness cost.
title: APBIO-MCQ-080

choices_json.rationale: This is the "runaway selection" or "sexy sons" hypothesis (Fisher's runaway) — not honest signaling. If ornaments are truly costless, they carry no information about male quality. The handicap hypothesis specifically requires that ornaments be costly so that only high-quality males can bear the cost without dying, making the signal reliable.
choices_json.choice_text: Ornaments persist because they are neutral traits with no fitness cost; females simply choose them by arbitrary preference without any information about male quality

choices_json.rationale: The handicap principle (Zahavian handicap): the cost is the mechanism of reliability. A signal is honest precisely because cheating (low-quality males faking the signal) is penalized by death or reproductive failure. High-quality males have excess resources/health to afford the cost; low-quality males cannot. Females who choose ornamented males therefore consistently obtain mates with superior genes (good genes hypothesis) or resources. The cost makes the signal stable evolutionarily — it cannot be faked without fitness consequences.
choices_json.choice_text: The cost of the ornament ensures signal honesty: only males with high genetic quality, parasite resistance, or resource acquisition ability can survive while bearing the ornament cost; low-quality males who attempt to display the ornament die before reproducing, making the ornament a reliable indicator of underlying fitness

choices_json.rationale: This mischaracterizes ornaments as functional traits rather than signals. Peacock tail feathers, for example, impair locomotion and increase predation risk — they are not functional tools. The paradox to be explained is precisely why apparently maladaptive traits are favored, which the handicap hypothesis resolves through signal reliability.
choices_json.choice_text: Females choose ornamental males because large ornaments directly help with nest building, foraging, or chick rearing — the ornament is a functional tool, not a signal

choices_json.rationale: Sexual selection and natural selection can work in opposite directions (runaway selection or handicap dynamics), but their interaction does not simply produce a fixed intermediate value. In honest signaling, ornament expression varies with male quality — high-quality males express larger ornaments, not a single population-wide fixed value. There is continuous variation linked to quality.
choices_json.choice_text: Sexual selection and natural selection always work in opposite directions and eventually reach a stable compromise where ornament size is fixed at a single intermediate value across all males in the population

stem: Which best describes why the bottleneck effect reduces genetic diversity in a population?
stimulus: In 1890, the northern elephant seal (Mirounga angustirostris) was hunted nearly to extinction — as few as 20–100 individuals survived. Legal protection allowed the population to recover; today over 170,000 seals exist. However, genetic studies show that modern northern elephant seals have extremely low genetic diversity (nearly zero heterozygosity at most loci), in stark contrast to their southern relatives, which were not similarly reduced. The eastern Pacific gray whale underwent a similar bottleneck and shows comparably reduced diversity.
title: APBIO-MCQ-081

choices_json.rationale: Recessive alleles are not inherently less fit — fitness depends on context. Recessive alleles are not specifically targeted during a bottleneck; the bottleneck randomly samples whichever alleles the few survivors happened to carry. Additionally, natural selection did not cause the bottleneck (hunting did); the reduction was not fitness-based.
choices_json.choice_text: The bottleneck eliminated all recessive alleles from the population because recessive alleles are always less fit than dominant alleles

choices_json.rationale: The bottleneck effect is a form of genetic drift — random sampling error. When a population crashes to a small number of survivors, many alleles present in the original large population (especially rare ones) are simply not present in any of the few survivors by chance. The surviving population has a much narrower allele pool. Even after population recovery (like the elephant seal), the genetic diversity remains low because all individuals descend from the same few founders. This is illustrated by the near-zero heterozygosity of modern northern elephant seals despite their large population size.
choices_json.choice_text: When population size is drastically reduced, the few surviving individuals carry only a random sample of the original alleles; rare alleles are likely lost by chance; the reduced gene pool becomes the basis for all future generations — a random, non-selective loss of genetic variation

choices_json.rationale: Bottlenecks primarily act through drift (random sampling), not selection. In a bottleneck, the few survivors may carry some deleterious alleles — these are not eliminated; rather, if the deleterious allele happens to be in a survivor, it can increase in frequency by drift. Bottlenecks often increase homozygosity for deleterious recessives (inbreeding depression), the opposite of purging all deleterious alleles.
choices_json.choice_text: The bottleneck increased natural selection intensity, rapidly eliminating all deleterious alleles from the population and fixing only beneficial alleles

choices_json.rationale: Bottlenecks do not increase mutation rates. Mutation is a distinct process from genetic drift. The low diversity seen in elephant seals is due to random loss of alleles during the population crash (drift), not to stress-induced mutations destroying existing alleles.
choices_json.choice_text: The bottleneck increased mutation rates as a stress response, which paradoxically destroyed existing allele diversity while generating new alleles

stem: Which prediction about allele frequencies in the island population is most consistent with the founder effect?
stimulus:
A remote oceanic island is colonized by 12 individuals that rafted from a mainland population of 50,000. In the mainland population, a particular blood group allele (allele M) has a frequency of 3%. The 12 founders happen to include 3 individuals who carry allele M (2 are heterozygous, 1 is homozygous).

The founders successfully establish a breeding population on the island that grows to 5,000 individuals over 20 generations.
title: APBIO-MCQ-082

choices_json.rationale: Natural selection does not "restore" mainland frequencies — there is no mechanism for the island population to know what the mainland frequency is. The island population evolves independently from its founding composition. If allele M is selectively neutral, drift (not selection toward 3%) will determine its fate.
choices_json.choice_text: Allele M will have a frequency of 3% in the island population because natural selection will restore mainland allele frequencies within a few generations

choices_json.rationale: Founder effect calculation: 12 founders = 24 gene copies. Allele M copies: 2 (from heterozygote 1) + 2 (from heterozygote 2) + 2 (from homozygote) = let's count carefully. 2 heterozygous individuals contribute 1 M allele each = 2 M alleles. 1 homozygous individual contributes 2 M alleles = 2 M alleles. Total M alleles = 4. Frequency = 4/24 ≈ 16.7%. This substantially exceeds the mainland frequency of 3%, illustrating the founder effect: by chance, the small founding group overrepresents allele M compared to the source population. The island population also has lower overall diversity (only 12 individuals' worth of alleles founding the gene pool, vs. 50,000 on the mainland).
choices_json.choice_text: The island population will have a higher frequency of allele M than the mainland (approximately 20.8%), and genetic diversity will be lower overall, reflecting the non-representative allele sample carried by the 12 founders

choices_json.rationale: Mutation rates are extremely low (roughly 10⁻⁸ per nucleotide per generation) — 20 generations is far too short for mutation alone to generate substantial new genetic diversity.
